detail.abstract: This paper argues that the next phase of artificial intelligence (AI) will not be about replacing humans completely. Instead, it will focus on "de-automation" and "re-humanization"-bringing humans back into the loop where they are needed most. As AI becomes more common, relying too heavily on AI-generated data creates serious technical risks, such as "model collapse." At the same time, using only machines for complex jobs is becoming too expensive and inflexible for businesses. By looking at computer science, economics, and consumer psychology, this research shows that AI actually needs human input and creativity to survive. This paper suggests a "bionic" way of working: AI should handle large, repetitive tasks, while humans should handle decision-making, unexpected problems, and ethical choices. Ultimately, keeping humans involved is a smart business move, not a step backward.

detail.abstract: This study tests whether the AIAS Presence Index ($C_P$) predicts Amazon Best Sellers Rank (BSR) across consumer-goods substrates. Four hypotheses were pre-registered under Protocol v1.6, testing per-substrate Spearman correlations, pooled cross-substrate correlation, Cell A separation, and absent-brand alignment. Three substrates (kitchen knives, audiophile headphones, skincare; N = 64 listed brands) provided within-substrate variance in $C_P$; one substrate (cosmetics; N = 24) exhibited a ceiling effect (all $C_P$ = 6). A fifth substrate (premium kitchenware) was excluded post-registration due to incomplete Phase A data. Results were uniformly null: within-substrate Spearman correlations ranged from -0.116 to +0.049 (all p > 0.65); the pooled correlation across 88 brands was -0.0002 (p = 0.998). All testable hypotheses were falsified. The null result constitutes discriminant validity evidence for the AIAS construct. Combined with convergent validity evidence from v0.25 (Google Trends; $\rho$ = 0.74), the findings support a Campbell-Fiske interpretation: AI Presence captures brand salience within large language model knowledge systems, a dimension that is independent of retail market performance. This distinction is foundational to the Tri-System claim that AI Availability constitutes a third measurable system alongside Mental and Physical Availability.

detail.abstract: In this chapter, we examine what generative AI is doing to medicine. Drawing on a body of recent evidence, we argue that technical progress is necessary but not sufficient: even as models improve, the institutional scaffolding that absorbs them will decide whether that progress translates into trustworthy care. Visible AI use can lower peer and patient ratings of physicians. Liability and reimbursement pressures distort when and how AI is used. Sustained reliance can corrode the skills clinicians still need. Today's generative AI systems produce what is plausible, not what is feasible under hard constraints, and the agent frameworks built around them do not close that gap. The enthusiasm for AI as a substitute for clinical judgment is, at best, premature and, at worst, a category mistake. Better models will help, but only alongside the procurement, workflow design, local validation, and auditable governance that turn a technical artifact into a clinical instrument. In medicine, trust has always been institutional. The question is not whether to use AI, but whether the surrounding clinical system has made that use worthy of trust.

title: 2025 Labour Market Review: Trade Uncertainty, Structural Pressures, and Policy Priorities for Canada
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute and C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: 2025 Labour Market Review: Trade Uncertainty, Structural Pressures, and Policy Priorities for Canada
detail.abstract:
• In 2025, Canada’s labour market cooled as employment growth slowed, unemployment rose, and job vacancies declined from the unusually tight conditions seen after the pandemic. Trade tensions with the United States, slower immigration-driven labour force growth, and technological change contributed to increasingly uneven labour market outcomes across regions, sectors, and demographic groups.
  • Despite growing trade uncertainty, the Canadian economy remained relatively resilient, supported by continued CUSMA protections and government support measures, with most sectors recording employment gains. However, some trade-exposed resource industries and business support services experienced notable employment losses, while businesses became more cautious about hiring and investment.
  • Ongoing challenges persist, including rising youth unemployment, long-term unemployment, immigrant overqualification, labour shortages in certain sectors, regional labour market imbalances, and weak productivity growth. Many recent immigrants and non-permanent residents continued to face weaker labour market outcomes than Canadian-born workers.
  • This labour market review emphasizes the need for policies that strengthen labour mobility, improve school-to-work transitions and immigrant labour market integration, support workforce adaptation to technological change, and encourage productivity-enhancing investment and innovation.

detail.abstract: Whether quantities derived from large language model (LLM) outputs are stable enough over time to function as brand-measurement instruments is an open empirical question. This study reports a pre-registered, two-wave longitudinal re-acquisition of the AIAS™ measurement protocol across five product-category panels (audiophile headphones, skincare, cosmetics, automotive, premium spirits; 112 brand units), re-running each panel's original acquisition pipeline verbatim 15–21 days after first measurement against a fixed six-model panel spanning three providers. Four hypotheses were pre-registered and externally anchored before re-acquisition. H_CPC_Temporal_Stability was CONFIRMED: per-brand rank order of the CV-based consistency quantity (CV-CPC) was stable in four of five categories (Spearman ρ = 0.76–0.96; the exception, the smallest panel, ρ = 0.42, n.s.). H_CPC_Drift_Beyond_Presence was MARGINAL by structural collapse: recognition saturation in four of five categories rendered Presence-residualization a no-op, leaving one informative category — in which residualized stability (ρ = 0.61) exceeded raw stability (ρ = 0.42). H_Presence_Temporal_Stability was MARGINAL by ceiling: rank stability was high wherever rank variance existed (ρ = 0.81–1.00), but two categories were recognition-constant in both waves. Phantom status (below-recall-floor) persisted in 56 of 57 brands. The findings characterize CV-CPC's temporal behavior without validating it as a Consistency instrument, document pervasive recognition-ceiling effects in consumer categories, and motivate the mean-independent instrument requirement of the forthcoming v1.8 methodology revision.

title: Causal Inference for Real-Time Decision Systems: Bandits, Interleaved Experiments, and the Bias-Speed Tradeoff

detail.title: Causal Inference for Real-Time Decision Systems: Bandits, Interleaved Experiments, and the Bias-Speed Tradeoff
detail.abstract: Decision systems in marketing and finance have moved from batch to streaming: attribution platforms recompute channel value in near real time, budget pacing reallocates spend within hours, and recommendation and pricing engines learn continuously from their own decisions. The descriptive literature has documented the operational gains of this real-time turn, but its inferential foundations are routinely violated in practice. Continuous monitoring with fixed-sample tests inflates false-positive rates several-fold; adaptive allocation algorithms bias the very estimates they generate, systematically understating the value of arms they learn to avoid; and high-frequency reallocation interferes with the stationarity and independence assumptions on which classical experiment analysis rests. This article treats the inferential problem rigorously. It develops the peeking pathology and its principled remedies, groupsequential designs, mixture sequential probability ratio tests, and always-valid inference via confidence sequences; the bandit family, Thompson sampling and upper-confidence-bound allocation, together with the negative bias of adaptively collected data and the adaptive-weighting corrections that restore valid confidence intervals; and the high-throughput designs, interleaving and switchback experiments, that trade estimand generality for sensitivity and speed. Simulation illustrations quantify the pathologies: in the article's A/A simulations, two hundred interim looks raise a nominal five percent error rate above forty percent, and a standard Thompson sampling deployment understates the inferior arm's conversion rate by more than a full percentage point on a ten percent base. The article's organizing contribution is the biasspeed frontier: a framework that locates each design by its rate of in-flight value capture and the validity of the estimates it leaves behind, distinguishes the attainable frontier from the invalid interior, and supplies a decision typology mapping reversibility, effect persistence, and downstream reuse of estimates to the appropriate design. Applications are developed for real-time attribution and continuously calibrated marketing mix models, extending the author's prior work on attribution systems from descriptive to inferential treatment.

title: The Desistance Presumption: The Emotional Stability Index (ESI) as a Clinical Tool for Federal Supervised Release Reform
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Desistance Presumption: The Emotional Stability Index (ESI) as a Clinical Tool for Federal Supervised Release Reform
detail.abstract: This paper is written for the United States Sentencing Commission. It proposes a clinical framework designed to implement the individualized assessment mandate the Commission established under Amendment 835. Specifically, the framework provides the standardized, objective tool that the Commission's November 2025 policy statement (Section 5D1.4) implicitly requires to execute the 12-month presumption of early termination for low-risk individuals. While the Sentencing Commission's new policy directs probation officers to proactively petition for early termination at the one-year mark, the system currently lacks any structured clinical instrument for making this individualized determination. This paper proposes the Emotional Stability Evaluation (ESE) and its composite Emotional Stability Index (ESI): a six-cluster, clinician-administered instrument grounded in validated psychometric measures, with differential weights derived from published meta-analytic effect sizes. A parallel Mini-ESE, administrable by judges and probation officers without clinical training, extends clinical utility to every actor in the supervision process while preserving judicial discretion. The paper proposes four reforms within the existing authority of the Commission under 28 U.S.C. Section 994(a)(3). First, the ESE should be administered during BOP custody, RRC placement, or home confinement, before supervised release begins, providing courts with clinical evidence at sentencing. Where the ESI demonstrates High Stability, the court should exercise its discretionary authority under Section 3583(b) to decline to impose supervised release or to impose a minimal term. Once supervision has begun, courts should apply the ESI to satisfy the 12-month early termination presumption. The paper also identifies the economic cost of prolonged unnecessary supervision, including lost tax revenue, reduced job creation, and suppressed commercial productivity. The author is an emergency physician who is presently in BOP custody serving the remainder of his sentence on home confinement. He entered a plea of guilty, accepts full responsibility for his past conduct, and does not seek to relitigate his case or challenge the validity of his conviction. The paper is submitted in the belief that the Commission's work in this area represents some of the most consequential justice reform in the federal system, and in the hope that this tool may help operationalize those reforms.

title: Self-Rescue Without Re-Employment: AI Displacement and the Shift from Job Creation to Individual Output Creation

detail.title: Self-Rescue Without Re-Employment: AI Displacement and the Shift from Job Creation to Individual Output Creation

detail.abstract:
The "AI layoff trap" literature shows that automation under competition is a dominant-strategy prisoner's dilemma whose demand externality cannot be closed by passive reabsorption, with a Pigouvian automation tax as the unique remedy. That result, however, holds in a static model with no new-task creation, treating displaced workers as passive demand holes — and the 2025–26 episode suggests a channel the model assumes away: some displaced workers may use the same AI systems that displaced them to build new forms of self-employment and micro-enterprise.

This paper opens that assumed-away door. It argues that reflexive niche-creation does not restore employment, for two reasons that operate at once: the same advancing frontier that lets a displaced worker build a niche also erodes it, and even genuinely new AI-native sectors may be born labor-thin — a pattern visible in government data long before AI sharpened it. Two optimistic escapes — that new sectors will hire as they always have, and that falling costs make a thin labor market tolerable — run into the same bottleneck: the human-time-intensive work that AI can neither automate nor cheapen. The result is not simple collapse but restructuring without reabsorption: a new configuration in which displaced workers can sometimes self-rescue while the employment-based distribution mechanism remains broken. The central shift is from employer-mediated reabsorption to AI-enabled individual output creation.

The argument is consistent with the layoff-trap result, reached by an independent route, and it relocates the policy problem from the over-automation incentive (which a Pigouvian tax can correct) to the reabsorption gap (which it cannot). The reasoning is conceptual and the evidence early; the claim is that worker agency is real but is not reabsorption — and that the difference is what to watch.

title: The Value of Modeling Enrollment Dynamics in School District Design
affiliations: , Loyola University Chicago and Northwestern University - Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences

detail.title: The Value of Modeling Enrollment Dynamics in School District Design
detail.abstract: Public school district design decisions, such as opening and closing schools and determining attendance boundaries, are long-term commitments that are difficult to reverse. Yet, student enrollment levels shift from year to year, and enrollment shifts are inherently uncertain. Large enrollment shifts can cause overcrowding or underutilization. Over the years, advances in optimization modeling have significantly improved decision-making in school district design, yet current practice typically relies on static enrollment estimates or, infrequently, deterministic multi-year projections. A natural question arises: what are the costs and benefits of further advancing school district design optimization by explicitly modeling uncertainty? Informed by school district practices, we develop a framework to explore this question. We formulate a series of optimization models whose treatment of enrollment dynamics progressively increases in sophistication from static point estimates to deterministic projections to probabilistic scenarios. We compare these approaches via a comprehensive computational study with district geographies and enrollment trajectories derived from historical data across a range of district sizes, locales, and enrollment trends. Given the nature of enrollment dynamics and the timeframe of design decisions, incorporating multi-year deterministic projections tends to consistently produce large benefits, with relatively limited additional gains from including probabilistic scenarios concentrated primarily in districts experiencing enrollment growth. Growing districts with sufficient resources can use stochastic optimization to alleviate the negative educational and financial impacts of overcrowding by incorporating uncertainty through a modest set of scenarios. For districts facing enrollment declines, deriving marginal value from stochastic optimization requires sophisticated probabilistic scenario generation beyond observed practical capabilities. If budgetary limitations prevent investing in the level of technical expertise required for stochastic modeling, as is likely for districts with declining enrollment, incorporating standard deterministic projections (which districts periodically generate for general planning purposes) can provide substantial improvements over a typical static approach.

title: Causal Attribution Under Data Missingness: A Unified Framework for Business and Policy Decision Systems

detail.title: Causal Attribution Under Data Missingness: A Unified Framework for Business and Policy Decision Systems
detail.abstract: High-stakes decision systems in business and public policy share a common inferential foundation: they attribute observed outcomes to candidate causes and allocate resources on the strength of that attribution. They also share a common pathology. In marketing and financial attribution, customer journeys are observed only in fragments, with offline interactions, cross-device behavior, and privacy-restricted signals systematically absent. In subnational policy measurement, the administrative indicators most relevant to accountability are precisely those that reporting units fail to compile. In both settings, missingness is not random noise around an otherwise complete record; it is structured, informative, and frequently correlated with the very outcomes under study. This article develops a unified framework, Causal Attribution under Missingness (CAM), that treats the missingness mechanism as a first-class component of the causal model rather than a preprocessing nuisance. The framework proceeds through five stages: explicit graphical encoding of both the causal structure and the missingness mechanism; recoverability analysis to determine whether the attribution query is identifiable from the data actually observed; estimation using methods matched to the diagnosed mechanism, including inverse probability weighting, multiple imputation, doubly robust estimators, and rank-based normalization; sensitivity analysis for departures from ignorability; and a decision-layer reporting protocol that publishes data-readiness diagnostics alongside causal estimates. The framework is illustrated through two contrasting applications drawn from prior work: multi-touch attribution in marketing and finance, and the construction of a composite index ranking fifty-three Indian cities on service quality under pervasive municipal data gaps. The comparison demonstrates that the same diagnostic logic governs both domains and yields transferable design principles for any organization whose decisions rest on causal claims computed from incomplete records.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether civil liberties reduce sovereign default risk in Africa using a panel of 49 African countries over 1995-2025 (1,519 country-year observations). Pooled logit, probit, conditional fixed-effects logit, and IV-Probit models with year fixed effects and a full set of macroeconomic controls all yield a negative, precisely estimated coefficient on the inverted Freedom House civilliberties score: a one-unit increase reduces the log-odds of external default by 0.625 (p < 0.01), equivalent to an average marginal effect of approximately 3.3 percentage points at the sample mean default rate of 5.3 percent. The finding is robust to political rights as an alternative institutional measure, alternative lag structures, random-effects estimation, and multiple subsample restrictions including Sub-Saharan Africa only, pre-and post-2010 splits, and high-debt country-years. The consistency of the civil-liberties coefficient across logit, probit, and random-effects probit specifications provides informal reassurance against rare-events bias. An IV-Probit strategy yields consistent estimates, and a Durbin-Wu-Hausman test fails to reject exogeneity (p = 0.219); we treat this as corroborating rather than fully identifying evidence, given the strong exclusion-restriction assumptions of lagbased instruments. Heterogeneity analysis reveals no significant moderation by debt levels, growth conditions, or IMF program participation, suggesting the protective effect operates primarily through direct institutional channels: government accountability, fiscal transparency, and policy credibility. These results strengthen the case for incorporating institutional quality into sovereign credit-risk assessments and carry direct implications for conditionality design in multilateral lending to Africa.

title: Traceability and Food Waste in Fresh Produce Supply Chains
affiliations: McGill University (Desautels),  and McGill University

detail.title: Traceability and Food Waste in Fresh Produce Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Grocery supply chains account for approximately 42% of global food waste. Policymakers and retailers increasingly view traceability technologies, process improvement, and waste penalties as tools for improving freshness and reducing waste. Yet traceability does not only improve information; it also changes supplier incentives. We study a fresh produce supply chain in which a retailer invests in costly and incomplete batch-level traceability, while a supplier chooses its wholesale price and invests in process conformance, which determines the likelihood that products arrive with high freshness. Consumer demand increases with freshness, and waste arises across the supplier, retailer, and consumer stages. We show that traceability has a non-monotonic effect on upstream process conformance. When conformance is costly, equilibrium freshness is low, and greater traceability induces the supplier to improve conformance. In this region, traceability and process conformance are strategic complements, so traceability improves freshness and can reduce waste. When conformance is less costly, however, equilibrium freshness is already high, and greater traceability can induce the supplier to reduce conformance in order to preserve information rents. In this region, traceability and process conformance are strategic substitutes, and traceability may backfire by lowering freshness and increasing total supply chain food waste. We then study two policy levers: a penalty on retail food waste and a subsidy for traceability investment. We identify conditions under which these policies simultaneously reduce food waste, increase food availability, and improve supply chain profits-a win-win-win for consumers, firms, and the environment. We also derive a threshold on traceability costs below which subsidizing traceability is more effective than increasing waste penalties. Overall, our results show that traceability is not a universal remedy for food waste; its value depends critically on supplier incentives, traceability costs, and consumers' sensitivity to freshness.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility and Assortative Matching in the Market for Interfirm Relationships *
affiliations: , University of Pittsburgh - Finance Group, Wayne State University - Mike Ilitch School of Business and

detail.title: Corporate Social Responsibility and Assortative Matching in the Market for Interfirm Relationships *
detail.abstract: We investigate the presence and consequences of assortative matching on corporate social responsibility (CSR) among firms in markets for interfirm relationships. Using observed customer, supplier, and collaborative relationships, we construct annual market-specific networks to identify feasible alternative pairings. We find that firms disproportionately pair with relationship partners that share greater similarity in their CSR policies. These tendencies are strongest in the tails of the CSR distribution, i.e., there are both high-CSR and low-CSR "tribes." Evidence from relationship outcomes, i.e., duration, stock returns around negative unanticipated firm, industry, and macroeconomic shocks, etc., indicates that low-CSR firms appear to generally benefit by forming relationships with other low-CSR firms whereas high-CSR firms are in some instances apparently worse off by forming relationships with other high-CSR firms. Taken together, our results reveal that CSR is a characteristic on which firms sort into distinct tribes with internally reinforcing complementarities and, thus, that CSR is not a simple scalar measure of a firm's quality as a potential relationship partner or merely a reflection of managers' nonpecuniary preferences.

title: Environmental Policy Design under Unionized Wage-Setting: Regulatory Timing and Green Preferences
affiliations: Swansea University and University of Macedonia

detail.title: Environmental Policy Design under Unionized Wage-Setting: Regulatory Timing and Green Preferences
detail.abstract: This paper examines how labor-market institutions shape environmental policy design when regulators choose the timing of command-and-control regulation. We develop a theoretical model of a unionized oligopoly in which a welfare-maximizing regulator imposes emission standards either before wage-setting or after wages have been set. The key mechanism is that environmental policy and wage bargaining interact strategically when unions attach value to environmental quality. Under ex-ante regulation, environmental standards influence subsequent wage-setting, whereas under ex-post regulation wage-setting influences the regulator’s policy choice. As a result, regulatory timing determines not only environmental stringency, but also wages, output, and welfare. We show, first, that union environmental awareness affects regulatory incentives through two opposing channels: greener unions moderate wage demands, reducing firms’ marginal costs and increasing output, but they also partially internalize pollution damages, thereby reducing the need for regulatory intervention. This interaction generates a non-monotonic relationship between union greenness and regulatory stringency. Second, ex-ante regulation is associated with higher wages and lower output, while the opposite holds under ex-post regulation. Third, the welfare effects of regulatory timing are conditional rather than uniform. For sufficiently small markets, ex-ante regulation can be locally welfare-superior when union environmental awareness is weak, whereas ex-post regulation becomes locally welfare-superior near full union internalization. These results imply that green unions partly substitute for formal regulation, so the value of regulatory commitment depends on how much environmental harm unions internalize. The mechanisms remain robust when unilateral union wage-setting is replaced by generalized Nash bargaining in a centralized right-to-manage environment.

title: Protected Areas and the Environmental Kuznets Curve in European Countries

detail.abstract: Protected areas are a natural instrument for preserving biodiversity and a major defence against climate change. This paper uses an Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) perspective to examine the relationship between the percentage of national territory under protection (PA%) and per capita GDP (GDPpc) in European countries. Building on the results of a previous study (Bimonte, 2002) that found a U-shaped relationship between GDPpc and PA%, it explores fate of this relationship two decades later, after two economic crises and a pandemic. It also investigates the effect of the European Union (EU) enlargement. In a dynamic perspective, it analyses the effect, if any, on national conservation policy. Due to the characteristics of the indicator chosen, which is stock-sensitive and subject to saturation effect, it verifies whether the relationship between income level and PA% is still an EKC, or whether a convergence in conservation policy has emerged and PA% is tending to a steady state. This is done by running regression models on the countries to test said EKC and β-convergence hypotheses. The results confute the persistence of an EKC and show a convergence in conservation policy in the last two decades, albeit with interesting differences between groups of countries, in particular latecomers as opposed to old member states of the EU. The results have important policy implications: when dealing with public or collective goods, or goods that produce externalities, centralised (federal) guidance is more effective than local and decentralised approaches (subsidiarity principle).

title: Episode Margin Ledger for Value-Based Care: An Economic Architecture for Prospective Payment Integrity and Risk Reconciliation

detail.title: Episode Margin Ledger for Value-Based Care: An Economic Architecture for Prospective Payment Integrity and Risk Reconciliation
detail.abstract: Payment integrity in U.S. healthcare is often treated as a claims-control function: identify coding errors, deny incorrect claims, recover overpayments, and monitor utilization after payment has already occurred. That approach remains necessary, but it is incomplete for value-based care and bundled payments. When providers, payers, and patients are accountable for outcomes across an episode of care, payment integrity must also ask whether dollars were allocated to clinically necessary care, avoidable waste, preventable failure, or administrative friction. This paper proposes the Episode Margin Ledger, an economic architecture for prospective payment integrity in value-based care. The model treats each episode as a financial object with three linked accounts: a risk-adjusted expected resource account, an avoidable variance account, and a quality-protected reconciliation account. The paper introduces the Prospective Integrity Margin, a formula that separates legitimate clinical intensity from waste-sensitive spending and preventable administrative loss. It also proposes a Reserve-to-Reconciliation Loop that allows organizations to set episode reserves at the start of care, classify spending variation while the episode is open, and settle financial performance only after quality and access safeguards are reviewed. The contribution is conceptual and technical: it offers equations, tables, a black-and-white operating diagram, governance gates, and an evaluation plan for organizations that want economic discipline in value-based care without turning payment integrity into blunt cost control.

title: The Procurement Purpose Gap: From Gatekeeper to Service Function to Invisible Infrastructure

detail.title: The Procurement Purpose Gap: From Gatekeeper to Service Function to Invisible Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests, employment-related sponsorship, or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual and theory-building work and does not involve human participants, patient data, identifiable personal information, experiments, surveys, interviews, or clinical research. declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was independently conceived, researched, and written by the author.

detail.abstract: Procurement literature traditionally describes the function's objectives as cost reduction, risk mitigation, compliance, and supplier management. These descriptions enumerate activities and constraints but do not state what procurement is for. This paper argues that the absence of an articulated terminal purpose-the procurement purpose gap-is a central cause of a familiar organizational pathology: procurement functions that optimize procedural compliance, are experienced by stakeholders as obstacles, and cannot explain their contribution in terms other than the controls they administer. Drawing on systems thinking, governance theory, and the sociology of goal displacement, the paper proposes that procurement's organizational purpose can be reduced, for analytic purposes, to two terminal outcomes: availability-sustained access to compliant, reputationally viable supply at acceptable total cost-and innovationaccess to capabilities the organization has not yet specified. Conventional governance outcomes-fair competition, financial stewardship, supplier resiliency, legal protection, ethical conduct, information security-are classified as availability factors rather than independent ends; the framework is positive rather than normative, and takes no position on the status of ethical obligations, which enter the model as determinants of supply availability. Building on this foundation, the paper introduces a three-stage maturity model describing procurement's evolution from Gatekeeper, to Service Function, to Invisible Infrastructure. The central claim is diagnostic and testable: procurement dysfunction occurs when governance mechanisms are mistaken for terminal outcomes, and procurement maturity is measured not by the visibility of controls but by the degree to which governance and stakeholder enablement coexist without friction.

detail.title: Democracy and Financial Intermediation: The Political Economy of Cryptocurrencies
detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency allows citizens to exit the formal financial system without leaving the state or the market. The exit choice runs along two dimensions: which currency instrument to hold (stablecoins or non-stablecoins) and which channel to use for exchange (intermediated or disintermediated venues). We argue that democratic institutions shape both dimensions. Where electoral accountability is strong, citizens remain in regulated intermediated channels; where it is weak, they shift toward dollar-pegged stablecoins routed through opaque venues, thereby reducing surveillance and currency debasement simultaneously. We build a model of democratic accountability and the cost(s) of financial legibility and derive hypotheses linking state power to exchange in cryptocurrency markets. We leverage unique transaction-level data from 110 emerging and developing economies, along with panel data and event study models, to test these hypotheses. Our findings show that behavior in cryptocurrency markets is directly tied to expectations regarding state power.

detail.abstract: Matching markets allocate scarce opportunities using performance metrics that agents can game. When does making a metric less gameable actually reduce gaming? We show that the answer hinges on how the market converts evaluations into stakes. Where evaluations assign prices-wages, credit terms, score-indexed paymentspartially purifying the metric raises gaming precisely when gameable variation dominates it: the market's trust in the metric then rises faster than its exposure to gaming falls. By contrast, where evaluations assign positions-fixed seats allocated by rankpurification never backfires: ranking cancels trust from the incentive, leaving a rank price that deflates with the metric's dispersion, so mean gaming falls monotonically. We solve both markets in closed form under a first-order equilibrium concept; transfers microfound the first regime, rank tournaments the second. A prize-curvature index then determines when gaming improves rather than harms sorting, and when perfecting the metric is itself sorting-suboptimal.

title: A Simulation Study Examining the Effect of Numbershire Video Game on Proximal Math Outcomes for K-2 Students with Math Learning Disabilities

detail.title: A Simulation Study Examining the Effect of Numbershire Video Game on Proximal Math Outcomes for K-2 Students with Math Learning Disabilities
detail.abstract: This stimulation study examines mathematics proficiency among U.S. early graders, particularly those with Mathematics Learning Disabilities (MLD). With only 39% demonstrating proficiency on the national test, early intervention remains essential. This simulation study investigates the impact of NumberShire, an instructional video game, on improving math outcomes for second-grade students with MLD. A randomized controlled trial was conducted with 100 students, divided into two groups: an intervention group that played the game and a control group that received traditional instruction. Students in the intervention group played for 12 hours over 12 weeks, aligning with the Common Core State Standards. Both descriptive and inferential results showed significant improvements in the intervention group, with positive effects across all MLD levels. Regression analysis was also performed to consider moderating factors. The study highlights the importance of game-based learning for students with learning challenges and its potential for broader use in inclusive educational settings.

detail.abstract: The federal government owns approximately 30 percent of the surface land area in the United States. Congress has allocated responsibility for managing these lands to four principal agencies: the National Park Service, the U.S. Forest Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Bureau of Land Management. Each agency operates under its own organic statute, which provides the standards applicable to management of the lands under its jurisdiction. These standards differ from agency to agency, as the organic statutes differentially prioritize some goals and uses while restricting or prohibiting others. Two of the agencies operate under multiple use, sustained yield standards. The others are governed by "dominant use" mandates, which seek to foster preservation, recreation, or wildlife preservation. The impacts of climate change are making adherence to the management mandates of the four agencies problematic. Lands that used to be suitable for preserving certain species are, or may soon become, inhospitable to these species. Areas that used to have sufficient water to promote certain uses have become, or may soon become, too arid to support them. Wildfires that devastate lands subject to climate-related aridification may alter vegetation regimes, rendering existing uses impossible or undesirable. These changes are transforming the jurisdictional boundaries of the land management agencies into obstacles to effective management of the federal lands, as conditions that were once thought to be relatively static are in considerable flux. This Article focuses on the challenges facing the four agencies in the face of climate change and suggests how policymakers may need to adjust the relationships among the agencies, the procedures they use in making management decisions, and the substantive criteria that guide management choices in response to those challenges.

title: The Sovereign Decline: Restoring Attributable Judgment in Professional Engagement With Patient-Led Innovation

detail.title: The Sovereign Decline: Restoring Attributable Judgment in Professional Engagement With Patient-Led Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper extends the Burgess Principle's binary test to a category of professional output the framework has not previously addressed: the decision not to engage. Patient-led proposals in assistive technology frequently meet non-response from the clinical professionals best positioned to assess them. The conventional framingsjustified gatekeeping on one side, individual negligence on the other-both miss the operative distinction. Professionals routinely face requests they cannot properly fulfil, because of scope of duty, regulatory constraint, indemnity limits, or evidence standards, and the test does not require them to fulfil such requests. It requires that the decision not to engage be itself an attributable output: a named, reasoned, recorded decline that registers the specific request and, where possible, signposts the pathway that could assess it. The paper terms this the SOVEREIGN decline.

title: The Concentric Value Model -A Modern Framework for Evaluating Public Companies and Stock Price Performance for Contemporary Capital Markets

detail.title: The Concentric Value Model -A Modern Framework for Evaluating Public Companies and Stock Price Performance for Contemporary Capital Markets
detail.abstract: Benjamin Graham's seven value-investing criteria were designed for an industrial economy of tangible assets, stable margins, and slow information diffusion. Contemporary capital markets are characterized by intangible-asset dominance, derivative-driven price formation, retail participation at scale, and rapid technological displacement-conditions under which traditional accounting metrics now explain approximately 5% of stock price variability versus roughly 90% in the mid-20th century (Lev and Gu, 2016). This paper introduces the Concentric Value Model (CVM), a six-layer evaluation framework integrating ten dimensions: Macroeconomic Trends, (Option) Market Dynamics, Financial Architecture, Corporate Positioning, Governance Structure, and Organizational Core-that synthesizes traditionally siloed bodies of research from agency theory, innovation economics, behavioral finance, organizational psychology, and derivatives microstructure into a unified lens. The model is structured as outside-in influence and inside-out performance: outer layers transmit market and macro forces, while inner organizational coherence determines whether those forces translate into sustainable value creation. The paper makes three contributions. First, it derives the ten dimensions from peerreviewed literature and a detailed scoring rubric (Appendix A). Second, it tests the framework against SAP SE's 2014-2024 cloud transition as a longitudinal embedded case study, demonstrating how cross-layer coherence, not any single dimension, explains outsized returns. Third, it proposes preliminary weightings (Governance Structure and Corporate Positioning at 25% each; Macroeconomic Trends 10%; Option Market Dynamics 5%; Financial Architecture 20%; Organizational Core 15%) calibrated from those case findings and judgment, explicitly inviting empirical refinement. Also, this research is accompanied with a scoring instrument, enabling third-party scoring, regression analysis, principal component analysis, and inter-rater reliability testing (Cohen's Kappa). The paper is positioned as a practitioner-first preliminary investigation: the framework, rubric, and tooling are released specifically to enable independent empirical validation across geographies, market caps, and industries.

detail.abstract:
Commander's Intent is a central concept in Mission Command within modern military organizations. Contemporary armed forces emphasize shared understanding and decentralized execution under conditions of uncertainty and friction. However, operational history repeatedly demonstrates that even clearly articulated Commander's Intent can produce divergent organizational behavior and outcomes inconsistent with operational objectives. 
Existing research has provided important insights into Mission Command, shared understanding, organizational control, uncertainty, and friction. Yet it has not sufficiently explained why intent that appears to have been shared is reconstructed as different meaning under friction. 
This study integrates Mission Command theory, Clausewitz's concept of friction, organizational interpretation theory, and command-and-control research to propose the Cumulative Distortion Model. The model argues that small distortions occurring across the stages of information, interpretation, acceptance, intent formation, transmission, reinterpretation, execution, and feedback accumulate over time and generate divergence in organizational behavior. 
This study further redefines Commander's Intent as a Compressed Operational Biography. Commander's Intent is not merely an order. It is a compressed expression of the commander's accumulated professional experience, education, organizational culture, risk perception, successes, and failures.
The central argument of this paper is that Commander's Intent is not transmitted. It is reconstructed. Military effectiveness therefore depends not merely upon information transmission, but upon the preservation of interpretive coherence under uncertainty.

title: Testing the Power of Herding Measures: Evidence from Dispersion Models and a Dynamic Convergence Approach

detail.title: Testing the Power of Herding Measures: Evidence from Dispersion Models and a Dynamic Convergence Approach
detail.abstract: This study reexamines herding behaviour in financial markets by comparing traditional dispersion-based models with a performance-driven convergence framework. Using daily stock data from five major equity markets-the FTSE 100, S&P 500, DAX 40, NIFTY 50, and the Chinese market-over the period 2018-2026, the analysis evaluates herding dynamics under both normal and crisis conditions. Herding is first assessed using the Cross-Sectional Standard Deviation (CSSD) and Cross-Sectional Absolute Deviation (CSAD) models, which infer behavioural convergence from reductions in return dispersion. Consistent with much of the existing literature, these models fail to provide statistically significant evidence of herding, even during the COVID-19 crisis. Although CSAD coefficients become negative during periods of market stress, the results remain statistically insignificant, indicating limited reliability of dispersion-based measures. To address this limitation, the study introduces a performance-based framework, the Relative Performance Convergence Index (RPCI), which conceptualises herding as a dynamic process of adjustment in which underperforming assets exhibit convergence toward strongerperforming assets over time. The empirical results reveal statistically significant convergence behaviour in most markets during the crisis period, providing strong evidence of herding that is not captured by traditional models. The findings highlight that herding is not a static phenomenon reflected in contemporaneous dispersion but a time-varying and dynamic process driven by performance-based imitation. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the effectiveness of herding detection is highly dependent on the measurement approach and that reliance on dispersion-based models alone may lead to misleading conclusions. Overall, this study contributes to the literature by providing a cross-market evaluation of herding measurement techniques and by offering a behaviourally grounded alternative that more accurately captures investor dynamics. The results suggest the need for a shift towards dynamic frameworks in future empirical research on financial market behaviour.

title: On Reference-Regulated Multiperiod Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization in High Dimensions

detail.title: On Reference-Regulated Multiperiod Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization in High Dimensions
detail.abstract: The multiperiod mean-variance (MV) portfolio optimization serves as a vital expansion of Markowitz's static MV portfolio selection framework. Just like its static counterpart, the multiperiod MV portfolio remains susceptible to estimation errors. We propose a reference-regulated multiperiod mean-variance (RRMV) framework that penalizes deviations from a reference policy. Therefore, this new optimization successfully combines the advantages of dynamic strategies and reference portfolios. A key contribution of this paper is the characterization of the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio under high-dimensional asymptotics with estimation errors in both the mean vector and the covariance matrix. We show how the reference penalty and the investment horizon jointly affect the optimized portfolio performance, and how regularization operates differently from the single-period portfolio optimization. Extensive simulation and real data studies demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the stability and out-of-sample Sharpe ratios of multiperiod policies significantly.

detail.abstract: We examine whether a commercial large language model (LLM) can match human analysts in numerical earnings per share (EPS) forecasting. Using 121,369 forecasts for 607 Korean listed firms over 2018-2025, we generate paired LLM forecasts utilizing only information publicly available as of the analyst forecast date, with external search disabled. Human analysts remain more accurate on average: median forecast errors are 1.9% of stock price for analysts and 2.3% for the LLM, implying that the LLM underperforms analysts by about 20%. The LLM outperforms consensus forecasts but remains less accurate than analysts' prior forecasts. The analyst advantage is larger for loss-making, highly leveraged, and smaller firms, as well as for firms with greater analyst disagreement. Comparing model generations under identical prompts, GPT-5.4-nano closes 68% of the gap between GPT-4.1-nano and human analysts. Overall, current commercial LLMs do not yet perform on par with human analysts, but their relative performance improves across model generations and is strongest in settings with richer public information and lower uncertainty.

detail.abstract: We study how tariff-attention shocks affect market-based inflation compensation in the United States. Using a Bloomberg-based tariff news index as a measure of attention to trade policy, we estimate local projections of Treasury TIPS breakeven inflation rates and inflation swaps across maturities ranging from one to thirty years over the sample period July 2018 to January 2026. In the full sample, a one-standard-deviation tariff news shock is followed by declines in both breakevens and inflation swaps, especially at short maturities. This pattern suggests that tariff news is not interpreted by markets as a pure cost-push inflation shock, but also operates through a risk-off or growth negative channel. Subsample analysis reveals an important contrast between the two Trump administrations. During Trump 1, both breakevens and swaps decline broadly across maturities. During Trump 2, short-end breakevens continue to fall, while inflation swaps rise across most maturities and medium-to long-maturity breakevens also turn positive. These results suggest that markets may have assigned greater weight to persistent tariff-driven price pressures during the second episode.

title: Asymmetric Iron-Ore Shock Transmission in Australian Mining Equities: A Nonlinear ARDL and Regime-Switching Analysis

detail.title: Asymmetric Iron-Ore Shock Transmission in Australian Mining Equities: A Nonlinear ARDL and Regime-Switching Analysis
detail.abstract: We examine whether iron-ore price shocks transmit asymmetrically to the equity returns of Australia's three largest listed iron-ore producers (BHP, Rio Tinto, Fortescue) over January 2011 to May 2026 (N = 3,013 trading days). Using a nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) framework, we find that positive iron-ore price movements transmit substantially more strongly to mining-equity prices than negative movements: the long-run multiplier on cumulative price increases (L⁺ = 0.720) exceeds that on decreases (L⁻ = 0.523), a gap of 0.197 that is statistically significant (Wald F = 13.90, p < 0.001). The asymmetry is robust across alternative market-control specifications and lag structures, and is sharply concentrated by business model: the pure-play producer (Fortescue) exhibits long-run multipliers three to four times those of the diversified majors. Evidence on a long-run cointegrating relationship is suggestive rather than conclusive-the bounds F-statistic is inconclusive at the 5% level, though a significantly negative error correction term and the bounds t-test point toward such a relationship. A two-state Markov-switching model identifies persistent calm and stress regimes; embedding the regime classification in the NARDL via filtered probabilities reveals a two-part structure: the long-run asymmetry is regime-invariant (the calm-stress difference in the asymmetry gap is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and survives a two-stage block bootstrap that propagates first-stage regime-estimation uncertainty), whereas short-run transmission intensity roughly triples in the stress regime. These findings indicate that the asymmetric structure of commodity-equity transmission is a stable feature of the relationship, while its immediate magnitude is state-dependent. The results imply that hedges built on symmetric, constant exposure are systematically miscalibrated, that the three producers are distinct rather than interchangeable instruments for iron-ore exposure, and that hedge levels can rest on stable long-run parameters while rebalancing intensity should rise in stressed markets.

title: Monitoring the Auditor: Evidence from Institutional Investors’ Votes

detail.title: Monitoring the Auditor: Evidence from Institutional Investors’ Votes
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how institutional investors monitor external auditors through proxy voting. Although auditors play a central role in corporate governance, ratification proposals typically receive near-unanimous support, raising questions about investors' oversight. Using over 3 million votes cast by 1,673 investors, we uncover substantial heterogeneity in monitoring approaches. Hand-collected voting policies reveal that many investors scrutinize non-audit fees and auditor tenure, and their votes generally align with these policies. When investors deviate to support an auditor despite a potential breach, they often publish voting rationales to justify the decision and maintain accountability. These signals have real effects: dissent on non-audit fees predicts lower subsequent fees, while dissent on tenure predicts higher auditor turnover. Based on voting patterns, we classify investors as automatic approvers, rule-based voters, and deliberate voters. Rule-based voters-those guided by explicit criteria-are the most informed, more likely to detect poor audit quality. In contrast, automatic approvers-the largest group-exert minimal oversight and are less likely to hold firms with high auditor tenure or non-audit fees.

detail.title: When Parents Stay Home: Work-from-Home and Sorting across Public, Private, and Home Schools
detail.abstract: Thus U.S. has recently seen a sharp, persistent decline in public school enrollment alongside a surge in homeschooling. This paper examines the role of work-from-home (WFH) in driving these changes. WFH may lower the cost of homeschooling through greater flexibility and reduced commuting, but productivity disruptions and shifts toward private schooling may offset these effects. We combine national data on public and private enrollments with newly assembled district-level homeschooling counts. Using variation in telework potential across local labor markets in a difference-indifferences framework, we find no aggregate decline in public school enrollment, but declines in private enrollment and corresponding increases in homeschooling that are temporary. The aggregate result masks heterogeneity: urban districts experience declines, partially offset by gains in more remote areas. These enrollment shifts are critical for school finance, as they directly affect state aid formulas and therefore local district spending.

detail.title: Temporal Dynamics of Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) in Semi-Arid Gadarif Region, Sudan (1985-2024): Implications for Landscape Monitoring and Drought Assessment

declarations.ethicsApproval: the research is about monitoring natural resources changes using RS

detail.abstract: Monitoring vegetation and hydrological dynamics in semi-arid ecosystems is critical for understanding responses to climate variability and anthropogenic pressures. This study employs multi-temporal Landsat satellite imagery (1985-2024) to examine spatiotemporal changes in the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) across three ecologically distinct localities-Al-Kayari, Alidedat, and Elsefia-within the Gadarif State, eastern Sudan. Image processing and spectral index computation were performed using Google Earth Engine (GEE) and ArcGIS Pro v3.4.0. NDVI analysis revealed a progressive increase in healthy vegetation cover (NDVI ≥ 0.3) in Elsefia (approximately 63 km² by 2024) and Alidedat (approximately 105 km² by 2024), indicating a positive greening trend over the study period. Conversely, Al-Kayari maintained comparatively drier conditions with persistently sparse vegetation. Parallel NDWI analysis demonstrated enhanced surface moisture and expanded flooded vegetation zones in Elsefia and Alidedat since the mid-1990s, while Al-Kayari continued to exhibit relatively low moisture availability. Pearson correlation analysis between NDVI and NDWI yielded a moderate positive coefficient (r = 0.63, R² = 0.40, p < 0.001), confirming coupled vegetation-moisture dynamics. These findings suggest a partial ecological recovery consistent with documented Sahel re-greening, potentially driven by rainfall variability, land use shifts, and hydrological feedbacks. The results provide a quantitative baseline for evidence-based land management, drought early warning, and climate adaptation planning in the semi-arid Gadarif region.

title: The Income Channel to Labor-Market Polarization
affiliations: Dartmouth College, Northwestern University and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Income Channel to Labor-Market Polarization
detail.abstract:
We study labor-market polarization by developing a framework with heterogeneous consumers, non-homothetic preferences, and endogenous labor supply a la Roy (1951). Because income-elastic sectors are intensive in high- and low-skilled occupations, shocks that raise either the average or the dispersion of income across households shift relative labor demand toward these occupations, generating an income channel to polarization. We quantify this channel by comparing the effect of shocks that affect the distribution of household income in our model and in a version with homothetic preferences in which the income distribution does not affect sectoral composition. The income channel is sizable: it explains 42% and 210% of the increases in the relative wages of high- and low-skill workers observed between 1980 and 2016, and 26% and 51% of the increase in their hours-worked shares. A quarter of its effect operates through income dispersion, highlighting the importance of departing from representative-consumer frameworks in non-homothetic environments.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of Fitch Ratings sovereign credit ratings for a balanced panel of 86 emerging market and low-income countries (LICs) over 1994-2023 (690 country-year observations). We estimate pooled OLS and country fixed-effects models for rating levels, probit models for upgrades and downgrades with a formal asymmetry test, and a local regression discontinuity (RD) design around the BBB-/BB+ investment-grade threshold. The macroeconomic core-GDP per capita (β = 1.227***), foreign exchange reserves (β = 0.198***), and external debt (β =-0.023***)-is robust across all specifications. Sovereign default episodes generate a persistent penalty of-5 to-7 notches, the largest single determinant in the model. The 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the 2014-2016 commodity price shock each depressed ratings by approximately one notch beyond fundamentals, with stronger effects for emerging markets than for LICs. The RD analysis finds no significant discontinuity in rating dynamics at the BBB-/BB+ threshold, suggesting that the cliff effect operates through sovereign spreads rather than through rating formation itself. Upgrade/downgrade asymmetry is partial, concentrated on foreign exchange reserves and GDP per capita. Results are stable across seven robustness specifications. These findings carry direct implications for sovereign debt managers: FX reserve accumulation, external debt management, and default prevention are the most actionable levers for preserving creditworthiness in developing countries.

This essay intentionally adopts the role of devil’s advocate to interrogate the credibility of privately regulated Voluntary Carbon Markets (VCMs) against the standards of science, economics, and justice. title: Beliefs and Actions under Government Policy Uncertainty: Evidence from Student Loan Forgiveness
affiliations: University of Chicago, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Beliefs and Actions under Government Policy Uncertainty: Evidence from Student Loan Forgiveness
detail.abstract:
How does uncertainty about future government policy affect households’ beliefs and subsequent borrowing, spending and debt payment behavior? We study these questions through the lens of student loan forgiveness in the United States, which following electoral promises, was announced in 2022 but never implemented due to judicial rulings. We conduct a customized information provision experiment embedded in a survey eliciting real-time beliefs about future debt forgiveness and repayment, which we link to credit bureau data, employment verification data, and nondurables consumption. Eligible borrowers who are more optimistic about forgiveness reduce payments on student loans by \$40 per month and increase non-durable spending by $100 per month. We also find some evidence optimistic borrowers may postpone durable spending waiting for uncertainty to resolve. Borrowers optimistic about future payment pauses make fewer payments on their student loans, reduce payment by $40 per month and are 7.5 percentage points more likely to be delinquent after payments resume. A quantification exercise finds welfare losses from incorrect beliefs can exceed 43 percent of the initial loan balance. Our results provide micro-evidence on the role of policy uncertainty in household decision-making, and have implications for government announcements and commitment policy.

title: Data-Driven Automation
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and

detail.title: Data-Driven Automation
detail.abstract:
We build a dynamic model of data-driven automation in which data (i) is heterogeneous and task-specific; (ii) accumulates endogenously as a byproduct of economic activity; and (iii) exhibits spillovers such that data generated by one task can augment the productivity of another. Along the transition path of automation, data plays a dual role in simultaneously augmenting the productivity of already-automated tasks and expanding the automation frontier. We derive tight conditions for the economy to be partially versus fully automated in the long-run. In the latter case, automation exhibits rich short-run dynamics that depend on the pattern of data spillovers but is always slow in the long-run: the share of tasks produced by labor decays asymptotically as a power law in time. We show that the economy is generically inefficient and analyze how a planner optimally tilts the direction of data accumulation. With endogenous capital accumulation, data-driven automation generates explosive growth but stagnant long-run wages.

detail.title: Quantifying relationships between U.S. regulatory zoning and landscape-scale trends in impervious surface development
detail.abstract: Zoning, a popular land-use policy tool in the United States (U.S.), regulates the type, intensity, and location of development, intended to serve broad objectives, from sustainable development to public health. To date, examinations of relationships between zoning and development outcomes in the U.S. have focused on small-scale case studies and/or disregarded rezonings (changes over time), preventing a generalizable understanding of zoning outcomes across regions. We address these limitations through a complementary, multi-scale approach that leverages two independent datasets; one prioritizing large spatial extent and the other offering temporal depth to overcome the common lack of temporal rezoning data at scale. For the large spatial extent dataset, we conduct a statewide cross-sectional analysis (2001–2023) of North Carolina relating zoning to impervious surface expansion, providing the first empirical assessment of 13 disaggregated zoning districts across a U.S. state. For temporal depth, we perform a local longitudinal analysis (2004–2023) that quantifies zoning–development relationships over two decades. Statewide and locally, Planned-Use districts experienced the largest growth, with urban development nearly tripling over 20 years, whereas Downtown, Parks and Recreation, and lower density Residential districts showed limited new development. Although effect directions were consistent across analyses, accounting for rezoning in the local case substantially reduced effect sizes, suggesting that static zoning designations alone may not fully capture development dynamics. By empirically quantifying zoning–development associations at multiple spatiotemporal scales, this study advances understanding of zoning outcomes and offers actionable insights for land-use policy, land-change science, and geospatial modeling.

title: Auditors' (Non-)Responses to Public Warnings of Audit Risk: Evidence from Short-Selling Campaigns
affiliations: Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Accounting, Business Law & Taxation, Harvard Business School and McGill University - Desautels Faculty of Management

detail.title: Auditors' (Non-)Responses to Public Warnings of Audit Risk: Evidence from Short-Selling Campaigns
detail.abstract: Using a novel setting, we examine auditors' responses to public warnings of audit risk and whether their non-responses are associated with auditor and client characteristics. Specifically, we focus on 243 short-selling campaigns from 2006 to 2020 in which short sellers make public, credible allegations of audit-related issues against listed companies. 48.3% of those companies' auditors do not take any observable actions in terms of raising audit fees substantially, terminating the engagement, issuing going concern opinions (GCO), or reporting internal control weaknesses (ICW) in the year after the short sellers' allegations. We further find that longer auditor-client tenure is the factor most consistently associated with auditors' non-response to public warnings of audit risk, a pattern arguably consistent with impaired independence. Additional analyses show that the litigation and reputation costs of auditors' inactions are minimal, further reducing auditors' incentives for responses.

detail.abstract: Present-bias, combined with the lack of commitment, can prevent individuals from sticking to their intended plans. Conventional wisdom suggests that when present-biased households are sophisticated, the economy achieves higher growth rates than when households are naive. We show that this result is driven by the Elasticity of Intertemporal Substitution (EIS). Specifically, in an AK-growth model, sophistication drives higher growth than naïveté only when EIS < 1; when EIS > 1, the relationship reverses. Our findings suggest that self-awareness of behavioral biases can undermine economic growth, depending on the prevailing intertemporal substitution motives. Our results allow us to quantify both the reduction in growth rates and welfare for both agents.

detail.abstract: This paper explores two scenarios for the potential economic effects of a Middle East war that causes a spike in energy prices. In the first, oil prices surge for one year to around $120 per barrel, while prices also rise sharply for liquefied natural gas, refined petroleum, and fertilizer; in the second, energy prices remain elevated for three years. We find in both scenarios, global growth slows relative to our baseline projection, but the effects are felt very unevenly. Countries dependent on Middle Eastern oil, petroleum, natural gas, and fertilizers experience the largest declines in GDP and increases in inflation. The effects on different sectors vary according to their energy sources, both directly through different energy dependence and indirectly through production networks. Also, trade relationships matter because as the global economy slows, countries such as China experience a decline in export demand, worsening GDP losses, even though China has large domestic supplies of oil, gas, and fertilizer.

title: The Rise of Online Dating and Heterogamous Marriages
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, University College London and Bates White Economic Consulting

detail.title: The Rise of Online Dating and Heterogamous Marriages
detail.abstract: We study how online dating shapes intermarriage by race and education in the United States. Using American Community Survey data and a continuous-treatment two-way fixedeffects (TWFE) design, we estimate sizable TWFE coefficients linking platform exposure to interracial marriage that vary across platforms, with weaker estimates for educational homogamy. To probe mechanisms, we surveyed retrospective dating histories, partner preferences, and online dating behavior. Individual fixed-effects panel regressions show that effects of meeting a partner online vary with users' preferences and filter usage: those with strong same-race preferences use a race filter to meet same-race partners. Thus, platform features and user preferences jointly shape dating patterns.

detail.title: The Cultural Trust Gap: Discrimination Across England's North-South Divide

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 08/2026

detail.abstract: Trust, the belief in another individual or organisation's intent to act in good faith, is a cornerstone of social prosperity. However, cultural norms significantly influence trust levels within and between groups, often leading to discriminatory behaviours that undermine cooperation. This paper investigates the impact of culture on trust using a novel experimental approach that isolates trust from confounding factors such as risk preferences and distributional concerns. The setting of the experiment is England, a culturally and economically divided nation. Focusing on self-identified Southerners and Northerners, I find evidence of a cultural trust gap. Specifically, while Southerners exhibit equal trust towards both groups, Northerners trust Southerners significantly less than their own group. By decomposing trust into its conditional and unconditional components, I show that this disparity is driven by unconditional trust: Northerners perceive Southerners as more selfish than their own culture.

title: Skill Formation with Siblings
affiliations: Stockholm University

detail.title: Skill Formation with Siblings
detail.abstract: This paper estimates a structural model of skill formation for children who grow up with siblings, introducing a novel variable, the "sibling bond," which captures how well siblings get along. Using data from the Millennium Cohort Study in the United Kingdom, I construct this measure from information on the frequency and quality of sibling interactions, such as enjoying playtime together and teasing each other. Descriptive evidence shows that a stronger sibling bond is associated with better child outcomes during adolescence. The structural estimates are consistent with the sibling bond being a productive input in the skill formation of both younger and older siblings, alongside parent-child interactions.

title: Pricing Job Amenities: A Practitioner's Manual

detail.title: Pricing Job Amenities: A Practitioner's Manual
detail.abstract: This paper provides a practical framework for estimating compensating differentials in the presence of unobserved worker ability. The approach treats ability as a structured residual that shapes access to both wages and non-pay job attributes. Job choice is assumed to be governed by a single vertical job-quality index, and—conditional on this index—an observed proxy for ability acts as an "anti-instrument" that allows researchers to recover amenity prices from standard observational data. Identification relies on a simple conditional independence assumption: if pay, amenities, and underlying job quality were fully observed, the anti-instrument would add no additional information. The paper emphasizes implementation and interpretation rather than technical proofs, offering a practical roadmap for applied researchers; adoption is supported by the companion aivreg Stata package, which enables estimation using standard cross-sectional datasets. An application to the experimental setting of Mas and Pallais (2017) shows that the pricing method reproduces experimentally measured willingness-to-pay patterns with observational data, further validating the strength of both the experimental and observational approaches.

title: Blindly Discriminating: The GI Bill and Racial Inequality
affiliations: Stanford University and

detail.title: Blindly Discriminating: The GI Bill and Racial Inequality
detail.abstract: The World War II GI Bill was the largest education subsidy in US history and a cornerstone of the postwar US transition to a knowledge economy. Although formally race-blind, the program's decentralized administration left implementation to local officials and segregated institutions, with sharply different consequences for Black and white veterans. This paper quantifies the GI Bill's impact on Black and white Americans' economic outcomes across two generations, using a regression discontinuity around WWII service eligibility cutoffs and a new data linkage from veterans in the 1940 and 1950 censuses to their sons' neighborhood outcomes between 1990 and 2025. The GI Bill widened racial inequality, doubling white veterans' college completion while steering Black veterans into often-fraudulent vocational programs with no earnings returns. The disparities persisted across generations, increasing the white-Black gap in sons' adult-neighborhood outcomes, including a 5-percentage-point (47 percent) widening of the racial college gap. Unequal returns to the same eligibility account for the intergenerational gap, with no contribution from prewar differences in socioeconomic status or geography. In sum, access to the GI Bill was not nearly the same economic opportunity for Black Americans as it was for white Americans, highlighting that race-blind policy does not guarantee racial equality.

detail.title: Central Bank Reserves and Banks’ Portfolio Rebalancing in the Euro Area

detail.abstract: An important consequence of unconventional monetary policy is a substantial increase in the amount of reserves held in banks’ balance sheets. In this article, we analyse whether a higher level of reserves affects credit supply to the real economy. Using data for euro area banks after the ECB initiated asset purchases in 2014-2015, we show that reserve creation related negatively to their security holdings and positively to bank loans, in line with portfolio rebalancing theories. The results account for endogeneity in reserve holding and are less pronounced for banks with higher risk of deposit outflows. However, reserve-induced lending is not limited to monetary easing. During the 2022-2023 ECB tightening cycle, reserve-rich banks mitigated credit declines to firms, impairing transmission. Results were stronger for banks facing frictions related to market fragmentation and financial constraints. Overall, our work implies that central bank reserves can have far-reaching consequences for monetary policy transmission through the bank lending channel.

title: Uncle Sam's Cut: A Century of the Federal Tax Drag on US Equity Returns
affiliations: Columbia University

detail.title: Uncle Sam's Cut: A Century of the Federal Tax Drag on US Equity Returns
detail.abstract: We estimate the Federal tax drag on US equity investors by simulating a taxable investor holding the market portfolio from 1926 to 2025, under the tax code in force each year with tax-lot accounting, holding-period rules, capital-loss limits, and carryforwards. Federal taxes reduce long-horizon equity wealth by more than one-third. Across overlapping 30-year windows, the annualized tax drag averages 347 bps, peaks at 538 bps in 1936-1965, and falls to 165 bps in 1996-2025. Dividend taxation is the dominant historical channel. The step-up in basis at death reduces embedded capital-gains liabilities, and for a 30-year-old investor, it lowers tax drag from 165 bps to 127 bps; by age 70, it lowers it to 103 bps.

title: Global Public Good Agreements: Is there Really a Paradox of Cooperation?
affiliations: FernUniversität in Hagen and FernUniversität in Hagen

detail.title: Global Public Good Agreements: Is there Really a Paradox of Cooperation?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
