detail.abstract: This paper applies self-enforcing agreements to the public good game of Bergstrom et al. (1986) and Cornes and Sandler (1984, 1985, 1986) with linear transformation technology. First, countries decide whether to sign a global public good agreement. Thereafter signatories choose their public good contributions as Stackelberg leader and nonsignatories choose their public good contributions as Stackelberg followers. A "paradox of cooperation", a term coined by Barrett (1994), ensues when the participation in the agreement is high only if the gains from cooperation are low. The paradox of cooperation may arise in case of linear-quadratic utility functions, but not in case of CES utility functions. This contradictory result is attributable to differing income expansion paths.

title: Estimating the Output Gap in a High-inflation Emerging Market
affiliations: Sabanci University

detail.title: Estimating the Output Gap in a High-inflation Emerging Market
detail.abstract: How should emerging market economies (EMEs) estimate potential output and the output gap in the presence of extreme volatility, frequent structural breaks, and policy regime shifts? This paper addresses this question by comparing a comprehensive menu of eighteen estimators-spanning univariate filters, survey-based measures, and open-economy statespace models-using Turkey (2005-2025) as a laboratory. I evaluate which methodologies are robust and which fail in volatile environments. While canonical filters (such as HP and Hamilton) and structural VARs are highly unstable or produce implausible trends, refined statistical filters offer reliable, low-volatility benchmarks. Cross-method disagreement is large: at end-of-sample the full eighteen-method range spans nearly 4 percentage points. For structural state-space models, I show that two adjustments matter most: regime-variance scaling is non-negotiable, preventing crisis outliers from contaminating potential GDP, and conditioning on the monetary policy stance via the ex-ante real rate is essential to avoid overstating the gap during tightening cycles. Crucially, this disagreement is not uniform: it concentrates at the sample edge and around crises, while estimates agree through the well-identified interior. EME central banks should therefore report the gap as a range that widens precisely where, and when, method choice bites.

title: Hold-up  in the Absence of Individual Rationality: Asymptotic Efficiency   and Gradualism

detail.title: Hold-up  in the Absence of Individual Rationality: Asymptotic Efficiency   and Gradualism
detail.abstract: The holdup problem has given rise to a large and influential literature. We consider a bilateral holdup problem where bargaining power is asymmetrically distributed among the agents, in particular investing at the efficient level is not "individually rational" for one of the agents. We demonstrate that in the presence of a rich natural setup-that allows for dynamics in transfers, investments and negotiations-there exist subgame perfect equilibria that achieve asymptotic efficiency. This is true both when investments by the two agents are substitutes, as well as when these are complements. Moreover, implementation requires gradualism, with sequential investments and transfers over several periods.

title: Bank Intermediation Costs and Monetary Policy Transmission: A Decomposition Across EU Member States

detail.title: Bank Intermediation Costs and Monetary Policy Transmission: A Decomposition Across EU Member States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses two questions about bank intermediation costs across the EU27. First, how much of the observed lending-deposit spread reflects structural bank pricing behavior, as opposed to sovereign risk and term premia? Second, what structural features of national banking systems explain persistent crosscountry differences in this cost? We construct a novel Cost of Bank Intermediation (CBI) measure using harmonized ECB data over January 2017-December 2025, decomposed separately for household deposits and NFC loans. During the 2022-2024 tightening cycle, the deposit-side CBI rose by nearly 400 basis points while lending margins were only moderately compressed, shifting the adjustment burden disproportionately onto household savers. Crosscountry heterogeneity is large and persistent: deposit margins are highest in peripheral economies; lending margins are highest in Eastern Europe, where limited competition sustains structurally elevated intermediation costs.

title:
How Bitter is the Pill?
State-dependent Sacrifice Ratios in a Small Open Economy: Evidence from Türkiye
affiliations: Sabanci University

detail.title:
How Bitter is the Pill?
State-dependent Sacrifice Ratios in a Small Open Economy: Evidence from Türkiye
detail.abstract: The cost of disinflation is not a fixed number: it depends on the inflation regime, the credibility of policy, and the open-economy channels through which monetary tightening affects prices. Using monthly Turkish data from 2006 to 2026, this paper studies this state dependence through a state-dependent Phillipscurve framework. I show that the Phillips curve is statistically flat in low-inflation periods, making the implied sacrifice ratio effectively uninformative. In high-inflation periods, however, the inflation-slack relationship becomes much steeper, implying an unemployment sacrifice ratio of about 0.4-0.7 percentage points of the unemployment-rate gap per percentage point of disinflation. Residualized Phillips curves and expectations-augmented specifications show that this steepening is not simply driven by inflation persistence, expectations, or imported costs. The results suggest a conditional view of disinflation: the early phase may be relatively cheap when credibility stabilizes the exchange rate and lowers inflation expectations, but the cost can rise if services inflation, dollarization, indexation, and FX balance-sheet risks keep inflation persistent even as activity slows.

title: Formal Labor Market Dynamics and Development

detail.title: Formal Labor Market Dynamics and Development
detail.abstract: This paper studies formal employment dynamics using linked employer–employee data from eight countries spanning a wide income range from Kenya to Chile. First, we show that formality rates increase with development, both between and within countries, because more workers enter the formal sector, not because they spend more time in formal jobs. Second, formal labor market fluidity increases with development, as workers hold more formal jobs, spend less time in each job, and less time between jobs. Third, greater fluidity is associated with higher life-cycle wage growth, which is largely accounted for by within- rather than between-firm wage gains.

title: Restart: Career Breaks, Upskilling and Employer Response

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: Family-related career interruptions are an important channel through which household responsibilities shape women's labour market trajectories. We study whether shortterm upskilling can offset the hiring penalty associated with such interruptions using a large-scale correspondence experiment on India's biggest online job portal. Submitting 15,872 applications to 3,968 vacancies, we randomize career-break status, upskilling certifications, and family signals across otherwise identical female profiles. A career break reduces callbacks by 49% relative to continuously employed applicants. The penalty is larger in finance (55%) than in HR (36%), consistent with employers placing greater weight on recent experience where skills may depreciate faster. Upskilling certifications do not reduce the penalty, despite improving measured resume-job fit, suggesting that short-form credentials are weak substitutes for employment continuity. The penalty is smaller at higher-paying jobs, in larger firms, and in southern cities. These findings imply persistent demand-side barriers to women's re-entry and limited gains from supply-side skilling alone.

detail.abstract: Banning Russia's access to SWIFT banking system and luxury goods and technology, Western countries hoped the Russian economy would crumble. However, by 2026, Russia has survived by using various strategies.The study identifies main structural vulnerabilities in Eurasia through which Russia can circumvent the global blockade. International card bans are avoided by strategic "card tourism" by Russians who open active foreign bank accounts at institutions, such as Bakai Bank in Kyrgyzstan.Also Russian citizens open Bank acount in CIS countries,Belarus. Off-the-grid banking systems clear payments in South Ossetia and Transnistria, both unrecognized territorial enclaves, where payments are routed through a banking system that is hidden from international compliance monitors. Russia operates a large fleet of so-called "maritime shadow ships" to evade the G7 oil price ceiling by facilitating "ship-to-ship" transfers to mask energy sources. Russia takes advantage of low energy prices and subzero temperatures to create large crypto-mining operations in Siberia, which are financed directly in foreign debt with the purchase of cryptocurrencies. The channels are made possible by China's new economic policies aimed at bypassing Western sanctions, which rely on thousands of well-structured Chinese middlemen to bring the world's best luxury cars and industrial parts into Russian dealerships by reclassifying them or similar means.Finally, this study provides evidence that today it is almost impossible to single out a single country in the face of fragmentation of global trade. These alternative networks achieve the state's survival, but impose the economic cost on the public through high inflation and reduced purchasing power.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates why the widely-used Big Three financial literacy index provides a reliable measure of financial literacy. Using an Item Response Theory framework, we estimate item difficulty and discrimination parameters and conduct a meta analysis to assess the stability of these properties across datasets and countries. Results confirm the scale's validity and reliability, with item characteristics that remain stable across populations and settings. We find no evidence of measurement differences across demographic subgroups or countries. Compared to the longer Big Five scale, the Big Three index performs similarly in measuring financial literacy and predicting financial behaviors.

title: A Comparative Assessment of National Competitiveness in Advanced Biotechnology, with Implications for South Korea

detail.title: A Comparative Assessment of National Competitiveness in Advanced Biotechnology, with Implications for South Korea

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/IER/31/2/1

publicationDetails.detailsText: KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 31 No. 2., pp. 6-18

detail.abstract:
As the advanced biopharmaceutical industry becomes a cornerstone of health security, cell and gene therapy (CGT) has emerged as a major sub-field with significant industrial and economic growth potential.

This paper analyzes the industrial competitiveness of the CGT sector in seven major countries, revealing that the South Korean CGT sector lags in terms of industrial competitiveness, with an industrial competitiveness index score of just 4.81 points, trailing the first-place United States (9.61) by a significant margin. The study also finds that Korea suffers from a brain drain of doctoral talent and a clinical trial structure skewed toward legacy therapies, and finds a lack of Korean products approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of the United States.

Korea also offers fewer government subsidies compared to its competitors. Furthermore, 12 of 16 key items in the materials, parts, and equipment (MPE) sector are import-dependent, creating a potentially fatal supply chain vulnerability.

To address these issues, Korea must focus on three short-term goals: cultivating a skilled workforce, localizing the production of key MPE, and diversifying imports. In the medium to long term, it is essential to foster domestic talent with skills across disciplines and promote mission-oriented R&D to widen competitive advantages and establish global supply chain leadership.

title: The Blind Spot in the Fight Against Inflation: The Perceived Inflation Gap
affiliations: Istanbul University

detail.title: The Blind Spot in the Fight Against Inflation: The Perceived Inflation Gap
detail.abstract:
Central banks primarily monitor price developments through headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation during disinflation processes. However, in the Turkish economy during the period February 2023–February 2026, households did not perceive an equivalent improvement in inflation conditions despite the observed decline in headline inflation. This pattern suggests the existence of a systematic divergence between measured inflation and perceived inflation.
This study examines this divergence through the economy-wide diffusion of price increases and provides the first quantitative measure of the commonly expressed household observation that “inflation is falling, but it is not being felt.” To this end, the difference between the Behavioral Diffusion Index (BDI), developed through the Behavioral Diffusion Channel (BDC) to capture the diffusion of price increases across CPI main expenditure groups, and the Diffusion Index (DI) is defined as the Perceived Inflation Gap (PIG).
The findings indicate that price increases exhibited a high degree of diffusion throughout most of the analysis period, with the BDI remaining at elevated levels for more than 90% of the observed period. These results suggest that the diffusion of price increases serves as a key reference point for households and functions as an indicator of perceived inflation. The study further shows that the PIG represents an important perceptual blind spot that may limit the effectiveness of monetary policy in combating inflation. Although this framework is developed using the Turkish case, the proposed mechanism is not necessarily country-specific and may also provide a broader perspective on the perceptual and behavioral nature of inflation.

title:
Decomposing the Ideological Divide in Perceptions of Inequality: 
A Signal Detection Approach
affiliations: ,  and Princeton University

detail.title:
Decomposing the Ideological Divide in Perceptions of Inequality: 
A Signal Detection Approach

detail.abstract: A central puzzle in the social sciences is that, despite high and rising inequality, democracies consistently under-deliver redistributive policies. Research in economics and political science has documented one explanation for this puzzle: beliefs about the extent of inequality are polarized along ideological lines, with liberals believing there to be more inequality than conservatives. We decompose this ideological divide in inequality perceptions into two sources: the decision threshold applied by liberals and conservatives when classifying possible instances of inequality ('criterion') and their tendency to perceive inequality to begin with ('sensitivity'). Across five studies (N = 1,962), we find that liberals consistently report seeing more inequality than conservatives when exposed to identical stimuli. A formal signal detection decomposition reveals that the effect size of the difference in criterion between liberals and conservatives is nearly twice the magnitude of the sensitivity difference. The ideological gap in perceived inequality disappears when stimuli depict inequality unambiguously-that is, when the signal is strong enough to clear even the strictest decision thresholds. Notably, we find that perceived inequality is associated with fairness concerns and support for redistributive policies above and beyond ideological orientation. These findings suggest that the everyday settings in which people encounter instances of social inequality are themselves likely to produce consequential differences in beliefs about the extent of inequality.

title: Comparing Market Mechanism Efficiencies

detail.title: Comparing Market Mechanism Efficiencies
detail.abstract: We develop a game-theoretic framework that compares welfare efficiency across three market mechanisms: continuous double auctions with transparent order books (lit exchanges), opaque order books (dark pools), and periodic batch auctions. Each mechanism is modeled as a queuing system where heterogeneous traders face trade-offs between the execution price, waiting costs, and transaction costs. Our main result establishes that under moderate arrival rates and bounded adverse selection, dark pools dominate both alternatives in aggregate ex-ante welfare. Observable order books create costly strategic timing games in which traders delay or rush submissions to optimize their position in the queue, generating wasteful social waiting costs. Opaque order books eliminate these timing games through information design. We formally characterize the equilibrium strategies in each mechanism and prove the welfare ranking W_DARK > W_LIT > W_BATCH. Extensions incorporate asymmetric information and endogenous venue choice. The results demonstrate how the information structure and the discipline of the service jointly determine efficiency in strategic matching environments.

title: The Elastic Capacity of Fiduciary Prudence: Operational Compression and the Expanding Burden of Institutional Scale in Defined-Benefit Pensions

detail.title: The Elastic Capacity of Fiduciary Prudence: Operational Compression and the Expanding Burden of Institutional Scale in Defined-Benefit Pensions

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Prudence in trust law is a proportional standard of fiduciary conduct evaluated relative to the character, aims, capacity, and circumstances of the fiduciary office.

Defined-benefit pension systems combine institutional magnitude, long-duration liabilities, broad authority, access to expertise, and significant economic consequence within a single fiduciary office. Those characteristics materially expand what fiduciaries may reasonably investigate, negotiate, structure, monitor, and foresee under prevailing conditions.

Yet pension administration evolved through Employee Retirement Income Security Act-era guidance, prudent-investor expansion, delegated asset-management structures, benchmark-oriented peer practice, and increasingly standardized forms of financial intermediation. Those frameworks supplied administrable methods for managing large pools of capital, but they do not necessarily capture the full implications of institutional fiduciary capacity under trust-law prudence.

This Article argues that prudence doctrine already contains an under-theorized principle of proportional inquiry. The claim is not that fiduciaries must pursue predetermined economic or political outcomes. It is that institutions possessing substantial fiduciary capacity may need to justify continued reliance on frameworks that do not fully reflect the practical capacities and consequences of the fiduciary office.

The problem is not that trust law lacks a standard for institutional pensions. It is that institutional pension practice frequently operationalizes prudence through market conventions that understate fiduciary capacity.

The Article’s contribution is not to announce a new fiduciary duty, but to show that existing doctrine has been applied through comparators and operational assumptions better suited to ordinary market participation than institutional-scale pension stewardship.

title: Caught in the Crossfire: Why the 2026 Energy Shock Hit Indian and Global oil Giants Differently
affiliations: Institute Of Management Development and Research (IMDR)

detail.title: Caught in the Crossfire: Why the 2026 Energy Shock Hit Indian and Global oil Giants Differently
detail.abstract: This study investigates the multi-dimensional corporate financial performance and operational resilience of global National Oil Companies (NOCs) and International Oil Companies (IOCs) during the 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis. Utilizing comparative fiscal benchmarking, Edward Altman's Z-Score model, and three-step/five-step DuPont financial analysis, we evaluate the systemic risk, capital structure efficiency, and profitability mechanics of energy majors including Saudi Aramco, ExxonMobil, Chevron, and the Indian public sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs: IOCL, BPCL, HPCL). Based on financial filings and macroeconomic data from the Q1 2026 conflict period, the empirical results identify a significant structural 'resilience gap.' State-backed NOCs exhibited superior capital efficiency and liquidity buffers, while private IOCs faced severe derivative timing mismatches. In India, OMCs navigated an extreme retailpricing paradox, absorbing substantial under-recoveries of ₹1,000 crore per day to shield consumers before implementing staggered retail fuel price hikes. The study demonstrates that geopolitical and logistical risk premiums have fundamentally transformed corporate risk management, cementing national energy security as the primary driver of capital allocation over traditional decarbonization pathways.

title: Dusting the Blurry Lens of Immunity in Nigerian Legal System
affiliations: Financial Crime Prosecutor

detail.title: Dusting the Blurry Lens of Immunity in Nigerian Legal System
detail.abstract: The doctrine of constitutional immunity under section 308 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended) remains one of the most controversial constitutional provisions within Nigeria's democratic structure. Although the immunity clause was designed to preserve executive stability and protect certain public office holders from frivolous litigation capable of disrupting governance, its practical application has generated serious concerns regarding accountability, corruption, abuse of office, and constitutionalism. This article critically examines the legal foundation, historical justification, judicial interpretation, and practical implications of executive immunity in Nigeria. The article further interrogates the widespread misconception that categories of public officers outside those expressly protected under section 308 also enjoy immunity from legal processes. Through doctrinal legal analysis and judicial authorities, the paper argues that constitutional immunity in Nigeria has increasingly evolved into a mechanism capable of frustrating anti-corruption efforts and weakening public trust in governance. The article concludes by advocating constitutional recalibration aimed at balancing executive protection with democratic accountability and the rule of law.

title: Relative-Price Skewness, Dispersion, and Inflation Regimes: Evidence from Europe
affiliations: Sabanci University

detail.title: Relative-Price Skewness, Dispersion, and Inflation Regimes: Evidence from Europe
detail.abstract: Ball and Mankiw (1995) argue that the shape of the relative-price distribution can matter for aggregate inflation. When price adjustment is costly, firms with large desired price increases adjust, while firms with smaller or negative desired changes may wait. Observed right-skewness can therefore reflect an asymmetric adjustment pattern in which positive relative-price shocks pass through more quickly than offsetting negative shocks. This paper asks whether this mechanism is stable across inflation regimes. The answer from European HICP data is no. Once inflation rises and repricing becomes more frequent, the skewness channel largely disappears. What remains informative is not the asymmetry of relative-price changes, but their scale: countries with wider cross-sectional price-change distributions have higher inflation, and this dispersion channel becomes stronger after the post-2022 inflation surge. A separate Turkish case study, using more granular CPI data in a much higher-inflation environment, shows the same pattern in sharper form. The evidence points to a state-dependent interpretation of the Ball-Mankiw mechanism: skewness matters most when non-adjustment is common, while dispersion becomes the more useful diagnostic when inflation is high enough that firms reprice more frequently.

title: Decomposing Shifts in the Beveridge Curve:  Implications for Labor Market Dynamics and Inflation
affiliations: University of Maryland - Joint Program in Survey Methodology and Department of Economics,  and Kenyon College

detail.title: Decomposing Shifts in the Beveridge Curve:  Implications for Labor Market Dynamics and Inflation
detail.abstract:
This paper explores the relationship between standard labor market tightness (vacancies divided by unemployment) and generalized labor market tightness (vacancies divided by a measure of effective searchers that accounts for potential hires from all sources including those out of the labor force or currently employed). We show that much of what the standard model attributes to variation in matching efficiency reflects changes in the ratio of effective searchers to unemployment rather than changes in “true” matching efficiency. Generalized tightness outperforms standard tightness in Phillips curve equations, both in models with tightness entering linearly and in better-fitting models with tightness entering nonlinearly. In models that distinguish between movements in generalized tightness due to movements along the generalized Beveridge curve versus Beveridge curve shifts (reflecting changes in generalized matching efficiency and other factors), changes in tightness due to Beveridge curve shifts explain more of the variation in inflation.

title: Air Pollution and Internal Migration in the United States
affiliations: University of Lucerne, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research (CEEPR), University of Basel and University of Lucerne

detail.title: Air Pollution and Internal Migration in the United States
detail.abstract:
We estimate the effect of PM2.5 pollution on migration between commuting zones in the United States from 2005-2019. To account for the correlation between origin and destination commuting zones’ pollution levels and potential endogeneity, we estimate a dyadic migration model and isolate permanent changes in origin and destination pollution emanating from distant coal-fired power plants. Annual panel and long-difference estimates indicate that air pollution plays a key role in relocation decisions. For the typical commuting zone, an isolated average 2005-2019 PM2.5 concentration decrease of 3.85 μg/m3 would avert out-migration and increase in-migration, totaling 2 percent of the population annually.

title: Sent Away: Displacement, Neighborhoods, and Children’s Outcomes under Slum Clearance Policies
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison and Reed College

detail.title: Sent Away: Displacement, Neighborhoods, and Children’s Outcomes under Slum Clearance Policies
detail.abstract:
We examine the difference between two policies that target urban slums, relocation versus redevelopment on-site, on children’s future outcomes. We use evidence from a slum clearance program in Chile between 1979 and 1984, where two-thirds of slum-dwelling families were relocated to housing projects on the city’s periphery, and one-third received housing through on-site redevelopment at their original locations. We find that 40 years post-policy, displaced children receive 0.62 fewer years of schooling, earn 10.2% less, experience higher labor informality, and live in higher poverty areas compared to non-displaced children. Relocation to lower-opportunity areas and disruption of social networks explain the negative displacement effects.

title: Characterizing the File Drawer: Evidence from a Meta-Analysis of Parent-Interventions Around the World
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin and University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Characterizing the File Drawer: Evidence from a Meta-Analysis of Parent-Interventions Around the World
detail.abstract: We conduct a meta-analysis of 82 randomized controlled trials across more than 20 countries to estimate the effects of low-cost, remote parental engagement interventions delivered through text messages, phone calls, and apps. We estimate a joint likelihood function that incorporates both written studies and unwritten studies identified through trial registries, funder records, research labs, evidence clearinghouses, and other sources. By also recording sample sizes for unwritten studies, the model estimates the distribution of standard errors, identifies write-up probabilities conditional on significance, and characterizes the file drawer by estimating effect distributions for written and unwritten studies. Bias-corrected effects are 0.05 SD for test scores, 0.07 SD for grades, 0.05 SD for attendance, and 0.03 SD for enrollment. In the best-identified domain, test scores, statistically insignificant results are still written up at high rates. We also find that larger studies tend to estimate smaller latent effects, which could indicate that true effects are correlated with study precision, violating a common meta-analysis assumption. In smaller-sample domains, our approach helps identify selection probabilities by anchoring the absolute write-up rates. Finally, we estimate the value of additional RCTs to inform adoption decisions. Any single study estimate is unlikely to dissuade adoption because parent interventions have high marginal value of public funds. Instead, future research is most valuable when it can explain heterogeneity across settings.

title: Climate Change in the Classroom
affiliations: Georgia State University,  and

detail.title: Climate Change in the Classroom
detail.abstract: Knowledge gaps and biased beliefs concerning both climate change and climate policy represent major obstacles to the decarbonization process. Climate education may offer a scalable solution to address such obstacles. In the context of a national reform of the school curriculum in Italy, we implemented a nationwide field experiment, training thousands of secondary school teachers across thousands of schools using a staggered design. Our intervention, a comprehensive course on climate change and climate policy, goes beyond the light-touch interventions typical in the literature. Using extensive survey data, we examine how training affects teachers' knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, behaviors, and policy preferences and, in turn, those of students. Our study highlights important initial knowledge gaps and biased beliefs about climate change among teachers and students, and provides evidence that climate education can address them at scale. Following our intervention, teachers and students also reconsider their support for climate policies.

title: The Gender of Opportunity: How Gendered Job Titles Affect Job Seeker Attraction
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Institute of Management, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and

detail.title: The Gender of Opportunity: How Gendered Job Titles Affect Job Seeker Attraction
detail.abstract: Recruitment signals shape applicant pools. Across three studies, we examine whether genderfair (vs. generic masculine) German job titles affect application behavior and job seekers' beliefs about organizational culture. In a large-scale pre-registered field experiment, gender-fair titles increase female applications and clicks in Business & Management where priors are flexible by about 50 %. There is no average effect in categories with less flexible priors consistent with a signaling model. Eye-tracking evidence shows effects reflect belief updating, not visual salience, and an online study supports gender-fair language as a credible equality signal. We find no male backlash.

title: One Great Pool or Many? Measuring Global Oil Market Integration Using a Dynamic Time Warping-Hierarchical Cluster Approach
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU) - International Business School Suzhou and

detail.title: One Great Pool or Many? Measuring Global Oil Market Integration Using a Dynamic Time Warping-Hierarchical Cluster Approach
detail.abstract: This paper measures global crude oil market integration using dynamic time warping combined with hierarchical cluster analysis. Using ten global crude oil prices (2000-2026), we find that markets cluster primarily by geography: West African, Middle Eastern, and U.S. markets each form distinct regional clusters: Brent occupies an intermediate position. A rolling window analysis reveals an increase in integration over time, but a remarkably stable regional structure. A subsample analysis shows that during the turbulent 2020-2024 period, integration increases but the clear geographical pattern weakens. Validation metrics such as silhouette width and cophenetic correlation confirm robust clustering across all periods.

title: Social Anxiety and Evaluative Interviews
affiliations: University of Chicago, Carnegie Mellon University and Hertie School

detail.title: Social Anxiety and Evaluative Interviews
detail.abstract: Evaluative social interactions are pervasive in labor markets. Inequality in these settings can arise not only from how individuals are treated or perform when evaluated, but from whether they enter evaluation at all. We study these margins in the context of social anxiety. In a controlled online experiment (N = 922), applicants decide whether to complete a live video interview that determines a monetary hiring bonus. We find that inequities associated with social anxiety are concentrated in participation rather than in performance or treatment. Socially anxious applicants are substantially less willing to interview, hold more pessimistic beliefs about being hired, and correctly anticipate a worse experience. Yet they perform no worse and are evaluated no differently. Interview experience does not attenuate the relative pessimism of socially anxious individuals, a pattern that is inconsistent with Bayesian updating under comparable signals. We use our rich audio-visual data and open-ended reflection texts to show that, instead, socially anxious applicants interpret similar interactions more negatively. We then provide evidence on organizational interventions aimed at closing social anxiety gaps. Finally, we show that social anxiety explains a meaningful share of inequalities commonly attributed to gender and social skill differences and is associated with significant earnings gaps in national data.

title: Risk Perceptions and Protective Behaviors at the Onset and Outset of the COVID-19 Pandemic
affiliations: London School of Economics, NHS England, University of South Carolina and Catholic University of Rome

detail.title: Risk Perceptions and Protective Behaviors at the Onset and Outset of the COVID-19 Pandemic
detail.abstract: We study the formation of risk perceptions— subjective probability beliefs— of three adverse events—COVID-19 contagion, influenza contagion, and food poisoning—at the onset and outset of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, using survey data. We show that perceived risk levels for COVID-19 are similar to those for influenza but are not significantly influenced by proximity to infection and are shaped instead by an individual's gender, education, and employment status. Using an instrumental variable strategy, we assess whether these perceptions influence a number of protective behaviors. Although risk perceptions are associated with various protective behaviors, we only find a causal impact in increasing the likelihood of phone or online medical consultations by only about a percentage point

title: Heterogeneity in Consumers' Economic Expectations Across Euro Area Countries
affiliations: Leibniz University Hannover, , Leibniz  Universität Hannover and Bank of Finland - Research

detail.title: Heterogeneity in Consumers' Economic Expectations Across Euro Area Countries
detail.abstract: This paper examines cross-country differences in consumer expectations about macroeconomic outcomes and mortgage borrowing conditions within a monetary union. Using harmonized microdata from the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey for eleven euro area countries, we document significant national disparities. By sequentially adding a rich set of consumer- and country-specific macro controls to pooled regressions with country fixed effects, we find that these factors account for much, but not all, of the cross-country heterogeneity in expectations. These remaining differences likely reflect unobserved country-specific factors, highlighting the need for country-tailored monetary policy communication to effectively stabilize consumer expectations.

title: Kindergarten and Career Comebacks for Mothers: Is Access to Public School Enough?
affiliations: Brigham Young University and Brigham Young University

detail.title: Kindergarten and Career Comebacks for Mothers: Is Access to Public School Enough?
detail.abstract: Over the last 70 years, there has been a dramatic increase in female labor supply. However, gender gaps in employment trajectories remain, in part because the role of childrearing has largely fallen upon women. Providing more publicly funded childcare could relax these constraints, which may have ramifications for mothers' labor supply decisions over time. We examine the dynamic effects of gaining childcare access earlier on mothers' labor supply. Using a regression discontinuity in kindergarten eligibility cutoffs for nearly 7.5 million U.S. mothers, we estimate how gaining access to childcare, through public school, one year earlier affects maternal employment over time. Enrolling a child in school one year earlier increases annual maternal employment by 2.2 percentage points, and the effect persists for two years, even though children born after the eligibility cutoff gain similar access the next year. However, employment effects eventually fade out, highlighting the limited role publicly-provided childcare plays in closing long-term gender gaps. We show that mothers take on additional family management responsibilities after childbirth, and these responsibilities are not relaxed by gaining childcare access. Moving childcare access earlier will not necessarily close gender gaps in employment as mothers still face these additional constraints.

title: How (Not) to Ask About Undeclared Work: Estimating Prevalence and Patterns Using a Survey Experimental Approach
affiliations: Walter Eucken Institute and Walter Eucken Institute

detail.title: How (Not) to Ask About Undeclared Work: Estimating Prevalence and Patterns Using a Survey Experimental Approach
detail.abstract: Reliable estimates of undeclared work in Germany are scarce, yet they matter for tax and social security policy. Using two large-scale surveys of the German general population and recipients of transfer benefits particularly, we elicit the prevalence of the supply and demand of undeclared work via direct questions, a crosswise model and a list experiment. In line with economic theory, opportunity and incentives shape the decision to work undeclared. The self- and marginally employed as well as transfer recipients who face high effective marginal tax rates are particularly likely to work undeclared. The potential, especially for envelope wages, is substantial. Methodologically, the crosswise model consistently yields higher prevalence estimates for both supply and demand than direct questioning. We discuss assumptions and challenges when implementing list experiments.

title: Household Behavior Below the Zero Lower Bound
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics, University of Oxford - Oxford University Centre for Business Taxation, ,  and University of Cologne

detail.title: Household Behavior Below the Zero Lower Bound
detail.abstract: How do households respond when deposit rates drop below zero? Using administrative micro data and exploiting cross-bank variation in interest rate policies, we study a major episode of negative deposit rates in Denmark affecting two thirds of household deposits. We find that households strongly reduced deposit balances when exposed to negative deposit rates, allocating funds to stock portfolios and consumption. In a large-scale survey, we document important roles for loss aversion, perceived unfairness, intertemporal substitution and return considerations in driving these responses. Our findings suggest that monetary policy can have strong consumption effects in negative territory.

title: Long Memory in Latin American Sovereign Risk: Daily Evidence on the EMBI
affiliations: University of Navarra - Department of Economics, Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance and

detail.title: Long Memory in Latin American Sovereign Risk: Daily Evidence on the EMBI
detail.abstract: This paper analyses the long-memory properties of sovereign bond spreads in 17 Latin American countries as well as two regional aggregates using daily EMBI (Emerging Markets Bond Index) data from April 2013 to January 2026 (3,163 observations per series). Parametric methods show that all 19 series are characterized by fractional integration with estimated orders ranging from 0.97 (Uruguay) to 1.22 (Honduras) for the log-transformed spreads. Nine series have confidence bounds above unity, indicating that shocks have permanent effects; under autocorrelated errors (as in the Bloomfield model), Uruguay is the only country whose series exhibits mean reversion (as the confidence bands for the fractional parameter are below unity). The results are robust to making different assumptions about the error terms (white noise or autocorrelation) and to allowing for non-linear deterministic trends.

title: Defaulting Investors Toward Sustainability: A Field Experiment
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology, Aarhus University and

detail.title: Defaulting Investors Toward Sustainability: A Field Experiment
detail.abstract: We provide the first field experimental evidence on how default options influence sustainable investment choices. Using a real-world investment setting that avoids experimenter demand effects and enables realistic estimates of effect sizes, we find that setting a sustainable investment as the default increases adoption from 23% to 36% relative to a conventional default. The effect is stable over time, consistent across investor subgroups, and persists in the long run. A follow-up survey shows that both sustainable and conventional investors expect their chosen portfolios to outperform, yet few are willing to sacrifice meaningful returns for sustainability. Overall, while sustainability preferences matter, investors' decisions remain primarily driven by financial return considerations under realistic market conditions.

title: Blockchains and Strategic Secondary Censorship
affiliations: and VU University Amsterdam

detail.title: Blockchains and Strategic Secondary Censorship
detail.abstract: Censorship resistance is widely viewed as a core attribute of distributed ledgers. Censorship resistance refers to the inability to selectively exclude technically valid but undesirable transactions from the blockchain. We examine blockchain censorship in a game-theoretic framework that allows for both primary and secondary censorship. The analysis identifies scenarios in which both inclusion and censorship equilibria can arise. Once an equilibrium with strategic secondary censorship is implemented, it may be hard to revert to inclusion: Censorship equilibria are perfectly coalition-proof if the negative impact of an undesirable transaction on block producers is sufficiently large. These results suggest an expanding role for research into methods shaping censorship resistance at the technical layer.

title: Monotonic Polynomial GARCH Models for Conditional Higher Moments
affiliations: and University of Leipzig

detail.title: Monotonic Polynomial GARCH Models for Conditional Higher Moments
detail.abstract: Density expansions such as the Gram-Charlier (GC) expansion allow for the modeling of time-varying higher moments. However, they can suffer from spurious multimodality, negative densities, and asymptotically light tails if truncated. This paper introduces monotonic polynomial generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models. They generate conditional skewness and kurtosis via a monotonic polynomial transformation of innovations. By construction, this approach guarantees a valid, unimodal probability density without requiring truncation. It naturally accommodates heavy Weibull-type tails. We provide a theoretical framework proving strict stationarity and ergodicity. In empirical applications to financial returns, the proposed estimator outperforms both GC-based and score-driven benchmarks in out-of-sample density forecasting. It demonstrates superior structural stability and robustness against overfitting.

title: The 1992 Democratic Party Platform: A Note
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The 1992 Democratic Party Platform: A Note
detail.abstract: In this note the author analyzes the portion of the Democratic Party Platform of 1992 devoted to economic and socioeconomic questions for its implications regarding both political-economic ideology and practical policymaking. On its basis the author concludes that in spite of considerable vagueness and even obfuscation, a certain amount of self-contradiction, and even specific promises of more progressive policy than his predecessors (which the administration of Bill Clinton was to break in office), a close reading of the note showed that where its fundamental premises were concerned it promised only conservative, and more specifically neoliberal, economic policymaking.

title: Internal Capital Markets and Production Disruptions *
affiliations: , University of Pittsburgh, Wayne State University - Mike Ilitch School of Business and

detail.title: Internal Capital Markets and Production Disruptions *
detail.abstract: We examine how negative cash flow shocks arising from production disruptions in one or more operating segments of a firm affect capital investment in other nondisrupted segments of the same firm. Relative to prior studies, our empirical design enables broader tests for the presence of both a causal investment-cash flow relation and the operation of active internal capital markets that reallocate scarce resources within multisegment firms. We find that a $1 decrease in cash flow at a disrupted segment is associated with a 16.2-cent reduction in investment at nondisrupted segments whose investment opportunities appear unaffected by the disruption. This investment-cash flow relation is concentrated among firms we expect to be more financially constrained, consistent with the identified relation reflecting in part a financial constraints channel. Additionally, the relation we identify is especially pronounced among nondisrupted segments that are subsidized by other parts of the firm or that exhibit relatively weak investment opportunities.

title: Price Rigidity and the Limits of Within Estimators for SKU-Level Demand Elasticity: An Empirical Bayes Approach Using Between-Estimators in Automotive Spare Parts Markets

detail.title: Price Rigidity and the Limits of Within Estimators for SKU-Level Demand Elasticity: An Empirical Bayes Approach Using Between-Estimators in Automotive Spare Parts Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest. The empirical analysis uses proprietary data from two automotive aftermarket firms in Chile. The firms did not influence the research design, analysis, or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses anonymized commercial transaction data. No human subjects, patients, or personal data were involved. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted at Vehmax AI with support from the Chilean Economic Development Agency (CORFO) under the Crea y Valida instrument, and in partial fulfillment of the requirements for a Master's degree in Artificial Intelligence at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Chile.

detail.abstract: Estimating price elasticity at the individual product (SKU) level is central to pricing optimization in distribution and retail markets. The standard within-group panel estimator  which exploits temporal price variation within each product  fails systematically when prices are rigid, a pervasive condition in automotive spare parts markets where demand is need-based rather than discretionary, catalogs span thousands of heterogeneous SKUs, and data infrastructure is structurally fragmented. We document this failure empirically across two independent market structures operating in the Chilean automotive aftermarket: an Independent Multi-Brand Distributor (imbd) with 3,576 SKU-pairs across 24 months, and an Authorized Chevrolet Dealership (acd) with 17,049 unique SKUs across 54 months. In both settings, 2455% of within estimates carry the wrong sign, consistent with reverse causality from demand-driven pricing, and LASSO regularization collapses an additional 45% of estimates to zero, signaling insucient temporal price variation for identication. We propose an alternative framework that combines cross-sectional between-estimators  which exploit cross-sectional variation in relative prices, competitive positioning, and market potential across products, rather than temporal price variation within products over time  with an Empirical Bayes shrinkage procedure that anchors individual SKU elasticities to hierarchical category-level priors. The between-estimator yields three complementary elasticity estimates. For the imbd, a consolidado specication maximizing sample coverage produces βˆ = −0.617 (p < 0.001, N = 66), consistent with the meta-analytic benchmark of [−0.5, −1.5] for durable goods (Bijmolt et al., 2005). The paired ORI/ALT specication yields βˆ = −0.238 (p < 0.001, N = 1,619)  an attenuated global estimate reecting the heterogeneous mix of product categories with structurally distinct demand elasticities; category-level disaggregation within the imbd conrms the benchmark positioning, with Front Suspension (βˆ = −0.801), Engine Distribution (βˆ = −0.551), Gaskets & Seals (βˆ = −0.538), and Rear Suspension (βˆ = −0.514) all within [−0.5, −1.5]; Brakes (βˆ = −0.449, p = 0.014) is signicant but marginally below the lower bound. For the acd, the between-estimator independently produces βˆ = −0.502 (p = 0.012, N = 170), also consistent with the meta-analytic range. The shrinkage estimator activates for 3.2% of imbd SKUs and 69% of acd active SKUs, reecting the dierential availability of within-product temporal signal. A complementary demand forecasting layer  evaluated using walk-forward validation across six model classes including gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) and a multi-layer perceptron  achieves MAPE of 34.0% for the imbd (LightGBM; 81% reduction relative to the naive baseline) and 16.6% for the acd (MLP; 27% reduction), forming the operational layer of a three-component pricing pipeline. We further document structural dierences in competitive positioning between market channels  systematic underpricing in the distributor channel (median RelPrice = 0.76) versus systematic overpricing in the dealership channel (median RelPrice = 1.29)  and discuss implications for a fully specied aftermarket pricing model incorporating vehicle age, vehicle value segment, and a three-tier quality taxonomy of Original (ori), OEM-Aftermarket (oem-am), and Generic Alternative (alt) parts.

title: Constraint-Based Computational Frameworks for Cross-Border Family Law Dispute Resolution: Toward an AI-Assisted Legal Innovation Model

detail.title: Constraint-Based Computational Frameworks for Cross-Border Family Law Dispute Resolution: Toward an AI-Assisted Legal Innovation Model

publicationDetails.detailsText: Law, Innovation and Technology, Vol. 19, No. 2, Autumn 2027 (Taylor & Francis)

detail.abstract: Cross-border family law disputes expose a structural gap in existing legal technology: the inability to reconcile heterogeneous mandatory rules from multiple jurisdictions in a principled, enforceable and transparent manner. This paper proposes a constraint-based computational framework that formalises jurisdiction-specific legal rules as machinereadable vectors, distinguishing between hard constraints that encode non-derogable obligations and soft constraints that represent discretionary policy preferences. Dispute outcomes are modelled as optimised outcome vectors that satisfy all hard constraints while balancing competing objectives including fairness and proportionality. The framework is built around three core principles, namely explainability, auditability and jurisdictional neutrality, and is designed to operate within emerging regulatory regimes for high-risk AI in the administration of justice. By reframing cross-border family disputes as structured decision problems, it advances the use of artificial intelligence in family law beyond document automation towards principled, jurisdiction-aware decision support with concrete implications for access to justice and cross-border legal governance.

title: Accounting-Based Distress Prediction Under Target Leakage: A Three-Estimand Framework with Evidence from Colombian Private Firms

detail.title: Accounting-Based Distress Prediction Under Target Leakage: A Three-Estimand Framework with Evidence from Colombian Private Firms

detail.abstract: Accounting-based distress prediction is methodologically delicate when predictors and outcomes share accounting variables: the resulting target leakage inflates apparent in-sample performance and obscures the genuine predictive content of the model. We propose a three-estimand framework - contemporaneous classification, forward-looking prediction, and transition prediction - that quantifies and partially neutralizes this dependence. Using 192,458 firm-year observations from the Colombian regulator Supersociedades for 2018-2024, we estimate a parsimonious two-ratio logit combining operating profitability (EBIT/Total Assets) and capitalization (Equity/Total Assets) on 37,653 unique formal corporates. The three estimands yield AUCs of 0.955 (contemporaneous, with definitional leakage), 0.826 (forward-looking, 95% CI [0.819, 0.829]) and 0.654 (transition, 95% CI [0.643, 0.661]); the 13-30 percentage-point gap quantifies the magnitude of the leakage component. Walk-forward out-of-time validation across 2019-2023 yields AUCs of 0.78-0.85, including the COVID-19 year. On a separate historical Colombian panel where all Altman (1968, 1995) inputs are available, the local logit improves AUC by 15-19 percentage points over correctly-oriented Altman benchmarks (paired-bootstrap p < 0.005). An external cross-reference against 3,575 legal insolvency events from the Supersociedades public registry (2022-2025) - events not used for estimation - finds that 80.5% of subsequent judicial liquidations had predicted PD >= 10% one year before opening; this is asymmetric evidence conditional on observed events and does not quantify false positives across the population. The framework is the primary contribution; the Colombian estimates illustrate its application. The score is not recommended for entities in CIIU divisions K64 and K66, where balance-sheet structures saturate the capitalization ratio.

title: The Family Long Cycle Hypothesis: Intergenerational Liquidity Lock-in, the Uncertainty Multiplier, and China's Fertility Dilemma

detail.title: The Family Long Cycle Hypothesis: Intergenerational Liquidity Lock-in, the Uncertainty Multiplier, and China's Fertility Dilemma
detail.abstract: Why have pro-natal subsidies persistently failed in China? Why do consumption and fertility contract across households even when net worth remains intact? This paper proposes the Family Long Cycle Hypothesis (FLCH), which extends the decision unit of the life-cycle hypothesis from the individual to the intergenerational family network and replaces the single lifetime resource constraint with a dual constraint of "total resources plus liquidity structure." The core mechanism is that intergenerational transfers for home purchases ("blood transfusion") mobilize the entire network's liquidity; the purchase event instantly transforms the balance sheet-total net worth unchanged, yet the liquidity ratio collapses and continues to be squeezed by mortgage payments. Under borrowing constraints, depleted liquidity endogenously amplifies effective risk aversion; combined with income uncertainty, it creates a multiplier effect that drives up the risk premium on all irreversible long-commitment decisions. Fertility, the longest commitment (18-25 years), is the first to be pushed into a corner solution: when the liquidity ratio falls below a critical threshold, the fertility risk premium diverges, and any finite cost subsidy cannot reverse the decision. This explains the systematic failure of consumption-side subsidies: they target direct costs while the binding constraint lies in the risk premium.

title: The Decentralization of Harmless Public-Good Provision

detail.title: The Decentralization of Harmless Public-Good Provision
detail.abstract:
This paper studies decentralized provision of harmless public goods under private information. In such environments, provision harms no one, yet privately informed beneficiaries must coordinate contributions to cover the cost. I identify a pivotal-failure-aversion rationale: a self-interested agent avoids actions that may cause the false failure of a provision opportunity she values when contribution remains within her valuation.

I develop a residual-cost mechanism that supports efficient provision under this rationale through a sequence of individual feasibility questions rather than valuation reports or assigned cost shares. The resulting decentralized questionnaire preserves agents' monetary property rights, keeps feasible provision opportunities from being lost, and implements efficient provision in finite time whenever surplus is strictly positive.

title: Equity Spillover Reconfiguration: Evidence from the United States and Asia-Pacific Markets, 1990-2026

detail.title: Equity Spillover Reconfiguration: Evidence from the United States and Asia-Pacific Markets, 1990-2026
detail.abstract: This paper examines long-run changes in cross-border equity return spillovers among the United States, Taiwan, South Korea, and Hong Kong from January 1990 to April 2026 using monthly MSCI equity index returns. We estimate a four-variable VAR model and apply the order-invariant Diebold-Yilmaz (2012) generalized connectedness framework across five regime windows (Pre-AFC, AFC-Pre-GFC, GFC-Pre-COVID, Post-COVID Transition, and the 2022-2026 Semiconductor Concentration window) to trace how directional spillover roles evolve over 1990-2026. The Total Connectedness Index rises from 21.77% in the Pre-AFC period to 62.87% in the GFC-Pre-COVID period and remains elevated at 53.13% during the 2022-2026 window. Directional measures show a marked reconfiguration: Hong Kong shifts from a dominant net transmitter in the early regimes (+2.59; +5.22) to the deepest net receiver in the 2022-2026 period (-15.64), while Taiwan becomes the strongest net transmitter (+13.30) and South Korea also moves toward a transmitter position. These results are consistent with a semiconductor-centered reorganization of Asia-Pacific spillover topology. The evidence identifies directional connectedness in forecast error variance rather than structural causality; semiconductor concentration is interpreted as an industry-regime context for understanding the observed spillover reconfiguration.
