detail.abstract:
This paper provides an exploratory index-based analysis of whether Hong Kong’s post-1997 economic trajectory can be interpreted as exhibiting regime-like K-shaped characteristics rather than merely episodic K-shaped recoveries following individual crises. Focusing on the period 1997–2025, the study examines how financialisation, housing commodification, asset-market cycles, and labour-market precarity have interacted across successive shocks, including the Asian Financial Crisis, SARS, the Global Financial Crisis, the 2019 social unrest period, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The paper constructs two original composite measures — the Hong Kong K-Shaped Economy Pressure Index (HK-KSEPI) and the Youth Precarity Index (YPI) — using annual macroeconomic, labour-market, housing, and retail data. The analysis is explicitly exploratory and diagnostic: the indices are used to describe structural patterns of divergence rather than to establish causal effects.

The empirical strategy combines descriptive phase analysis, correlation analysis, ordinary least squares regressions with Newey-West heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent standard errors, unit-root diagnostics, variance inflation factor checks, and crisis-year exclusion tests. Because several variables are non-stationary and the sample consists of only 29 annual observations, all regression results are interpreted as associational rather than causal. The paper also acknowledges the partial circularity involved in regressing composite indices on their own components; accordingly, the HK-KSEPI regressions are treated as component-sensitivity diagnostics, while the YPI is externally compared with the pre-tax Gini coefficient as a preliminary consistency check.

The results suggest that Hong Kong’s post-1997 economy displays recurrent K-shaped patterns in which asset-market recoveries are often more rapid than improvements in labour-market and affordability conditions. HSI return and real wage growth are the strongest correlates of annual HK-KSEPI variation, while the YPI is positively associated with the pre-tax Gini coefficient, providing limited external consistency evidence that youth precarity is linked to broader inequality dynamics. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the use of aggregate annual data, preliminary or estimated observations for 2024–2025, possible interpolation in some inequality measures, and the limited scope for causal identification. The paper contributes conceptually by proposing the notion of a “K-shaped economic regime” and methodologically by developing exploratory indices that may be adapted for comparative studies of financialised global cities.

title: Financial Inclusion and Small Business Innovation: Evidence from China's Specialized Bank Branches
affiliations: Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, South China University of Technology and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Financial Inclusion and Small Business Innovation: Evidence from China's Specialized Bank Branches
detail.abstract: This paper examines how financial inclusion impacts small business innovation by exploiting China’s staggered rollout of Specialized Bank Branches (SBBs) dedicated to micro and small enterprises (MSEs). Using this quasi-natural experiment, we find that SBB presence significantly increases MSE patent applications. This effect operates through three channels: improving credit access, fostering local technology-driven entrepreneurship, and attracting external venture capital and M&A investments. The positive effect is most pronounced for firms with low asset tangibility, industries with high start-up capital barriers, and regions with less bank competition, particularly in central and western China. Furthermore, SBBs enhance patent quality and stimulate local GDP growth. Our findings demonstrate that government-promoted, proximity-based specialized banking effectively alleviates financing constraints and cultivates a dynamic innovation ecosystem.

title: Birds of a Feather Flock Together: the Coupling of Innovative Banks and Innovative Firms
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Birds of a Feather Flock Together: the Coupling of Innovative Banks and Innovative Firms
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of Fintech innovation in borrower monitoring on banks’ ability to extend credit to Italian firms, with a particular focus on small innovative firms. We combine Credit Register data on outstanding bank–firm loans in Italy with bank-level information on Fintech investments from the Bank of Italy’s Regional Bank Lending Survey and the classification of innovative young firms under the Italian Start-up Act. We find that banks investing in Fintech monitoring technologies extend more credit and charge lower interest rates to innovative firms. In addition, lending relationships with Fintech-monitoring banks are less likely to be terminated. Finally, we find no evidence that Fintech monitoring increases the probability that loans to innovative firms become non-performing. Overall, our findings suggest that Fintech monitoring technologies mitigate information asymmetries, allowing banks to expand lending to innovative firms without increasing credit risk.

title: Biodiversity Risks and Global Lending
affiliations: University of Southampton, University of Milan - Department of Economics, Management and Quantitative Methods (DEMM), University of Florence, University of Science and Technology Beijing and University of Southampton

detail.title: Biodiversity Risks and Global Lending
detail.abstract: The rapid and alarming decline of biodiversity poses significant risks to businesses and financial institutions that rely on natural resources derived from plants, animals, and microorganisms. Using an international sample of syndicated loans, we find that firms with greater biodiversity impact and dependency face higher interest rate spreads on bank loans. We examine whether eternal stakeholder pressure and the institutional environment influence how lenders price firms’ biodiversity risks. Biodiversity dependency risk is priced more strongly in countries with stronger environmental institutions and governance quality. We also show that banks adhering to sustainability frameworks such as the Equator Principles apply stricter loan pricing to biodiversity-exposed firms, while only concrete biodiversity mitigation actions by borrowers partially reduce the associated loan spreads. Our results are robust to an instrumental variable approach, alternative measures of biodiversity risk and controlling for firm-level climate risk exposure and Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance.

title: Maturity Mismatch and Bank Systemic Risk During Monetary Tightening
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Macquarie University

detail.title: Maturity Mismatch and Bank Systemic Risk During Monetary Tightening
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the systemic consequences of maturity mismatch during monetary tightening reflect individual bank fragility or shared exposure to interest-rate risk. Using U.S.-listed banks from 2020 to 2023 and the Federal Reserve’s 2022 tightening cycle in a difference-in-differences framework, we find that banks with greater pre-existing maturity mismatches experience larger increases in systemic risk following the tightening cycle. Decomposing systemic risk into tail risk and systemic linkage, we show that the increase is mainly associated with stronger systemic linkage rather than higher individual tail risk. The effect is weaker among banks with stronger liquidity, higher capital, and more stable deposit funding. We also find that banks expand maturity mismatches during accommodative periods, which is associated with greater risk-taking and, subsequently, higher systemic vulnerability during tightening. Overall, the evidence suggests that maturity mismatch contributes to systemic vulnerability primarily through correlated exposure to common interest-rate shocks.

title: Shifting IPO Syndicate Structure and Loss of Non-Manager Underwriters
affiliations: Auburn University Montgomery and University of North Alabama

detail.title: Shifting IPO Syndicate Structure and Loss of Non-Manager Underwriters
detail.abstract: This study investigates the structural evolution of U.S. IPO syndicates, focusing on the disappearance of non-manager underwriters and the rise of multiple bookrunners. Using 2,666 IPOs from 1998–2015, we apply instrumental variables and robustness checks to establish a causal link between multiple bookrunners and syndicate contraction. Our findings show that adopting multiple bookrunners significantly reduces the number of non-manager underwriters, often eliminating them entirely. We further examine the effects of syndicate structure on share allocation, offer price revisions, initial returns, and underwriting fees. Leaner syndicates are associated with more concentrated allocations and improved pricing efficiency, but have no meaningful impact on gross spreads or first-day returns. These results suggest that syndicate consolidation has not increased issuance costs and may benefit issuers through more accurate pricing. The study offers new insights into underwriter incentives and IPO market dynamics, with implications for issuers, underwriters, and regulators.

title: When Do Banks Reduce ESG Disagreement? Evidence from Environmentally Sensitive Industries
affiliations: Lingnan University, Lingnan University, Lingnan University and Lingnan University

detail.title: When Do Banks Reduce ESG Disagreement? Evidence from Environmentally Sensitive Industries
detail.abstract: We examine whether bank sustainability governance reduces disagreement among third-party ESG raters by converting soft environmental signals into harder information. Using borrower exposure to Equator Principles (EP) lead arrangers, which standardize environmental due diligence, we find that EP exposure lowers environmental-pillar disagreement only for environmentally sensitive borrowers, with null effects for clean-industry firms. The full-sample average effect is also null, consistent with attenuation from pooling active and inactive borrowers. Cross-sector results persist across robustness tests. Disclosure evidence from S&P shows EP exposure increases external CSR audits and quantified emission-reduction targets in sensitive sectors only. Despite small sample sizes, these findings suggest bank sustainability governance generates information externalities beyond loan contracts by improving environmental auditability.

title: Investor Valuation, Taxation, and Time Varying Expected Returns
affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Business and Management Science and NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Business and Management Science

detail.title: Investor Valuation, Taxation, and Time Varying Expected Returns
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the valuation of publicly traded stocks subject to capital income and wealth taxation when expected returns are time-varying. We show that, in an efficient capital market, investor valuation coincides with the market price under a broad class of tax systems, including accrued and realized capital gains taxation. The result holds for arbitrary holding periods provided that tax shields are set equal to the investor's after-tax risk-free rate. The key mechanism is that taxation introduces a deterministic payoff component that can be replicated using traded assets, leaving the pricing of the stochastic return component unaffected.

title: From Coins to Cays: Using Crypto to Channel Funds Offshore
affiliations: Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt and Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt - Ingolstadt School of Management

detail.title: From Coins to Cays: Using Crypto to Channel Funds Offshore
detail.abstract: We provide evidence that individuals use cryptocurrencies to channel funds into and out of tax havens. Exploiting the Panama Papers (2016) and Paradise Papers (2017) leaks as shocks to offshore detection risk, we compare prices of cryptocurrency–fiat pairs involving Singapore and Hong Kong dollars — the two haven currencies with sufficient trading data — to those involving non-haven currencies on the same exchanges. Prices denominated in haven currencies rise by approximately 10% relative to non-haven currencies following the leaks, consistent with increased demand for crypto originating in tax havens. Effects are concentrated on smaller, less liquid exchanges where arbitrage is constrained, and dissipate within two months, consistent with market efficiency and limits-to-arbitrage theory. These findings suggest cryptocurrencies serve as an alternative channel for capital flows that bypass conventional anti-money-laundering infrastructure.

title: Trust and Non-Bank Financing: Evidence from Chinese Households
affiliations: Beijing Technology and Business University, Singapore Management University - School of Social Sciences and Nanjing Audit University

detail.title: Trust and Non-Bank Financing: Evidence from Chinese Households
detail.abstract: This study investigates the interplay between generalized trust, social relations, and financing choices among Chinese households, utilizing biennial data from the China Family Panel Studies (2014–2022). Our findings reveal that households with lower generalized trust invest more in insular social networks, leading to increased reliance on informal loans from family, friends, or private lenders. We extend Guiso et al. (2004) by incorporating social relations as a key mechanism, showing that low-trust households incur significant implicit costs—both monetary, through social investments like gift-giving, and psychological, evidenced by reduced happiness and increased smoking. Additionally, while trust initially appears linked to formal financial participation, this association di- minishes when controlling for individual fixed effects, suggesting that unobserved time-invariant traits—particularly financial literacy—drive this correlation rather than trust itself. Our findings highlight the dual role of social trust in shaping informal credit access while questioning its independent causal impact on formal financial markets.

title: Clouded Minds: Air Pollution and Student Cognitive Performance
affiliations: University of Milan - Department of Economics, Management and Quantitative Methods (DEMM),  and

detail.title: Clouded Minds: Air Pollution and Student Cognitive Performance
detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of air pollution on primary school students' cognitive performance in Italy, exploiting daily within-municipality variation in pollution across exam dates. Using INVALSI administrative data on the universe of students over ten cohorts and a specification with individual fixed effects, we find that a 10 μg/m³ increase in PM2.5 reduces test scores by 4.4% of a standard deviation. Effects are concentrated in reasoning-intensive items, with no significant effect on knowledge-based items, are stronger for lower-achieving and emotionally vulnerable students, and are substantially mitigated by school mechanical ventilation and air-conditioning systems. These results highlight the cognitive costs of short-term pollution exposure and the potential of targeted infrastructure investments to reduce environmental inequality in education.

title: The Internal Memory Network of the Economy
affiliations: KU Leuven

detail.title: The Internal Memory Network of the Economy
detail.abstract: This paper develops a new theoretical framework that changes the primitive object of persistence analysis from economic variables and frictions to the internal propagation architecture of the economy. Memory is a feature of the economy that allows to retain the imprint of past disturbances even after the original cause has disappeared. It is the economy’s capacity to retain the impact of past events through its internal organization. This paper advances a framework in which memory is an architectural property of economic systems, not a property of particular variables, frictions, or microeconomic mechanisms. The economy is treated as a black-box dynamical system and macroeconomic persistence is traced to internal macro architecture. This perspective unifies DSGE models or VARs and also problematic heterogeneous-agent environments within a single conceptual language. Rather than deriving persistence from micro heterogeneity and aggregation, the framework reverses the logic: internal macroeconomic architecture gives rise to macroeconomic persistence - while at the same time micro structures are fully consistent with the same architecture and its outcomes. We no longer need to know who the agents are in order to know whether the economy remembers. Memory capacity is fully characterized at the level of internal propagation architecture. Moreover, I provide explicit mappings from leading macroeconomic frameworks into the memory architecture. I introduce Macro Duration as the economy’s intrinsic memory horizon. Macro Duration measures how long past events remain economically relevant in principle. It does not describe how slowly any particular variable adjusts; it describes how persistent the economic system itself is. This perspective opens a fundamentally new margin for economic policy. Policy is no longer only about stabilizing flows or correcting local distortions, but about shaping the economy’s internal memory architecture. Financial regulation, market design, industrial policy, and labor- market institutions can be evaluated by how they reconfigure the economy’s capacity to store, amplify, or dissipate history. In this sense, policy becomes, in part, the design of economic memory.

title: Monetary Policy and Inflation Heterogeneity: The Role of Income and Price Elasticities of Demand
affiliations: Bank of Korea - Economic Research Institute, The Bank of Korea and Bank of Korea

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Inflation Heterogeneity: The Role of Income and Price Elasticities of Demand
detail.abstract: This paper examines the distributional effects of monetary policy shocks on inflation heterogeneity using Korean household data. Combining a sign-restricted VAR with local projections, we find that contractionary monetary policy widens inflation inequality: high-income households experience larger price declines than low-income households. To explain this pattern, we develop a theoretical framework based on Stone–Geary preferences that yields two opposing transmission channels — an income elasticity channel that amplifies price declines for luxury goods, and a price elasticity channel that partially offsets them. We show analytically that the income elasticity channel strictly dominates when the two elasticities are proportionally linked, a prediction confirmed by item-level evidence across 66 CPI subcategories. Our findings highlight that the distributional consequences of monetary policy on inflation are country-specific and depend critically on the structure of household demand.

title: Climate Policy and the Cost of Capital in Private Infrastructure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and EDHEC Business School

detail.title: Climate Policy and the Cost of Capital in Private Infrastructure
detail.abstract: How does climate policy affect the valuation and financing conditions of infrastructure assets? This paper examines how climate transition risk influences private infrastructure markets using a global dataset of project-level valuations and realized returns. We analyze how climate policy stringency affects asset values in an illiquid setting where infrastructure investment plays a central role in the energy transition. We find that higher policy stringency is associated with lower valuation multiples, consistent with higher required returns and an increase in the cost of capital for exposed assets. In addition, unexpected increases in policy stringency are associated with negative adjustments in realized returns, indicating that regulatory changes trigger ex post valuation revisions. Overall, the evidence suggests that transition risk is incorporated primarily through valuation levels, with more limited adjustments in realized returns. Importantly, the magnitude of these effects depends on policy credibility These findings highlight the role of policy expectations in shaping infrastructure valuation and financing conditions, with implications for the design of credible climate policy frameworks to support the energy transition.

title: Perception Biases and Residential Electricity Demand under Nonlinear Pricing
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City

detail.title: Perception Biases and Residential Electricity Demand under Nonlinear Pricing
detail.abstract: Under nonlinear pricing, households may hold inaccurate beliefs about both electricity consumption and electricity prices. Such misperceptions can distort consumption decisions, yet existing studies typically infer perceptions indirectly from observed behavior or focus on a single dimension of misperception. As a result, few studies directly measure consumption and price misperceptions, and their relative importance for electricity demand remains unclear. This paper develops a behavioral demand framework that separates consumption and price misperceptions, directly measures both using matched household survey and utility billing data, and evaluates their relative importance for electricity demand.We test the framework using matched survey and administrative billing records from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The results indicate that consumption and price misperceptions have different relationships with electricity demand. While both biases are present, only consumption misperception remains predictive of future electricity demand. A 1% increase in consumption perception bias reduces subsequent electricity usage by roughly 0.3%, whereas the estimated effect of price misperception is weak and statistically unstable. These results are robust to instrumental-variable estimation that addresses price endogeneity under increasing block tariffs.These findings suggest that behavioral distortions under nonlinear pricing arise primarily from persistent errors in tracking electricity consumption rather than misunderstandings of electricity prices. Policies that improve households’ awareness of electricity usage and provide timely consumption feedback may therefore be more effective than efforts focused solely on communicating tariff schedules.

title: Inattention region and consumption response to income windfalls
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Economics

detail.title: Inattention region and consumption response to income windfalls
detail.abstract: Consumers often ignore small changes in their environment but update their expectations when these changes are large enough. I attribute this behavior to adjustment friction in expectations. In the model, consumers incur a fixed cost to adjust cash-on-hand expectations and choose adjustment dates based on noisy signals of expectation error—the difference between actual and expected cash-on-hand. This results in an inattention region where consumers ignore news and continue to act on outdated beliefs if the signal remains within the region boundaries. Evidence from expectation surveys and experimental data supports this departure from Bayesian updating. I explore the implications for the marginal propensity to consume, showing that selective expectation adjustment generates a mass of zero MPCs and a decline in zero responses as windfall size increases. A quantitative version of the model replicates key features of the MPC distribution.

title: The Effects of Diagnostic Expectations in Small Open Economies

detail.title: The Effects of Diagnostic Expectations in Small Open Economies
detail.abstract: In this paper, I explore the implications of incorporating representativeness, in the form of Diagnostic Expectations (DE), into a small open economy model. Using Sequential Monte Carlo methods, I estimate the model on quarterly data for New Zealand and Chile. The results suggest that DE: (i) generate asymmetric volatility amplification, (ii) play a quantitatively larger role in Chile than in New Zealand, and (iii) interact with monetary policy design. The first finding helps reconcile exchange rate puzzles, including excess volatility, disconnection from fundamentals, and the forward premium anomaly. Through a modified uncovered interest parity condition, DE offer an alternative, behaviourally grounded explanation for these violations that differs from other deviations from rationality. The second result suggests that belief distortions are more pronounced in emerging markets, with the diagnosticity parameter approximately twice as large for Chile. The third result shows that central bank responses to nominal exchange rate movements shape both the identification and magnitude of diagnostic effects. The paper further documents that DE reallocate the relative importance of domestic and foreign shocks in historical decompositions, and that the estimation results are robust across alternative Bayesian estimation methods.

title: Consumer Learning and Strategic Entry of Technology Platforms in Emerging Automotive Markets
affiliations: University of South China and University of South China

detail.title: Consumer Learning and Strategic Entry of Technology Platforms in Emerging Automotive Markets
detail.abstract: Abstract: This paper investigates the optimal entry strategies for technology platforms in emerging automotive markets (e.g., new energy vehicles and autonomous driving). In these markets, consumer purchase decisions are influenced by past sales (social learning), technological spillovers evolve endogenously with market output, and multiple platforms and automakers form competing alliances. We develop a game-theoretic model that embeds consumer learning from the start, then successively analyzes no-spillover benchmarks, dynamic spillover evolution, and network stability. Without spillovers, consumer learning alters the thresholds for equilibrium entry structures (, , , ) and alliance stability. Introducing dynamic spillovers (learning-by-doing with depreciation) yields a non-monotonic “wait‑or‑enter” timing window: low initial spillovers favor delaying the alliance to build market experience, intermediate levels make immediate alliance optimal, and high levels render alliance never optimal. In a two-platform, two-automaker network, stable exclusive alliances exist only at intermediate network densities (a “Goldilocks” region), explaining why single‑alliance configurations are common. Extensions to the infinite-horizon setting, asymmetric networks, and logit demand confirm the robustness of these findings. We provide closed-form thresholds and actionable guidance to platforms, automakers, and policymakers for the intelligent transformation of mobility.

title: Regulatory Simplification and Climate Accountability: The Legal and Litigation Risks of Eliminating Article 22 CS3D

detail.title: Regulatory Simplification and Climate Accountability: The Legal and Litigation Risks of Eliminating Article 22 CS3D

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Genoa EUSFiL Law Research Working Paper Series No. 4/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Genoa EUSFiL Law Research Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
On February 26, 2025, as part of its ambition to deliver a “simplification revolution” aimed at creating a clear, streamlined regulatory framework and reducing administrative burdens to the benefit of competitiveness, the European Commission proposed a number of amendments to the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D), which had only recently entered into force. Among the amendments was the proposal to revise Article 22 of said directive, initially requiring in-scope companies to adopt and put into effect a climate transition plan outlining strategies to achieve the greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction targets established by the Paris Agreement, by limiting the obligation to the mere adoption of such plan. On December 16, 2025, the EU Parliament and the Council approved the final version of the so called “Omnibus Package I”, completely eliminating art. 22 and, therefore, any obligation referred to the transition plan. 

While according to the EU legislator such adjustment will enhance legal certainty and improve coherence across the EU sustainability framework, this paper argues that eliminating art. 22 CS3D is likely to create more issues than it solves, particularly from a litigation-risk perspective. On the one hand, by increasing the probability of strategic lawsuits seeking national courts to provid'2e the same normative gap-filling role art. 22 CS3D seemed to have partially taken away from them, thus fostering – absent a common legal framework – outcome uncertainty; on the other, paving the way for climate-washing and climate-washing related claims. On a further note, the amendment seems likely to undermine one of the very goals of the CS3D: ensuring that corporate strategies are compatible with Paris-aligned GHG reduction pathways.

Following an overview of the route that led from the approval of the CS3D to its revision, the paper explores why eliminating any obligation to produce a transition plan is likely to backfire and negatively affect EU companies with respect to climate-related lawsuits, suggesting that a “smarter” regulatory framework – one that reduces burdens without sacrificing effectiveness – should prioritize clarifying existing provisions to guide companies in implementing their net-zero commitments, rather than exempting them from execution altogether.

title: Does LLM-Graph Fusion Help Fraud Detection? A Reproducibility Audit and Negative Result with Implications for Financial AI Deployment

detail.title: Does LLM-Graph Fusion Help Fraud Detection? A Reproducibility Audit and Negative Result with Implications for Financial AI Deployment
detail.abstract: Recent fraud-detection papers report sizeable accuracy gains by fusing large language model (LLM) text encoders with graph neural networks (GNNs). We tried to reproduce this story under joint stress tests – adversarial perturbation of features, structure or text, and temporal concept drift – and arrived at three findings, all of which complicate the dominant narrative. (1) Reproducibility audit: we identify three silent bugs in the standard fraud-GNN evaluation stack – a pseudo-text label leak when YelpChi/Amazon are used for LLM-fraud evaluation despite shipping no native text, an autograd disconnect in the reference BWGNN implementation that silently zeroes adversarial gradients, and a deterministic scatter add that out-of-memories at the standard graph sizes – each of which materially distorts published numbers. (2) Negative result on the LLM–Graph Pareto frontier: after the fixes, on the only dataset that admits an honest joint attack/drift comparison (Elliptic, the others either ship no text or are PGDimmune at the standard budget), the LLMGNN fusion sits inside the Pareto frontier – dominated by vanilla GraphSAGE on both the attack-robustness axis (clean→adv AUROC 0.850 → 0.498 vs LLMGNN’s 0.843 → 0.491) and the drift axis (early-to-late ∆AUROC = 0.110 vs 0.152). (3) On BAF we test whether drift and PGD compound super-additively; the interaction term is small and slightly positive (+0.007 for both CARE-GNN and GraphSAGE) – damage is sub-additive, not compounding. Adversarial training (PGD-AT, TRADES) reduces the attack-axis drop by +0.172 AUROC but worsens the drift axis by −0.042 AUROC: it shifts the frontier without expanding it. Five seeds, FraudPareto release.

title: Giving Life to Private (Rated) Credit
affiliations: Imperial College London, Imperial College Business School,  and Indiana University - Kelley School of Business

detail.title: Giving Life to Private (Rated) Credit
detail.abstract: We study how ratings inflation can undermine financial regulation and inadvertently fuel the growth of privately rated credit. We exploit the 2021 Risk-Based Capital reform for U.S. life insurers, which aimed to curb reaching-for-yield through its treatment of credit ratings. Following the reform, more exposed insurers-especially those with tighter capital constraints-shifted toward privately rated bonds. These bonds exhibit within-issuer ratings inflation and offer higher yields within rating categories, consistent with greater underlying risk behind similar regulatory labels. Accounting for this inflation substantially attenuates the reform's apparent improvement in portfolio risk. Despite targeting ratings rather than market structure, the reform indirectly increased demand for private bonds. Consistent with this demand shift, firms more connected to exposed life insurers increased their private debt issuance.

title: The Application of Lean Manufacturing Principles in the Automotive Industry: A Comparative Study of Ford Motors and Bentley Motors
affiliations: Abertay University

detail.title: The Application of Lean Manufacturing Principles in the Automotive Industry: A Comparative Study of Ford Motors and Bentley Motors

declarations.ethicsApproval: i

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how lean manufacturing principles are applied across two contrasting automotive organizations Ford Motors, a high-volume producer, and Bentley Motors, an ultra-premium luxury marque with the aim of understanding what drives implementation success, what creates resistance, and how context shapes outcomes.

The research draws on a mixed-methods design combining a quantitative survey (n=60, response rate 68.9%) with semi-structured interviews (n=14). Stratified sampling ensured representation across organizational levels and experience bands. Survey data were analyzed descriptively; interview data were processed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis.

Four findings stand out. Lean generates real operational gains in both organizations’ higher productivity, less waste, and better quality though the path to those gains differs substantially between them. Leadership is the strongest predictor of whether lean sticks: roughly a third of survey respondents felt leadership engagement was insufficient, a concern that echoed through the interview data as well. Neither organization applies lean off-the-shelf: Ford integrates it with Six Sigma to manage variation at scale, while Bentley adapts it carefully to avoid threatening the craft identity that underpins its brand. Resistance, whether rooted in institutional habit at Ford or craft pride at Bentley, remains the most persistent barrier in both cases.

The paper contributes a comparative empirical perspective that is largely missing from lean literature dominated by high-volume manufacturing studies. The findings carry practical implications for manufacturers across the automotive spectrum, and for premium-segment producers in other industries where craftsmanship and operational efficiency must coexist.

title: When Less is More: School Schedule Reform and Student Outcomes
affiliations: University of Connecticut - Department of Economics and University of California, Riverside (UCR)

detail.title: When Less is More: School Schedule Reform and Student Outcomes

keywords: JEL Classification: H75 I21 I28 four-day school week

detail.abstract: We examine how school schedule reforms shape students' outcomes by studying the four-day school week, in which students attend school four rather than five days per week. We use comprehensive administrative data from Colorado, where this schedule is most prevalent in the United States. The dataset spans nearly two decades of entry cohorts and more than one million unique student records, providing us with a unique opportunity to study the policy's long-run effects. Leveraging quasi-random variation in adoption across districts in a difference-indifferences framework, we estimate how a shortened school week affects students' educational trajectories. In contrast to much of the existing literature, we find modest improvements in standardized test scores, lower dropout rates, and higher on-time and overall graduation rates. The duration of exposure plays a key role: students with longer and more consistent exposure experience the largest gains in persistence and attainment. Improvements in teacher retention and classroom expenditures also contribute to these gains. At the same time, heterogeneous effects indicate that disadvantaged students benefit less, raising concerns about equity. Overall, the findings suggest that a shorter school week need not necessarily harm student outcomes and can improve both performance and completion when designed and implemented carefully.

title: How Do Passive Investing Strategies Through Etfs Compare To Active Stock Picking In Terms Of Returns, Costs, And Risk Management?
affiliations: and

detail.title: How Do Passive Investing Strategies Through Etfs Compare To Active Stock Picking In Terms Of Returns, Costs, And Risk Management?
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the financial trade-offs between passive ETF strategies and active stock picking, focusing on long-term returns, costs, and risk management. Active investing promises portfolio autonomy and the allure of market-beating returns. Yet landmark empirical data from Fama and French (2010) and Barber and Odean (2000) reveal a harsher reality: most active managers consistently lose to broad market benchmarks over extended periods. This drag is not a mystery. High management fees, constant trading frictions, and psychological traps like panic selling systematically erode active gains. Passive ETFs solve these vulnerabilities by offering broad market diversification and rock-bottom expense ratios. This paper also weighs modern alternatives, including Smart Beta, robo-advisors, and ESG integration. Ultimately, the numbers favor simplicity. While expert stock pickers can find success in specific market pockets, a low-cost passive ETF framework remains the most reliable wealth-building machine for the everyday investor.

title: FCCL: The Fear-Control Capture Loop of Immediate Meaning Compensation (IMC) A Dynamical Model of Neural × Narrative × Market Coupling

detail.title: FCCL: The Fear-Control Capture Loop of Immediate Meaning Compensation (IMC) A Dynamical Model of Neural × Narrative × Market Coupling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None. The author declares no conflicts of interest relevant to this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical/conceptual paper and does not involve human participants, patient data, or experiments requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This work received no external funding.

keywords: Yongming Yuan. 2026. "FCCL: The Fear-Control Capture Loop of Immediate Meaning Compensation (IMC)." Working paper / preprint

detail.abstract: Background. Under high uncertainty, decision-making often shifts from truth-seeking to "bleeding control": rapid arousal reduction and restoration of perceived control, increasing demand for short-latency certainty and meaning. Model. We propose the Fear-Control Capture Loop (FCCL) linking arousal A(t), horizon compression H(t), control need C(t), narrative closure N(t), dose D(t), and structural action S(t), with NFCC(t) (need for closure) as the A→N bridge. FCCL predicts surface relief cycles can coexist with monotonic latent accumulation R(t) when relief substitutes for structural action (Delay(S)). Taxonomy/Costs. IMC implementations cluster into sedative, stimulant, and attachment-identity families mapped onto arousal regulation × social attachment. We add a panacea economics layer: low marginal cost and cure-all positioning incentivize dose expansion and relapse monetization; placebo-compatible relief can be real yet capture-prone under high closure and exit penalties. Case. A bounded mechanism anchor (Steve Jobs) illustrates acute FCCL dynamics under health threat via strong control preference and low tolerance for probabilistic ambiguity. Measures/Predictions. We introduce NFI-E/NFI-S (epistemic vs social closure), a mixed Structural Action Index (S), and operational inputs PN-Total (pathologizing/threat marketing), PE-Total (expectancy/ritual/authority), and Ad-NFI. We outline content-analysis, PN×PE experiments, and longitudinal designs to test dose escalation, S suppression, and R-proxy trajectories.

title: The Out-of-Pocket Cost of Rehabilitation: A Telerehabilitation Case Series

detail.title: The Out-of-Pocket Cost of Rehabilitation: A Telerehabilitation Case Series

detail.abstract: Background and Objective. After orthopedic surgery, much rehabilitation is done at home, and many patients do not finish the prescribed program. Cost and travel are named as barriers, but few studies measure what young post-surgical patients actually pay out of pocket, how much time they lose, or what a home telerehabilitation app might save. This matters in China, where patients carry a large share of health costs. I measured the out-of-pocket and time burden of inperson rehabilitation in these patients and what they reported saving with a home app. Methods. This retrospective case series analyzed de-identified baseline and endpoint survey data from seven post-surgical patients (three shoulder arthroscopy, four ACL reconstruction; ages 19-30) who used a smartphone rehabilitation app over an 8-12 week program. Patients reported two figures directly: avoided in-person visits and time saved; the cost figures are those visit counts multiplied by each patient's stated per-visit price, not verified spending. Results. All seven patients paid the full cost out of pocket (¥250-600 per visit), and six had to take leave from work or school. On average, patients reported avoiding six in-person visits and saving 10.4 hours, ¥2,559 in direct cost, and ¥2,963 in total out-of-pocket cost including travel (about US$437; range ¥1,464-4,900). Conclusions. In this small sample, in-person rehabilitation was a large self-paid burden in both money and time, and patients reported sizable savings with the app. These are preliminary single-arm findings; larger controlled studies are needed to confirm them.

title: TOPIC-Behavioural Nudges and Overspending in Digital Payments
affiliations: Indraprastha College for Women, University of Delhi and Indraprastha College for Women, University of Delhi

detail.title: TOPIC-Behavioural Nudges and Overspending in Digital Payments
detail.abstract: This study examines how behavioural nudges influence overspending in digital payment systems. With the rapid adoption of digital payment methods, understanding their impact on consumer spending behaviour has become increasingly important. The objective of this research is to analyse how digital payment frequency affects spending, along with the role of behavioural factors such as induced spending, cashback incentives, and habitual financial behaviour. The study uses a cross-sectional design and a mixed-method approach, with primary data collected through a structured survey of individuals aged 18-30 years. Regression analysis is employed to assess the relationship between digital payment usage and changes in spending behaviour. Secondary data from the World Bank is also used to provide a macroeconomic perspective. The findings indicate that digital payment usage is associated with increased spending, with induced spending emerging as a significant behavioural driver. However, cashback incentives do not show a significant impact. While macro-level trends suggest stable consumption patterns, micro-level evidence points to behavioural shifts in spending. The study highlights the need for further research on behavioural mechanisms within digital financial systems and their long-term implications for consumer financial decision-making.

title: Support Failure and the Value of Experimental Authority

detail.title: Support Failure and the Value of Experimental Authority
detail.abstract: Policy reforms often extend treatment to populations untreated under the assignment rule. The resulting problem is missing counterfactual support, not estimation noise alone. This paper develops a theory of welfare-oriented data acquisition when the information technology constrains which arm can be observed at each policy location. Observed anchor values are fixed as data; the design determines the local residual Lipschitz ambiguity around them. The zero-noise minimax-regret component equals one half of a sum of arm-specific, welfare-weighted distances to support. Optimal acquisition is therefore a constrained facility-location problem. Under a sharp pre-policy status quo, passive acquisition can improve support for the observable arm but cannot create treated support inside an expansion region. Experimental authority relaxes this constraint; its value is the minimax-regret gap between the passive and two-arm frontiers. A stylized Medicare eligibility-expansion calibration illustrates how this gap varies with welfare weights, pre-existing untreated support, acquisition budgets, and smoothness ratios.

title: Competencies and Classroom Management Skills among Teachers: A Comparative Study among ODL and Traditional Teachers
affiliations: University of Delhi

detail.title: Competencies and Classroom Management Skills among Teachers: A Comparative Study among ODL and Traditional Teachers
detail.abstract:
What happens to the art of teaching when you trade a physical room for a computer screen? This investigation explores that exact puzzle, looking at how the learning environment shifts the way educators connect with students, guide behaviour, and handle job stress. Rather than looking at dry data, this study focuses on the daily lived experiences of fifteen active instructors. The participants ranged from 23 to 52 years old, with career histories spanning from newcomers to veterans with over twenty years on the job. To get a complete view, the group included brick-and-mortar teachers, purely online distance instructors, and those who teach in both formats.

The field data brought five major insights to light. First, communication is completely transformed; traditional teachers read facial expressions instantly, whereas online instructors operate in a visual vacuum of turned-off webcams, forcing them to over-communicate through voice and chat text. Second, technology shifts from being a helpful, optional tool in a physical school to becoming the absolute framework of the virtual classroom, making technical fluency a strict requirement. Third, discipline changes shape; face-to-face teachers manage loud, active disruptions, while distance educators must fight passive withdrawal and student ghosting. Fourth, while in-person classrooms benefit from natural group accountability, online spaces require teachers to intentionally build digital checkpoints to keep students from becoming passive viewers. Finally, professional burnout manifests differently, showing up as physical exhaustion from large class sizes versus the psychological fatigue of screen isolation.

Ultimately, the study shows that traditional teaching strengths do not automatically ensure success on a digital platform. Online instruction requires a distinct professional toolkit centered on media comfort, creative digital design, and the unique ability to project human empathy through a glass screen. To support this shift, the study suggests that teacher training programs must treat digital pedagogy as a primary discipline, mandate split internships in both physical and virtual settings, automate administrative tasks to reduce workloads, and set clear communication boundaries to protect teacher well-being.

title: Proximity as Advantage: Why a Brazilian Private Health Insurer Presence at a Technology Park is a Decision of Industrial Economics, not Institutional Generosity

detail.title: Proximity as Advantage: Why a Brazilian Private Health Insurer Presence at a Technology Park is a Decision of Industrial Economics, not Institutional Generosity
detail.abstract: This essay argues that Unimed Fesp’s strategic positioning at Supera Parque, a technology park anchored by the University of São Paulo’s Ribeirão Preto Medical School (FMRP/USP), constitutes a decision of industrial economics, not institutional philanthropy. Drawing on four independent layers of empirical evidence derived from the Annual Social Information Report (RAIS 2024) and Brazilian Federal Agency for Support and Evaluation of Graduate Education (CAPES) graduate program data (2024), the paper demonstrates that a health cluster exists in Ribeirão Preto (RP) that is spatially demonstrable and quantitatively robust. The Location Quotient (LQ = 1.531) confirms productive specialization above the conventional cluster threshold. The Global Moran’s I (I = 0.107, p = 0.032), calculated over log-transformed LQ values with a critical mass filter (total employment ≥ 5,000; health employment ≥ 150), confirms statistically significant positive spatial autocorrelation. LISA quadrant analysis positions RP as a dominant pole in the High-Low quadrant, the spatial signature of a cluster in growth stage, where specialization is concentrated at the core before diffusing to the surrounding territory. Finally, a composite R&D index derived from CAPES data places RP third in the state of São Paulo in academic health capital, with 510 permanent faculty and 739 enrolled doctoral students in health sciences programs, surpassed only by São Paulo and Campinas. Together, these findings support the claim that health insurers occupying the institutional node of a growing health cluster are not acting charitably but, they are internalizing agglomeration externalities that would otherwise benefit their competitors.

title: Variance Risk Premium in Nifty 50 Weekly Expiry Cycles: VIX Calibration Bias and Regime Dependence

detail.title: Variance Risk Premium in Nifty 50 Weekly Expiry Cycles: VIX Calibration Bias and Regime Dependence
detail.abstract: This paper asks a simple question: does India VIX actually predict how much the Nifty 50 moves each week? Using 380 weekly expiry cycles from February 2019 to June 2026, I find that it does not, at least not accurately. Implied volatility overstates realized weekly moves in nearly three out of four cycles. The mean Variance Risk Premium (VRP), defined as the difference between implied and realized weekly volatility, is +0.70% per cycle (t = 8.40, p < 0.001). Beyond this central finding, I show that conditioning on volatility regimes derived from a pre-sample period (2011-2018) reveals meaningful structure. VIX retains some predictive power for move magnitude at the aggregate level (ρ = 0.228, p < 0.001), but this relationship breaks down entirely within the Low VIX regime. Only the High VIX regime produces realized volatility distributions that are statistically distinct from the other two regimes. Perhaps most interestingly, High VIX weeks show a significant upward directional bias of 62.6% (p = 0.021), a pattern consistent with fear-driven selloffs partially reversing before expiry. These findings hold when the COVID-19 period is excluded. Taken together, the results point to a structural and persistent VRP in Indian weekly equity market data.

title: Lawyer CEOs, Context-Dependent Conservatism, and Workplace Safety
affiliations: , ,  and Oklahoma State University

detail.title: Lawyer CEOs, Context-Dependent Conservatism, and Workplace Safety
detail.abstract: We examine the effect of CEOs' legal expertise (hereafter, "lawyer CEOs") on workplace safety. Using establishment-level workplace injury data from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, we document that firms led by lawyer CEOs exhibit significantly higher total case incident rate (TCR). Specifically, establishments of lawyer-CEO firms have a 20.6% higher TCR relative to the sample mean. Our further analysis shows that lawyer CEOs are more conservative in worker-related expenditure and investment. However, lawyer CEOs are not significantly associated with more fatal workplace injuries. Using the Ninth Circuit ruling in 1999 and Universal Demand laws as exogenous litigation risk shocks, we find that the effect of lawyer CEOs weakens when litigation risk increases but exhibits no change when litigation risk decreases. Labor union coverage and regulatory inspections can also mitigate the detrimental effect of lawyer CEOs. Overall, our evidence shows that CEOs' legal expertise shapes workplace safety in a nuanced manner, reducing exposure to severe liability while exacerbating workplace injuries through managerial conservatism.

title: Do Aggregate Risk Factor Disclosures Predict Market Volatility?
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Joseph M. Katz Graduate School of Business, University of Colorado at Boulder and

detail.title: Do Aggregate Risk Factor Disclosures Predict Market Volatility?
detail.abstract: Market-wide risk information is critical to investor decision making. In this study, we aggregate risk factor disclosures across firms to predict future market-wide risk. For an aggregate risk signal to exist, two conditions must hold: first, firms must identify novel and material risks in their risk disclosures; second, the risks must be similar across firms and therefore non-diversifiable. Consistent with this expectation, we provide evidence that aggregate risk disclosure is positively associated with future market-wide volatility when the amount of new risk disclosed is high and these risks are similar across firms. Sector-level tests corroborate the results of our market-wide analyses: sector-quarters with high aggregate risk disclosure and high disclosure agreement are positively associated with future volatility at three and six month horizons. This association is weaker for sector-quarters with high litigation risk, suggesting risk disclosures used to shield against litigation can obscure the macroeconomic risk signal. Our results suggest that firm-level narrative disclosures, when appropriately aggregated, can improve predictions of future market volatility beyond that already priced by investors.

title: The Plumbing Beneath Private Credit

detail.title: The Plumbing Beneath Private Credit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Adjunct Assistant Professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. The author has prior and ongoing professional relationships with institutions active in private credit and alternative investments; no funding, data access, or editorial input was received from any such institution in connection with this paper. The views expressed are the author's own.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Concerns about systemic risk in private credit intensified in 2025-2026 after Jamie Dimon's "cockroach" warning and mounting redemption pressure across non-traded BDCs. The asset class had by then expanded well beyond institutional investors, into insurance balance sheets and private wealth portfolios through semi-liquid structures. Recent regulatory commentary, including the Financial Stability Board's May 2026 assessment, highlights concerns around layered leverage, insurance-sector linkages, and limited transparency into underlying portfolio risk.

Framing private credit as "the next 2008" mischaracterizes the mechanism through which stress propagates. Unlike banks, most private-credit capital sits in locked, gated, or permanent-capital structures rather than runnable liabilities. Using a return-on-equity decomposition calibrated to a representative large-scale levered direct lending fund, the paper demonstrates that even severe stress assumptions imply return compression rather than principal impairment for diversified senior-lending portfolios. The more significant vulnerabilities sit in the tail of the market: smaller lenders with concentrated sponsor relationships, weaker diversification, and more fragile refinancing capacity.

The real story is spread compression. The cushion provided by risk spreads has narrowed materially. Headline yields stayed near 11% across a sharp rise in SOFR, but the underlying risk premium compressed by roughly 1.3 percentage points against long-run averages and nearly 3 points against the 2020 peak, leaving 2023-2025 vintages particularly exposed if the cycle turns. Rising base rates masked deteriorating lending economics by sustaining headline yields even as credit spreads compressed.

Rising redemption pressure in Q1 and Q2 2026 provided the first significant stress test of the perpetual structures that facilitated private credit's rapid expansion into wealth-management channels. Gating mechanisms — often interpreted as signs of fragility — are designed precisely to prevent the fire-sale dynamics associated with runnable banking systems. The episode revealed meaningful differences in portfolio quality, diversification, funding flexibility, and sponsor support across platforms, with peers including Apollo, Ares, BlackRock, and Blue Owl applying the standard 5% quarterly cap and Blackstone ultimately doing the same in Q2 after a more accommodative Q1 response. The evidence points toward platform differentiation and consolidation rather than banking-style contagion.

This paper is interpretive and framework-based: a market-structure analysis grounded in institutional mechanics, a return-on-equity decomposition, and observable spread and secondary-market data. It is not an econometric study and offers no causal identification or formal statistical testing.

title: GEMA v. OpenAI (Munich I Regional Court, 2025): Doctrinal, Comparative, and International Perspectives on Copyright and Generative AI
affiliations: Universitat Pompeu Fabra - Department of Law, Leibniz University Hannover and Columbia University - Law School

detail.title: GEMA v. OpenAI (Munich I Regional Court, 2025): Doctrinal, Comparative, and International Perspectives on Copyright and Generative AI

publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the Regional Court of Munich I’s decision in the GEMA v. OpenAI case, examining whether training generative AI models on copyrighted works constitutes infringement. The Court held OpenAI liable, finding that AI training creates copyright-relevant reproductions inside generative models not sheltered by text and data mining exceptions under EU and German law. The authors explore the ruling‘s implications, compare current US fair use litigation, and assess both against the background of international copyright law, particularly the Berne Convention’s three-step test.

title: Market Synchronization with Changing Economic Conditions
affiliations: and Universidad Europea de Madrid

detail.title: Market Synchronization with Changing Economic Conditions
detail.abstract: This paper examines the performance of a large sample of mutual funds in 35 countries worldwide, both overall and by decomposing it into its two components: market synchronization capabilities and stock selection. Both analyses are based on traditional measures and measures that consider the variation of returns and risk over time by incorporating macroeconomic variables representative of the economic cycle across countries. The incorporation of these variables leads to an improvement in overall performance and a decline in the manager's stock selection capabilities. We find no conclussion regarding market synchronization capabilities. However, we observe an improvement in the explanatory power of the models as a result of this incorporation across countries, which allow us to advocate for conditional models. Furthermore, this paper corrects for multicollinearity problems among these variables through factor analysis.

title: On the Short-Run Insufficiency of the Effective Federal Funds Rate as an Inflation Predictor: National and Regional Evidence

detail.title: On the Short-Run Insufficiency of the Effective Federal Funds Rate as an Inflation Predictor: National and Regional Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper examines the short-run and long-run relationship between the Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) and the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for Urban Consumers across national and regional U.S. markets from March 2020 to January 2026. Using monthly time series data spanning a full monetary policy cycle, from near-zero accommodation through aggressive tightening and into subsequent rate cuts; we employ a two-stage analytical framework. At the national level, a Vector Autoregressive (VAR) model and Johansen cointegration test motivate a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM), while a fixed-effects panel regression with cluster-robust standard errors is used at the regional level. Key findings reveal that EFFR does not Granger-cause CPI in the short run (F = 0.187, p = 0.666), and forecast error variance decomposition shows that EFFR accounts for less than 1.1% of CPI forecast variance at all horizons up to 12 months, while autoregressive CPI momentum explains 97.7%. Johansen cointegration confirms a long-run equilibrium relationship between EFFR and CPI, with reverse causality dominating the short run; CPI explains 89.8% of EFFR forecast variance at 12 months. At the regional level, fixed-effects models identify statistically significant heterogeneity in EFFR sensitivity (p < 2.2 × 10-16), with the West and South exhibiting consistently stronger responses than the Midwest and Northeast across both the full sample and a post-2022 robustness check. These findings suggest that while EFFR anchors long-run price stability, it 1 functions as an insufficient short-run inflation control instrument, with CPI momentum and reverse causality dominating the transmission mechanism.

title: Value Displacement Theory: Realization Mechanisms, Minority Claims, and the Transformation of Equity Value

detail.title: Value Displacement Theory: Realization Mechanisms, Minority Claims, and the Transformation of Equity Value
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that the value of a passive minority equity claim is not a property of the underlying enterprise alone, but a function of the interaction between the enterprise and the realization mechanism available to the holder. Two investors holding legally identical claims in structurally analogous enterprises can experience categorically different outcomes from the same price event if one realizes value through distribution and the other realizes value only through sale.

The paper argues that U.S. equity ownership has undergone a categorical transformation across identifiable historical regimes. In the original model of equity ownership, stocks functioned primarily as yield instruments: corporate earnings became shareholder wealth through recurring dividend distributions. For a large and economically dominant portion of modern public equity markets, that mechanism has been displaced. Many passive minority shareholders now realize value primarily through market-mediated price appreciation, buyback participation requiring sale or partial sale, acquisition, liquidation, or other realization events they cannot compel.

Value Displacement Theory argues that this shift renders earnings-based valuation frameworks incomplete when they are applied to passive minority claims in non-distributive public companies without specifying how enterprise earnings become shareholder-realizable value. The paper does not claim that earnings are irrelevant, that discounted cash flow analysis is useless, or that market prices are always durable or correct. It argues that enterprise value, control value, and minority shareholder-realizable value are distinct categories that conventional analysis often compresses into a single concept of equity value.

The paper develops this claim through historical regime analysis, a comparison between yield-mediated and resale-dependent shareholders, the control/minority distinction, legal and institutional evidence that minority shareholder harm is operationalized through price, and the Liquidity Event Horizon thought experiment. It further argues that narrative, liquidity, attention, thematic scarcity, and reflexive valuation-capital effects are not merely behavioral anomalies adjacent to value. In price-realization markets, they are part of the mechanism through which value becomes realizable.

Using an original daily U.S. equity database spanning 1815 to 1925, reconstructed from primary newspaper sources, and modern equities data extending to the present, the paper proposes a research agenda for testing the long-run transition from yield-mediated ownership to price-realization ownership.

title: Subnetwork Analysis for Neural Network Interpretability - A Survey and Experimental Study
affiliations: , Jönköping University and Jönköping University

detail.title: Subnetwork Analysis for Neural Network Interpretability - A Survey and Experimental Study

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Knowledge Foundation, Jönköping University, and industrial partners through the Knowledge Intensive Product Realization SPARK research and education environment at Jönköping University, Sweden [grant number 20200223] (Project: AFAIR).

detail.abstract: Subnetwork analysis has emerged as a growing research area with connections to the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, mechanistic interpretability, compositionality, and explainable AI. However, the field lacks a unified framework for comparing methods across these different research areas. In this study, we make four contributions: (1) we develop criteria and evaluation protocol for systematically comparing subnetwork analysis methods from an interpretability perspective; (2) we survey state-of-the-art methods spanning diverse focuses and purposes; (3) we experimentally compare two identified comparable methods — Differentiable Weight Masking (DWM) and our own Cumulative Subnetwork Analysis (CSA), extending CSA to image domains and adapting DWM from its original study; and (4) we demonstrate the practical utility of subnetwork analysis for neural network interpretability. Our results show that training-based methods such as DWM lack fidelity to the underlying model, as their performance does not reflect the original model's reasoning. CSA produces larger subnetworks but achieves performance closer to the original model, indicating greater fidelity. Using CSA, we further identify critical channels whose removal significantly degrades model performance, and show that subnetwork overlap is greater between semantically similar classes than between dissimilar ones. These findings support subnetwork analysis as a promising tool for bridging the interpretability of neural networks and human-understandable explanations.

title: Beyond Numbers: How Corporate Integrity Shapes Analysts' Earnings Forecasts
affiliations: , KU Leuven - Faculty of Business and Economics (FEB) and Central South University - School of Business

detail.title: Beyond Numbers: How Corporate Integrity Shapes Analysts' Earnings Forecasts
detail.abstract: We examine whether and how analysts incorporate corporate integrity into their earnings forecasts. Exploiting the staggered implementation of China's Social Credit System (SCS) reform, a national initiative aimed at enhancing societal integrity, we find that the reform improves integrity perceptions and commitment among local residents, governments, and firms. Analysts following affected firms subsequently issue significantly more optimistic earnings forecasts. This optimism appears to be driven by increased trust in these firms, rather than by optimistic expectations of improved performance. The effect is stronger for firms operating in weaker institutional environments, those that are financially constrained, firms operating in highly competitive industries, and for analysts with limited access to information. Overall, our findings highlight that corporate integrity constitutes an essential consideration in analysts' forecast behavior, and forecasts issued for high-integrity firms are more optimistic.

detail.abstract:
Background: The WHO prioritizes encephalitis as an urgent and global public health imperative with serious consequences for survivors. Socioeconomic outcomes remain poorly studied yet are imperative to addressing the WHO recommendations. No population-based studies have systematically assessed and compared individual consequences and societal outcomes of infectious and autoimmune encephalitis.

Methods: Patients with serologically confirmed autoimmune encephalitis (AE) and patients with microbiologically confirmed herpes simplex type 1 encephalitis (HSE) were matched with general population controls on sociodemographic characteristics. Differences in societal costs, personal socioeconomic outcomes and mortality were analyzed using regression-based statistical models.

Findings: A total of 117 AE patients were matched with 70,994 controls, and 112 HSE patients with 47,659 controls. Both groups incurred substantially higher societal costs compared to controls, averaging €134,000 per patient [95% CI 109,000 to 160,000] for AE and €113,000 [90,000 to 135,000] for HSE over a six-year period.Five years after diagnosis, individual socioeconomic outcomes remained markedly worse compared to background population controls. Absolute risk difference of labor market participation was reduced by 31% [16 to 45] and 28% [10 to 46], for AE and HSE, respectively. The probability of receiving disability pension increased for both AE (11% [2 to 20]) and HSE (28% [9 to 46]) and institutionalization was 13% [3 to 23] higher in HSE patients than in controls. Annual transfer income increased considerably, particularly among HSE patients. The 5-year cumulative mortality risk difference was 22% [14 to 30] for AE and 34% [24 to 44] for HSE.

Interpretation: Encephalitis is associated with substantial long-term mortality and individual and societal burdens regardless of etiology. These observations advance WHO advice by providing population-based quantification of the consequences of this condition which is likely to become an increasing global concern.

title: Communication Infrastructures for One Health Governance in Latin America and the Caribbean: A Comparative Multi-Actor Study across Five Countries
affiliations: University of Montpellier III Paul Valéry, University of Montpellier - CREEC/CANECEV (CREES), University of Montpellier and

detail.title: Communication Infrastructures for One Health Governance in Latin America and the Caribbean: A Comparative Multi-Actor Study across Five Countries

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study followed principles of voluntary participation, transparency, and collective validation. Participants were informed of the research objectives prior to the workshops and consented to the aggregated and anonymised use of results. No individual-level data are reported. The roadmaps and strategic outputs developed during the workshops remain the property of participants and national institutions. Analytical findings were shared with stakeholders to ensure reciprocity. The study aligns with the principles of equitable partnership, with the majority of authors based in the participating countries and substantively involved in design, facilitation, analysis, and interpretation.
