detail.abstract:
Background: Despite the Pan American Health Organization’s 2021 One Health Policy and broad endorsement across the Americas, the operationalisation of One Health remains uneven across countries. Existing assessments focus on surveillance systems and regulatory frameworks, with comparatively little attention paid to the communication infrastructures that enable intersectoral and multi-level coordination. We examined how communication dynamics among institutional, scientific, and territorial actors shape the implementation of One Health in five Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) countries.

Methods: We conducted a comparative qualitative and semi-quantitative study based on structured multi-actor workshops in Costa Rica, Cuba, Guatemala, Mexico, and Panama (October 2024 – June 2025). We used the Compass, a deliberation-based assessment tool covering twelve systemic indicators across environmental, economic, socio-political, and health dimensions. We documented 280 recorded interactions among 87 participants, and combined inductive comparative analysis of qualitative materials with descriptive interaction-flow and network analyses.

Findings: Three communication configurations recurred across countries. A nationally driven configuration, observed in Cuba and Panama, organised deliberation around interministerial commissions, shared conceptual frameworks, and legal instruments, with discussions starting from institutional conditions before considering territorial experimentation. A territory-rooted configuration, observed primarily in Guatemala, anchored discussions in local issues—zoonoses, environmental vulnerabilities—addressed through interactions among universities, NGOs, and ministerial representatives, before integration into broader national frameworks. A hybrid deliberative configuration, observed in Costa Rica and Mexico, articulated institutional structuring and collective deliberation simultaneously, with phased roadmaps connecting national coordination and territorial action.

Interpretation: The implementation of One Health in the Americas depends less on additional technical coordination than on the institutionalisation of intermediated communication infrastructures - boundary actors, committees, and translation devices that connect national policy frameworks with territorial action. Strengthening these mediation infrastructures is as critical to addressing zoonotic risks as reinforcing surveillance or laboratory capacities, and offers a tractable lever for the regional implementation of the PAHO One Health Policy.

title: Free-Riding on the Wind: Strategic Emissions at Administrative Boundaries
affiliations: Jinan University, Jinan University - Management School and Guangdong University of Finance

detail.title: Free-Riding on the Wind: Strategic Emissions at Administrative Boundaries
detail.abstract: Environmental enforcement is usually organized by administrative boundaries, whereas air pollution is transported by the atmosphere. This paper studies whether firms exploit this institutional-physical mismatch by timing emissions to wind conditions that can move pollution away from the home jurisdiction. We combine hourly SO2 emissions from the continuous emission monitoring system for 303 key polluters in Shandong Province in 2015 with ERA5 hourly wind fields and city-boundary geometry. For each firm-hour, we measure whether wind lies in a boundary-oriented sector and construct a transport-geometry index that combines distance to the nearest city boundary with the wind-speed component along that path. High-dimensional fixed-effects regressions show that firms emit more SO2 when wind points toward the nearest boundary. Conditional on boundary-oriented winds, emissions also vary systematically with the transport-geometry index, indicating that firms respond not only to wind direction but also to the broader atmospheric opportunity for exporting pollution. The response is stronger at night, on high-rainfall days, and among economically important firms; it is weaker in cities subject to environmental enforcement interviews, in the provincial joint prevention and control city cluster, and where regional circulation limits boundary-oriented dispersion. The findings document a form of atmospheric regulatory arbitrage and show how decentralized enforcement, jurisdictional borders, and natural dispersion jointly shape firms' compliance behavior.

title: When Protection Hurts: Labor Market Consequences of Mandatory Heat Allowances in China
affiliations: National University of Singapore and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Protection Hurts: Labor Market Consequences of Mandatory Heat Allowances in China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the unintended labor-market consequences of mandatory heat-protection policies in China. Exploiting a mid-2010 policy that doubled the statutory heat allowance in a major Chinese city, we combine a continuous difference-in-differences design with employer-employee-matched panel data covering over two million employees from 2008 to 2013 to conduct the analysis. The robust findings suggest that firms offset the extra allowance burden by implicitly slowing wage growth for employees. In a representative outdoor-exposed firm (with 34% outdoor exposure), post-policy nominal wage growth decreases by about 1.8 percentage points relative to unaffected firms. At the same time, dismissal probability rises by approximately 2.5 percentage points. Both adverse effects are concentrated among private firms, while state-owned firms remain unaffected. We further show that smaller firms rely more on wage reduction, whereas larger firms adjust through lowering employment. These baseline results remain consistent using a multi-city sample of listed firms. Additional analysis suggests that firms absorb the increased labor costs through two concurrent adjustments: fine-grained wage moderation targeted at employees subject to the mandated benefits and broader employment contractions at the firm level. These findings underscore a tension between climate-driven labor protection mandates and firm financial fragility to highlight the importance of complementary policy instruments to mitigate adverse employee outcomes.

title: Boon or Bane? Retailer Channel Mode Selection and Pricing Strategy Under the Dual Influence of Information and Service
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Boon or Bane? Retailer Channel Mode Selection and Pricing Strategy Under the Dual Influence of Information and Service
detail.abstract: With the development of emerging network information technology and changes in consumer shopping behavior, an increasing number of retailers are exploring omni-channel retailing. This paper considers the dual influence of service level and information sharing degree. Based on demand functions for online, offline, and BOPS channels, we construct profit function models for retailers under multi-channel and omni-channel scenarios with both uniform pricing and differential pricing strategies. We analyze the impact of parameters such as cross-price elasticity of service level and information sharing degree on retailer pricing and profit, and investigate the optimal pricing strategy. Key findings include: (1) Online channel demand is positively correlated with online price and negatively correlated with offline price; a higher consumer channel switching coefficient leads to a larger price difference between the two channels. (2) Service level and information sharing degree are positively associated with channel prices and profits; under omni-channel uniform pricing, both prices and profits are higher than those under multi-channel uniform pricing. (3) Retailer profit is higher when service level is high and information sharing degree is low than the opposite case; profit is maximized when both are high. (4) When both the cross-service-level elasticity coefficient and the information sharing coefficient are high, the price difference between online and offline channels is small, and retailer profit is optimal. This study provides managerial insights for retailers’ channel mode selection and pricing decisions.

detail.abstract: This report examines the role of enterprise applications in achieving operational excellence and customer closeness, with a focus on Girltrend’s Cosmetics and Skincare Manufacturing in the Philippines. Operational impacts include improved coordination, reduced delays, and personalized customer engagement, while stakeholders benefit from efficiency, compliance, and stronger collaboration. The findings suggest that digital transformation through enterprise systems can significantly strengthen productivity, maintain product quality, and foster long-term growth in competitive private-label cosmetics manufacturing.

title: Stop Detecting AI Authorship, Start Verifying Logical Alignment: A Methodological and Governance Framework for Scientific Research in the Generative AI Era

detail.title: Stop Detecting AI Authorship, Start Verifying Logical Alignment: A Methodological and Governance Framework for Scientific Research in the Generative AI Era
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has driven the marginal cost of producing scholarly text toward zero, while leaving the cost of verifying scholarly claims essentially unchanged. This asymmetry, not the existence of AI tools as such, is the structural problem confronting contemporary science. The dominant institutional response-mandating disclosure of AI use and deploying AI-text detectors-fails on three counts: detection is technically unstable and demonstrably biased; disclosure encodes too little information to inform either editorial decisions or epistemic trust; and both rest on a category error, treating the provenance of text as a proxy for the validity of an argument. We argue that the locus of scientific quality control must shift along two axes simultaneously: from authorship provenance to logical structure, and from post-hoc peer review to pre-submission verification. We develop an integrated, three-layer framework. (i) As an evaluative standard, we define Logical Alignment: a manuscript is logically aligned when its premises are transparent, its inference is traceable, its predictions are falsifiable and discriminatory, its boundary conditions are explicit, and its epistemic increment is identifiable. (ii) As a methodological pipeline, we introduce the Minimum Viable Idea (MVI) → Minimum Viable Theory (MVT) workflow, preceded by an Explanation-Depth Test that prevents premature termination of inquiry at proximate explanations, and validated through Heterogeneous Multi-Model Cross-Examination (HMCE), which treats the alignment differences across large language models as epistemic probes rather than as noise. (iii) As a governance interface, we introduce Cognitive Auditability as scholarly metadata-distinguishing cognitive amplification from cognitive substitution-and a lightweight Logic Alignment Report (LAR) that reduces the marginal cost of expert evaluation for editors, reviewers, supervisors, and funders. We provide formal definitions, multiple worked examples spanning evolutionary biology, the social sciences, the formal sciences, and the physical sciences, a full HMCE protocol with annotated transcripts, completed LAR templates, an explicit analysis of failure modes (including model homogeneity and the suppression of genuine novelty, for which we propose a High-Divergence Preservation Principle), and a voluntary, additive implementation pathway requiring no change to copyright law or existing authorship norms. The framework does not legitimize careless AI use; it makes such use structurally visible while routing rigorous use through transparent, inspectable verification channels. It is released as a preprint to establish methodological priority for its constructs and to invite open replication and critique.

detail.abstract: The first two papers in this series established, respectively, an execution architecture for fully-collateralised binary prediction markets and the Authority-Driven Development Model (ADDM), a prompt-engineering governance framework in which a large language model (LLM) acts as a read-only institutional auditor that never modifies the system under examination. This third paper advances the programme along two axes simultaneously. First, it extends the ADDM from passive audit to governed autonomous execution: the model is no longer restricted to witnessing evidence but is permitted to act-to plan, build, test and audit atomic tasks-while remaining bound by the same authority document, phase gates, forbidden-path constraints and controlled verdict vocabulary. We name this operating mode bounded autonomy and distinguish it sharply from the unconstrained agentic loops that dominate informal practice. Second, it transplants the method from a high-stakes execution domain into a research-grade, strictly read-only observation domain: a live data-collection system whose sole purpose is to test whether a directional signal D, derived from the net buying pressure of Bitcoin options order flow on Deribit, predicts the resolution of fifteen-minute 'BTC Up or Down' markets on Polymarket better than the price the market itself already carries. The empirical contribution of this paper is not the trading result-that question is deliberately left open and reserved for a future paper-but a detailed, honest account of how a contemporary agentic operator (running on the OpenClaw gateway over Anthropic and OpenAI models) actually performed when held to an authority document: where it succeeded, where it failed, where it silently approached premature closure, and how human-imposed gates caught those failures. We additionally introduce a juridical reading of prompt engineering, drawn from the author's legal training, in which the authority document functions as constitutional text, the prompt as procedural law, evidence categories as rules of admissibility, and the model's verdict as testimony rather than judgment. The contribution is methodological and institutional: it shows that autonomy and control are not opposites, and that the governing structure which makes an LLM a trustworthy auditor is the same structure that makes an autonomous agent safe to deploy.

detail.abstract: The Infinite Game OS is a framework for individuals who want to design their entire life as one of Carse's infinite games rather than only operate within finite ones. This paper synthesizes the framework's architecture, vocabulary lattice and operational primitives. It positions the work relative to Carse's original distinction between finite and infinite games (1986), Sinek's corporate adaptation (2019) and contemporary work in personal knowledge management and AI-native practice (Forte 2022, Karpathy 2024). The framework's primary structural move is counter-positioning to productivity AI: it opens at the question of whether a practitioner can distinguish authentic desire from conditioned programming before any optimization layer is built on top. Three structural commitments distinguish it from adjacent frameworks. Data sovereignty as foundation, expressed as a file-first knowledge architecture with the AI as a swappable interface. Counter-positioning rather than competition, expressed as sovereignty before optimization. Conductive rather than accumulative growth, expressed as a practitioner building a structured body of work that is locatable rather than building an audience to monetize. The framework is presented as the author's working position. Its primitives are documented for researchers, practitioners and AI-mediated indexing systems. The framework runs live in the author's operational environment and is offered as a starting point inviting practitioner application and extension rather than as a finished doctrine.

title: From Attitudes to Infrastructure: A Multilevel Review of AI Adoption in Healthcare
affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology and Middle Tennessee State University

detail.title: From Attitudes to Infrastructure: A Multilevel Review of AI Adoption in Healthcare
detail.abstract: The development and advancement of AI have been progressed since 1955. Its growth in the healthcare system has resulted in more improved and efficient patient care. For example, a neural network used to diagnose liver diseases caused by the hepatitis virus achieved 97.59% accuracy and exceeded human diagnostic performance in specific contexts. While these advancements have resulted in a rapid adoption rate by hospitals in the 21 st century, a holistic view encompassing both individual and organizational aspects of AI adoption can help healthcare organizations become more informed and take a proactive approach for unexpected events during the adoption process. The current study used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis' (PRISMA) guidelines to review articles applying the Theory of Planned Behavior and the Technology-Organization-Environment framework in medical settings. Results showed that, among individual factors attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control affect AI adoption. Among technological factors, while perceived usefulness, data quality, data accuracy, and interoperability drive adoption, technological complexity and lack of transparency in AI systems hinder adoption process. Among organizational factors, organizational readiness, leadership support, training availability, and digital infrastructure facilitate adoption; and limited resources, resistance from healthcare professionals, workflow misalignment hinder adoption process. Among environmental factors, government regulations and legal frameworks, external pressures, policy support, and trust in AI systems may drive or hinder adoption. This combination integrates literature by providing an overview of both micro-level psychological factors and macro-level structural factors. Practically, the synthesis of diverse research results can help healthcare organizations, medical AI developers, and policymakers to develop a realistic perspective toward AI adoption.

title: Strategic Throttling in Large Cloud Computing Platforms
affiliations: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, University of Texas at Austin and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Information, Risk and Operations Management

detail.title: Strategic Throttling in Large Cloud Computing Platforms

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted to appear in Information Systems Research.

detail.abstract: Large cloud providers compete on price and service quality while serving customers who differ in willingness to pay and delay sensitivity. We model this competition for cloud platforms where computing time is non-storable and service quality depends on processing speed and interruption risk. When the customer base is large enough, aggregate uncertainty in capacity utilization vanishes in steady state, so that static pricing and precise segmentation by quality become viable. The provider leverages this predictability by partitioning capacity into service tranches that throttle lower-tier users, inducing self-selection into contracts that differ in speed and interruption probability. A pay-as-bid auction implements the provider-optimal allocation while preserving incentive compatibility. Under duopolistic competition, efficient quality provision emerges when switching costs are low or vertical heterogeneity is large-driven either by competitive pressure or by a platform's incentive to expand coverage. Our results reveal a key trade-off: scale reduces demand uncertainty and improves operational efficiency, but the resulting market power sustains service throttling. Lowering switching costs or promoting interoperability improves welfare more effectively than structural interventions that reduce scale.

title: How AI Agent Deployment Structure Shapes Investor Evaluations: A Processing Fluency Perspective on One-Person Companies
affiliations: , , , Independent and University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)

detail.title: How AI Agent Deployment Structure Shapes Investor Evaluations: A Processing Fluency Perspective on One-Person Companies
detail.abstract: The One-Person Company (OPC) is an emerging human-AI collaboration model referring to a venture in which a single founder coordinates an ensemble of specialized AI agents that perform all operational work. Despite growing real-world adoption, how structure design shapes the cognitive responses of external evaluators remains theoretically unexamined. Drawing on complex adaptive systems (CAS) and processing fluency theory (PFT), we propose that agent control mode (centralized vs. decentralized) and workflow pattern (sequential vs. parallel) in OPC differentially influence investors' processing fluency, which in turn drives investment intentions and investors' word-of-mouth. We further theorize that agent control mode and workflow pattern operate as cognitive substitutes rather than complements. We test our hypotheses in an online experiment with 274 investors. Results show that centralized control and sequential workflow each independently enhance processing fluency, which in turn improves investor evaluations. However, when both features are present at the same time, each one's marginal contribution to fluency is reduced. Our findings contribute to Information Systems research by extending human-AI interaction research from dyadic to one-to-many configurations, integrating CAS and PFT to explain external cognition of complex AI-driven organizations, and revealing a substitution dynamic in how conjunctive structural properties jointly shape evaluative outcomes.

title: Designing for Structural AI Failure: Interface Stress Testing the Gap Between AI Capability Claims and Grounded Reality

detail.title: Designing for Structural AI Failure: Interface Stress Testing the Gap Between AI Capability Claims and Grounded Reality

detail.abstract:
Current multimodal AI systems exhibit reproducible, diagnosable architectural class failures in spatial reasoning, physical coherence, and temporal consistency. These represent hallmarks of current transformer architectures rather than model-specific artifacts. These failures are collectively described as the Inversion Error, a diagnosis independently supported by Ma et al, who report that current 3D large language models systematically fail to understand 3D spatial relationships. The failures are invisible from within the systems that produce them not only because the architecture lacks the physical grounding layer (Enactive floor) that detection would require, but because that absence is structural rather than incidental. They are visible from outside them because the embodied human observer stands on exactly that layer. This position paper proposes to exploit this diagnostic asymmetry by reorienting AI-focused Human-Computer Interaction design practice: from designing interfaces that smooth over AI failure modes, to interfaces that deliberately expose them.

The Inversion Error position paper established the first designer role in this two-paper socio-technical systems research program: the socio-technical systems designer as diagnostic architect, exposing the structural condition in current transformer architectures from outside the engineering system. That paper diagnosed and named the condition; this paper proposes the intervention at the level of the second designer role. Where the diagnostic architect identifies what is wrong with the architecture, the interface designer as More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) provides what it structurally lacks: the embodied physical grounding that makes AI outputs coherent in a physical world. The mechanism for the embodied physical grounding is Reinforcement Learning from Physical Feedback (RLPF): encoding physical constraints as differentiable priors inside the neural architecture rather than imposing them as post-hoc corrections on its outputs.

Building on the HCI tradition, within which screen-based interaction remains the dominant paradigm, I propose a two-phase stress testing program. Phase 1, the Spaghetti Table Protocol Challenge, operates at the screen-based level: a distributed research effort that scales diagnostic methodology across the design and HCI research communities using existing interfaces. Phase 2, the Universe Falling Apart Protocol, extends this program into embodied XR environments, grounded in the emerging premise of Human+Computer (H+C) Immersion: that the human user and the computational system can be co-present in a single environment where the symbolic and the embodied are united rather than separated by an interface layer. Where screen-based interaction exposes AI grounding failures symbolically, embodied interaction exposes them physically, generating the RLPF signal at the level of direct sensorimotor engagement. Shneiderman's principle that governance must match autonomy level provides the regulatory frame; H+C Immersion provides the ontological one. 2D screen-based HCI interface stress testing offers an excellent starting point for the methodology; 3D multimodal immersion is the next step.

Drawing on the Chaos Engineering tradition in software reliability, I introduce the Chaos Monkey for the Inversion Error: a class of interface designs that leverage human embodied cognition as a diagnostic instrument for detecting AI architectural failures. I present the Spaghetti Table Protocol as a proof-of-concept screen-based stress testing methodology, reporting an aggregate diagnostic score of 4 out of 30 across three leading multimodal systems. The logged outputs of this stress testing constitute training data for RLPF: the mechanism through which the interface designer as MKO provides the physical grounding signal that current AI training pipelines do not collect. Phase 2, the Universe Falling Apart Protocol, is inspired by Philip K. Dick's argument about the ontological persistence of reality turned into a diagnostic criterion: an AI-generated environment passes the stress test if it holds together under embodied, multimodal human interaction.Together, the two phases produce the dataset and the RLPF training signal that foundation model architectures require to address the Inversion Error at the level of structure rather than output.

detail.abstract: The Optimizing the Human Weapon System (OHWS) program was one of the most developed examples of integrated wearable-technology monitoring in U.S. Army formations. Originating in 2020 in response to a request from the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology, OHWS was deployed across operational units and institutional training environments and placed wearables on more than two thousand warfighters across a roughly six-year program life. Barring extraordinary intervention from Congress or Army leadership, OHWS is scheduled to conclude at the end of Fiscal Year 2026. I served as a primary advisor to the program during its first four years (2020–2023) and produced an internal return-on-investment review for the program’s institutional sponsor in 2023. This paper draws on those four years of observation and reframes them for an academic audience as the program approaches sunset. I describe the program’s four-phase assess–prescribe–implement–reassess ecosystem, the device suite and the Holistic Health Performance and Data Management System that aggregated it, and the flagging architecture that converted individual physiological data into actionable command and clinical signals. I report three categories of findings: an illustrative leadership decision in the 4th Battalion, 31st Infantry Regiment (4-31 IN) in which sleep data drove a unit-level shift schedule revision; the data flow architecture and the routing of individual-level information to medical and human-performance staff; and the participation, withdrawal, and consent patterns observed across the program. I close with implications for leaders considering similar programs and locate the observations within the Performance-Responsive Leadership Framework developed in a companion theoretical paper. The intent is to elevate the lessons of a six-year public-sector wearable-monitoring program for the next generation of public-sector practitioners who will design and lead similar efforts.

title: From Artifact Governance to Institutional Cognition: A Governance Ontology for AI-Native Organizational Systems

detail.abstract: AI governance still often treats models, applications, and outputs as the primary objects to be evaluated, certified, monitored, or controlled. That orientation was plausible for many bounded software artifacts whose functions, interfaces, and organizational roles were comparatively stable. AI-native organizational systems create a different governance problem: organizational knowledge, judgment, action, and memory are increasingly routed through dynamic configurations of models, retrieval, memory, tools, interfaces, workflows, human roles, generated artifacts, and downstream reliance. This paper develops a governance ontology for this shift. It argues that the relevant object is the institutional cognition pathway: the socio-technical pathway through which AI-mediated behavior is produced, represented, stored, reused, and relied upon inside organizations. On this view, organizationally consequential AI behavior is configuration-produced rather than model-contained. It emerges from conditioned assembly across model capability, context, orchestration, interaction, artifact formation, and organizational uptake. The paper distinguishes stochastic output, adaptive response, and emergent pathway behavior as analytically different governance phenomena. It then derives bounded emergence as the design objective for AI-native institutional systems: preserving useful adaptive latitude while maintaining behavioral envelopes, admissibility, recoverability, contestability, and institutional legitimacy. Orchestration is theorized as the runtime constitution layer through which those bounds become executable, while epistemic artifacts are theorized as the persistence layer through which AI outputs become organizational memory and knowledge infrastructure. The paper's payoff is governance engineering as pathway stewardship. Rather than proposing a static compliance checklist or one-time certification model, it offers a foundational theory for governing AI-native organizational systems by identifying, bounding, observing, intervening on, and learning from institutional cognition pathways over time.

title: Digital Washing in Global Logistics: How the Absence of Standardised DSCC Disclosure Frameworks Creates an Unverifiable Performance Narrative

detail.abstract: Digital transformation has become the defining strategic narrative in global logistics, with leading firms routinely asserting that investments in artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, blockchain, and predictive analytics are delivering measurable operational improvements. Yet a fundamental question persists: how do these firms actually demonstrate that claim, and can it be independently verified? This study investigates precisely that tension. Through qualitative thematic analysis of annual reports and sustainability disclosures published by four global logistics leaders, DHL, FedEx, Maersk, and UPS, between 2021 and 2025, this paper examines how digital supply chain capabilities (DSCCs) are disclosed and whether those disclosures establish verifiable links to operational key performance indicators (KPIs) including delivery accuracy, cost per shipment, inventory turnover, and order fulfilment rates. The analysis is grounded in three complementary theoretical frameworks: the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and the Technology-Organisation-Environment model. Findings reveal a persistent and consequential asymmetry in disclosure practice across the four firms. While all four assert the strategic value of their digital investments, they differ substantially in whether and how those investments are connected to measurable performance evidence. UPS provides quantifiable, traceable metrics linking specific digital tools to concrete operational outcomes. DHL, FedEx, and Maersk rely predominantly on qualitative narratives, strategic language, and case studies that describe digital activity without establishing performance accountability. In the absence of standardised disclosure frameworks for DSCC performance, digital transformation claims in logistics remain structurally unverifiable, a condition that limits investor accountability, obstructs cross-firm benchmarking, and leaves regulators without the evidentiary basis needed for meaningful scrutiny. The paper argues that the logistics industry requires independently developed, sector-specific reporting standards that treat digital capability claims with the same rigour currently applied to financial disclosures.

title: More Channels, Lower Scores: Entertainment Television and Student Achievement

detail.abstract: We study the effects of expanded entertainment television on children's academic performance leveraging the staggered transition from analog to digital TV across Italian provinces between 2008 and 2012, which greatly increased children's entertainment content, and administrative data on standardized test scores for entire cohorts of primary and middle school students. Availability of digital TV reduced literacy and math performance by 0.08 and 0.12 standard deviations, respectively, implying effects of −0.20 and −0.30 standard deviations among children who acquired access to digital TV along the transition. Effects are larger among younger children and among students attending school only in the morning.

detail.abstract: This paper documents the unintended consequence of fiscal rules in the form of tax expenditures using both theory and data. We first introduce a simple fiscal model where the government has time-inconsistent preferences with a present bias toward public spending in line with Halac and Yared (2014). We then empirically validate the main prediction of the model by providing evidence that the adoption of a binding fiscal rule on public spending leads to an increase in tax expenditures, whereas revenue rules, which do not constrain spending, leave them unaffected. Our findings suggest the existence of a robust "innovation channel" in the fiscal domain—paralleling regulatory capital requirements in banking.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolution and current state of Russian-Syrian trade and economic cooperation against the backdrop of the radical geopolitical and political transformations in late 2024. Long established as a key strategic and economic partner for Russia in the Middle East, Syria’s recent regime change raises critical questions regarding the future stability of bilateral trade flows, particularly in essential sectors such as grain, fuel, pharmaceuticals, and industrial equipment. Additionally, this study analyzes how ongoing international sanctions complicate logistics, banking transactions, and major infrastructure investment. Ultimately, the paper provides a practical and theoretical framework for understanding how political transitions reshape foreign trade priorities and the displacement or retention of traditional international partnerships in the region.

detail.abstract: The aim of this research is to investigate the critical HR factors that have the greatest impact on employee retention in School Bus Companies in Panama City. This gives the opportunity to identify and address different internal and external environmental factors that can impact employee retention based on managers' and drivers' opinions. This research also allows the researcher to identify organisational variables that affect the drivers' satisfaction and motivation levels. This research is also aiming to determine the impact of leadership on employee retention and the preferable leadership styles among drivers in the School Bus Companies in Panama City. In addition, it also looks into understanding the job and role demands that can affect employee retention. The literature review identified several factors that seem to have an influence on employee retention. These internal and environmental factors have been implemented as the base of the research. These factors include Recruitment and Selection, Training and Development, Work-Life Balance, Job Satisfaction, Leadership, Motivation and Performance as well as Organisational Culture and Work Environment, Psychological Contract and Commitment, Compensations and Rewards, and Communication. This study is carried out in three School Bus Companies in Panama City, focusing on the four owners acting as managers as well as the 53 drivers. Managers together with drivers share their opinions regarding different internal and external factors but most importantly about employee retention. Based on the findings, the researcher was able to identify four main variables that had the greatest influence on employee retention. These elements are communication, motivation, job satisfaction and leadership. Similarly, the findings also conclude that in the school bus driving industry in Panama City, nonmonetary rewards seem to be more important than monetary rewards highlighting that compensation is not as important as communication. In addition, this research also proposes a theoretical working model in order to increase employee retention levels. The model focuses on the four key elements (communication, leadership, motivation and satisfaction) found throughout this research and includes different internal and external factors that can have an impact on employee retention.

title: Twin-Anchor Fair Volatility and Cascaded Gate Selection for Short-Volatility Option Structures Public Release

detail.title: Twin-Anchor Fair Volatility and Cascaded Gate Selection for Short-Volatility Option Structures Public Release
detail.abstract: Short-volatility selection usually stacks uncoupled rules: IV rank, delta strikes, return-onrisk, and a single probability heuristic. We specify an alternative coupled pipeline: Gatheral SVI defines fair implied vol σ IVfair ; Longstaff-Schwartz Monte Carlo prices American legs at σ IVfair (not at market IV); per-leg volatility edge uses joint vol-dollar residuals net of costs; a three-stage probability cascade (P RN → P real → P eff) feeds both managed-loss expectancy and Kelly sizing; expected shortfall normalized by structure max loss gates tail risk before booking; competing structure classes share one gate algebra and lexicographic rank. We contrast this framework with conventional practice, state eight methodological contributions (twin-anchor fair pricing, dual-channel edge, cascaded probability, managed-loss entry, structure ES gate, unified competition, regime-split prescreen vs gates, American-European consistency boundary), and derive the pricing operators (Black-Scholes, Crank-Nicolson, Dupire, SVI, LSM, binomial). Operational calibration is omitted (Section 1).

title: When to Broaden, When to Focus: Job Search and Market Tightness

detail.title: When to Broaden, When to Focus: Job Search and Market Tightness
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether directing job search toward tight labor markets improves re-employment. Such targeting is theoretically attractive as it reduces aggregate congestion. I link Swiss unemployment records to clickstream search data to measure which markets jobseekers target. To address selection, I exploit quasi-random assignment to caseworkers differing in their tendency to redirect clients toward tight markets. Moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile raises six-month job-finding by 2.7%. The channels are heterogeneous: jobseekers who become unemployed in slack markets gain from mobility, consistent with prior findings from policies that encourage broader search. The new insight is that jobseekers who become unemployed in tight markets benefit from a narrower focus on this initial market. Effects are orthogonal to other caseworker behaviors and do not come at the expense of job quality. My findings suggest that market tightness offers a simple basis for targeted search advice.

title: Recursive Intelligence in Medicine: A Human-AI Synergy Framework for the EHR Era

detail.title: Recursive Intelligence in Medicine: A Human-AI Synergy Framework for the EHR Era

declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Context: As artificial intelligence becomes deeply integrated into clinical practice, the medical profession faces a choice that has not been adequately framed in either the health policy or informatics literature. This article introduces Human-AI Synergy as a framework for that choice, grounded in a model of Recursive Human-AI Interaction that reconceives the relationship between physician and AI as iterative and mutually generative rather than competitive or simply assistive. 

Methods: Drawing on industrial organization theory, cognitive science, and institutional economics, the article develops a structural analysis of how electronic health records have created the informational architecture that currently shapes AI integration in clinical settings, and why that architecture, left unreformed, produces what this article terms the validation trap. 

Findings: EHRs have gradually shifted the physician's epistemic role from primary evaluator to interpreter of a pre-structured record over three decades. AI systems are optimized for exactly the standardized environment EHRs have created, accelerating a narrowing of clinical judgment that is individually unremarkable but cumulatively transformative. Errors embedded in the longitudinal record are not merely propagated across encounters but operationalized through AI training, compounding the structural risk. 

Conclusions: The dominant automation-versus-augmentation frame in healthcare AI policy is inadequate. Human-AI Synergy, realized through Recursive Human-AI Interaction, offers a superior framework for EHR and AI system design. Four design principles and policy recommendations for healthcare organizations, regulators, medical educators, and technology vendors are offered.

title: Acuity Adjusted Nurse Staffing and Patient Processes and Outcomes in an Emergency Department: A Retrospective Longitudinal Study

detail.title: Acuity Adjusted Nurse Staffing and Patient Processes and Outcomes in an Emergency Department: A Retrospective Longitudinal Study
detail.abstract: Background: Emergency departments are experiencing crowding and delays in care, which are associated with poorer patient outcomes. Nurse staffing is a key determinant of patient throughput and outcomes, but much of the existing research relies on indicators such as average nurse-to-patient ratios that do not account for daily variation in patient acuity. Acuity-adjusted measures of staffing that reflect the balance between available nursing hours and patient care requirements may provide a more accurate understanding of how nurse staffing affects emergency department performance.Objective: To examine the association between nurse staffing, adjusted for daily case-mix acuity, and patient processes and outcomes. Design: Retrospective longitudinal study.Setting: Emergency department of a university hospital. Participants: Administrative data from 67,010 patients corresponding to 115,078 adult visits over 787 consecutive days.Methods: Routinely collected emergency department data from January 2018 to February 2020 were analysed, with each 24-hour period as the unit of analysis. Actual nursing hours were taken from rosters. Required nursing hours were estimated by linking each patient’s Manchester Triage System category to a pre-determined nursing care time. A staffing deficit was defined as actual minus required hours. Process measures were time to triage, and wait to be seen; outcome measures were patient experience time, and leaving without being seen. Models were run unadjusted and adjusted for potential confounders.Results: On average, 85% of visits were triaged as urgent or very urgent. On 88% of days, actual nursing hours were below the estimated requirement. Median times were 21 minutes to triage, 2.1 hours to be seen, and a median of 7.0 hours total patient experience time. Staffing deficits were associated with poorer patient processes and outcomes (p < 0.001). Each 5-hour deficit (versus no deficit) in nurse staffing was associated with a 21% increase in time to triage (RGM 1.21; 95% CI 1.19 to 1.23), a 12% increase in wait to be seen (RGM 1.12; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.14), a 7% increase in patient experience time (RGM 1.07; 95% CI 1.05 to 1.09), and 16% higher odds of a patient leaving without being seen (OR 1.16; 95% CI 1.11 to 1.22). Conclusions: Lower nurse staffing relative to patient acuity was associated with delays across all stages of care and more patients leaving without being seen. An acuity-adjusted staffing metric provides a more accurate relationship between staffing and patient need than simple nurse-to-patient ratios supporting its use in determining safe emergency department staffing.

title: The Information Curse in Turbulent Supply Chains: Expectations-Based Reference Dependence and Operational Efficiency
affiliations: ,  and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: The Information Curse in Turbulent Supply Chains: Expectations-Based Reference Dependence and Operational Efficiency

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: To navigate unpredictable supply chain turbulence, firms increasingly invest in advanced predictive analytics, operating on the classical assumption that more information enhances supply chain decisions. However, this paradigm overlooks the behavioral realities of corporate planning, where managers evaluate realized outcomes against anticipated operational targets. We investigate this dynamic using a principalagent model in which a manager chooses between a conservative supply chain option with certain returns and an aggressive alternative with higher operating benefits but uncertain disruption costs. Crucially, before the manager forms a plan, the Board of Directors determines the firm's information architecture: they decide whether to adopt an advanced system that provides the complete probability distribution of the disruption risk, making the manager fully informed, or to rely on a basic system that yields only a single deterministic signal, leaving the manager partially informed. Assuming the manager exhibits expectations-based, reference-dependent preferences, our analysis reveals a novel "information curse": providing complete predictive transparency often degrades the firm's supply chain efficiency while simultaneously increasing the manager's ex-ante expected utility. For the manager, full information acts as a psychological buffer that perfectly calibrates expectations and minimizes painful gain-loss shocks. Yet, this stabilization induces behavioral hesitation, driving sub-optimal physical execution. In contrast, a partially informed manager treats a limited signal as deterministic, bypassing the burden of over-comparison and frequently achieving higher objective efficiency. Finally, we establish that structural cost reductions inversely impact efficiency and managerial utility across information states. Our findings caution that corporate boards must strictly coordinate policy levers with their push for digitization, ensuring that advanced transparency does not merely create "illusive happiness" for the agent at the expense of the firm.

title: Strategic Intelligence Architecture for Business Intelligence-Enabled Supply Chain Intermediation in Emerging Markets: Insights from Vietnam's Agricultural and Chemical Sector

detail.title: Strategic Intelligence Architecture for Business Intelligence-Enabled Supply Chain Intermediation in Emerging Markets: Insights from Vietnam's Agricultural and Chemical Sector
detail.abstract:
Business Intelligence (BI) has become a critical strategic capability for supply chain intermediaries operating in volatile commodity markets, yet evidence from asset-light trading firms in Southeast Asia remains limited. This study develops and validates a four-layer Strategic Intelligence Architecture (SIA) for LAEXIM, a Vietnamese startup engaged in agricultural inputs, industrial chemicals, and premium wines.

Using ten proprietary Vietnamese customs datasets (2015–2025) covering 31,259 shipment records across agricultural chemicals, fertilizers, rice, cashew kernels, feed ingredients, coated paper, and industrial chemicals, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of price volatility, supply concentration, and working capital risks within Vietnam’s commodity trading ecosystem.

Key findings indicate: (i) heavy dependence on China for critical agricultural chemicals (SA: 91.2%; NH4Cl: 95.8%); (ii) substantial commodity price volatility affecting procurement costs; (iii) strong growth in the hydrogen peroxide market; (iv) significant pricing variation across export destinations for cashew products; (v) large-scale rice export flows requiring advanced logistics and compliance capabilities; (vi) complex multi-origin sourcing structures in coated paper imports; and (vii) persistent information asymmetries disadvantaging domestic SME traders.

The proposed SIA combines an ETL-based data warehouse, predictive pricing models, supplier reliability scoring, and executive KPI dashboards. Financial simulations suggest net margin improvements of 1.5–2.0 percentage points, inventory cost reductions of 15–20%, and a payback period of less than one month. The study contributes to BI strategy, supply chain analytics, and emerging-market SME research by offering an empirically grounded framework applicable to commodity trading firms across Southeast Asia.

detail.abstract: We document regime-dependent predictability in the U.S. SBIR Phase II to venture capital pipeline. On 8332 Phase II SBIR/STTR awardees indexed 2010-2022, concordance falls from 0.668 under random crossvalidation to 0.565 under strict time-split validation; within-regime validation partially recovers it, localising the implied regime change to 2018-2019. The gap survives nine robustness corrections and replicates on the broader Phase I sample (n = 14 156): the predictive axis (firm-trajectory and embedding features) replicates there, while the behavioral axis (grant cadence, submission timing) attenuates, consistent with survivor selection. A regime-aware specification yields a top-decile lift of 1.50× (95% CI [1.06, 1.99]).

title: The Digitalization of Arbitration in Africa: Enhancing Access to Justice or Entrenching Inequality?

detail.title: The Digitalization of Arbitration in Africa: Enhancing Access to Justice or Entrenching Inequality?
detail.abstract:
The digitalization of arbitration has emerged as one of the most significant developments in contemporary dispute resolution. Accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, arbitral institutions and practitioners across the world have increasingly adopted virtual hearings, electronic filings, and online case management systems.2 In Africa, where arbitration continues to grow as a mechanism for resolving commercial disputes, digital technologies present an opportunity to improve efficiency and expand access to justice.3 However, the shift towards digital arbitration also raises critical concerns regarding fairness, equality, and inclusivity.

This paper examines whether the digitalization of arbitration in Africa enhances access to justice or risks entrenching existing socio-economic inequalities. It argues that while digital arbitration has the potential to democratize dispute resolution by removing geographical barriers and lowering procedural costs, its benefits remain unevenly distributed due to infrastructural disparities, technological illiteracy, and the persistent digital divide. Through an evaluation of African arbitration institutions, the paper demonstrates that digital arbitration must be implemented cautiously to safeguard procedural fairness. The paper concludes that digitalization should complement rather than replace traditional arbitration mechanisms. This piece further suggests that regulatory reform and digital infrastructure development is essential to ensure that technological innovation strengthens access to justice.

title:
Bifurcated Cross-Sectional Inference on Continuous Commodity Futures

A Roll-Aware Fusion Architecture with Mandatory Directional Exposure and Orthogonal Priority Ranking
affiliations: Yale University

Bifurcated Cross-Sectional Inference on Continuous Commodity Futures

A Roll-Aware Fusion Architecture with Mandatory Directional Exposure and Orthogonal Priority Ranking
detail.abstract: We present a mathematical proof-of-concept for daily cross-sectional scanning of vendor-spliced commodity continuous futures. The framework departs from the dominant long-flat-short paradigm: every symbol receives a mandatory Buy or Sell label-there is no neutral, hold, or abstain state at the inference layer-while conviction magnitude lives in a continuous composite C i and an orthogonal priority score Opp i. The contribution is architectural. We show how roll-calendar skepticism, disciplined volatility state estimation, dual-layer headline sentiment, short-horizon drift, and simulated path diagnostics can be fused into a signed decision rule whose internal disagreements are surfaced but not silently overridden. This manuscript supplies conceptual equations, explanatory figures, and descriptive documentation for interpreting cross-sectional scan outputs. Calibrated parameter values are application-specific and omitted here for brevity.

title: Investor Disputes in Nigeria: Arbitration, Litigation and Enforcement Risks Every Investor Should Understand

detail.title: Investor Disputes in Nigeria: Arbitration, Litigation and Enforcement Risks Every Investor Should Understand
detail.abstract: Foreign investors should plan carefully for disputes in Nigeria, a large emerging economy with a pro-arbitration stance. Nigeria is a party to the ICSID Convention and the New York Convention 1 , 2 and its modern Arbitration and Mediation Act of 2023 (AMA) incorporates these treaties into domestic law 3. 4. In practice this means that, when properly structured, arbitration agreements and awards are generally upheld and enforceable. Below we examine key aspects of dispute clauses, forum and law choices, enforcement of awards/judgments, interim relief, and common pitfalls for foreign parties. All points are supported by Nigerian statutes and case law or expert commentary, as cited. Arbitration Clauses in Contracts Nigeria's arbitration law is now largely based on the UNCITRAL Model Law.

title: Internal vs. External Barriers to Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM): An Empirical Study of Egypt's Petrochemical Sector
affiliations: , Effat University and

detail.title: Internal vs. External Barriers to Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM): An Empirical Study of Egypt's Petrochemical Sector
detail.abstract: This study addresses the critical problem of barriers hindering Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM) adoption in Egypt's petrochemical sector, a major economic driver that produces approximately 4.5 million tons annually but generates significant GHG emissions and hazardous waste. The objective is to identify, rank, and analyze the hierarchical relationships among internal and external barriers using a mixed-methods approach. This study focuses on the full petrochemical supply chain in Egypt, encompassing upstream (raw material sourcing), midstream (manufacturing/refining processes), and downstream (distribution, waste management, reverse logistics), with an emphasis on emission/waste reduction practices. Data were collected via a structured questionnaire from 400 employees in Egyptian petrochemical firms and analyzed using Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM). The findings showed that internal impediments, such as a lack of corporate leadership and support (IB1), a critical shortage of resources (IB6), and the absence of green initiatives (IB5), serve as driving forces that exert a cascading influence over the external barriers, which include insufficient government support (EB1), a lack of markets for recycled materials (EB5), and human resources or expertise shortages (EB7). The study contributes to the existing literature on GSCM by incorporating international trends and specifically addressing Egyptian issues, including weak policies, difficult supply chains, high energy-intensive operations, and costly operations. The study suggests that sending clear messages from the top and providing financial incentives can help push the obstacles aside and guide the industry down the path of environmentally responsible operations.

title: A Multi-Dimensional Labeling System for "Fixed Income Plus" Fund Managers: An Integrated Approach Combining Quantitative Metrics, Portfolio Structure, and Large Language Model Analysis

detail.title: A Multi-Dimensional Labeling System for "Fixed Income Plus" Fund Managers: An Integrated Approach Combining Quantitative Metrics, Portfolio Structure, and Large Language Model Analysis
detail.abstract: Background: With the rapid expansion of "fixed income plus" (FI+) fund products-including secondary bond funds and convertible bond funds-investors increasingly demand tools for manager style identification and performance attribution. Conventional fund evaluation relies on single quantitative metrics or opaque qualitative ratings, which fail to capture the multi-dimensional nature of FI+ strategies. Objective: This study constructs a six-dimensional labeling system for FI+ fund managers by integrating quantitative metrics, portfolio structure, and large language model (LLM) textual analysis, and systematically compares fund performance across label combinations. Methods: We select 25 representative FI+ funds (15 secondary bond funds + 10 convertible bond funds) from January 2022 to December 2024. Three analytical layers are employed: (1) nine quantitative indicators computed from daily net-asset-value (NAV) data; (2) bond-type classification and credit-downgrade analysis based on portfolio holdings; and (3) structured text analysis of 224 fund periodic reports using DeepSeek Chat large language model via API (temperature = 0.1). A six-dimensional label system is built covering "return-risk profile," "operating style," "drawdown control," "equity style," "interest-rate band," and "credit style." Findings: (1) Low-volatility funds (annualized volatility < 3%) achieved an average return of 2.4%, significantly outperforming high-volatility funds at-2.33% (Kruskal-Wallis test, *p* < 0.05). (2) "Left-side layout" funds exhibited a significantly higher Sharpe ratio (0.38) than "right-side follower" funds (-0.13)(Wilcoxon rank-sum test, W = 15, p = 0.042). (3) Managers with a neutral sentiment expression outperformed those with dominant optimism (annualized 0.58% vs.-1.72%). (4) Credit-downgrade strategies did not generate excess returns during the sample period. Implications: The labeling framework provides an objective, quantifiable toolkit for fund screening, performance attribution, and product design. The methodology is replicable and extensible to other fund categories.

title: Aid Transitions and Agricultural Productivity: Evidence from Zimbabwe and Zambia after 2000

detail.title: Aid Transitions and Agricultural Productivity: Evidence from Zimbabwe and Zambia after 2000
detail.abstract: This paper describes the structural impacts of foreign aid delivery methods on agricultural sector performance, distinguishing between long-term development capital and short-term humanitarian relief. Leveraging a post-2000 policy divergence where donors redirected Zimbabwe's capital aid entirely into humanitarian relief for political reasons while maintaining Zambia's structural lines, I evaluate a macro-panel of caloric land productivities (1980-2024). Panel estimations (FGLS and autoregressive) show that shifting to humanitarian aid correlated with a severe structural contraction: an immediate 41.32% yield drop that deepens to a 47.78% long-run cumulative loss. These results formalize the "humanitarian trap," demonstrating that emergency relief cannot substitute for capital accumulation.

title: Machine Learning for Predictive Analytics for Agricultural Water Sustainability
affiliations: The British University in Dubai

detail.title: Machine Learning for Predictive Analytics for Agricultural Water Sustainability
detail.abstract: Agricultural water sustainability has become a critical global concern due to climate change, increasing water scarcity, population growth, and the rising demand for food production. Traditional irrigation and water management approaches often fail to optimize water use efficiency and respond effectively to dynamic environmental conditions. This study explores the role of machine learning (ML) in predictive analytics for improving agricultural water sustainability through intelligent decision-making, real-time monitoring, and data-driven forecasting models. The research examines how advanced ML algorithms, including regression models, neural networks, decision trees, and deep learning techniques, can analyse large-scale agricultural and environmental datasets to predict irrigation requirements, soil moisture levels, crop water demand, drought risks, and climate variability. Furthermore, the study highlights the integration of Internet of Things (IoT), remote sensing technologies, geographic information systems (GIS), and big data analytics to enhance precision agriculture and sustainable water resource management. The paper also discusses the benefits of predictive analytics in reducing water waste, increasing crop productivity, improving resource allocation, and supporting environmental sustainability objectives. In addition, challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, infrastructure limitations, model uncertainty, and implementation costs are critically evaluated. The findings indicate that machine learning-driven predictive systems can significantly improve agricultural water management efficiency and contribute to resilient and sustainable farming ecosystems. The study concludes by emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, policy support, and technological innovation to accelerate the adoption of intelligent water sustainability solutions in modern agriculture.

title: Anti-Camping Ordinances, State Preemption, and the Arrest of People Experiencing Homelessness: Evidence from Orange County, Florida
affiliations: University of Central Florida and University of Central Florida

detail.title: Anti-Camping Ordinances, State Preemption, and the Arrest of People Experiencing Homelessness: Evidence from Orange County, Florida
detail.abstract: Anti-camping laws have proliferated across American state and local governments, intertwined with the Supreme Court's 2024 Grants Pass v. Johnson decision that further allowed their legal authority. Research has documented the harmful effects of these laws and others targeting behaviors associated with homelessness for unhoused persons from their perspectives, but little has analyzed the enforcement patterns. We examine this question using administrative jail booking records from Orange County, Florida (N = 96,669 bookings, January 2022-June 2025), including both the implementation of a local anti-camping ordinance in January 2024 and a statewide preemption law in January 2025. Using an interrupted time series design, we estimate the association between each policy's implementation and weekly homeless bookings and the composition of charges. Although camping charges about tripled after the state preemption law compared to before, the local ordinance associates with no detectable change in homeless bookings or camping-specific enforcement, making attribution to the ordinance uncertain. The rise is likely a result of a rising rate of arrests prior to the law. However, there are large increases in arrests of unhoused persons from open-container laws (400%) and share of arrests that are homeless-targeting charges (38%). Collectively, these findings imply that post-policy enforcement dynamics likely reflected a combination of ongoing trends, broader policing or governance changes, and evolving homelessness conditions rather than a singular causal effect of the local ordinance or state law.

title: Quantifying Digital Harm to Minors: A Risk-Scoring Framework for Litigation, Insurance, and Policy

detail.title: Quantifying Digital Harm to Minors: A Risk-Scoring Framework for Litigation, Insurance, and Policy

detail.abstract: The adolescent mental health crisis attributable to social media platform design has generated one of the most consequential waves of mass tort litigation in American legal history. Yet the field lacks a standardized, defensible methodology for quantifying the magnitude of harm that individual platforms impose on minors-a gap that impedes litigation strategy, insurance underwriting, school procurement decisions, and evidence-based policy. This paper proposes the TeenAegis Digital Harm Index (DHI), a multi-dimensional risk-scoring framework adapted from financial risk quantification methodology and applied to the specific harm vectors documented in academic research, regulatory findings, and litigation discovery. Drawing on credit risk scoring architecture, Basel III operational risk principles, and ESG materiality frameworks, the DHI scores platforms across five harm dimensions: algorithmic amplification, design exploitability, data extraction intensity, crisis response adequacy, and jurisdictional compliance posture. The framework produces a composite score on a 0-100 scale, enabling comparative platform benchmarking, trend monitoring, and expert witness testimony grounded in a reproducible, peer-reviewable methodology. Applications for plaintiff counsel, reinsurance underwriters, school district procurement officers, and state legislators are discussed.

title: An Analytical Framework to Analyze Challenges and Opportunities for Medical Tourism in Host (Developing) Countries

detail.title: An Analytical Framework to Analyze Challenges and Opportunities for Medical Tourism in Host (Developing) Countries

detail.abstract: Medical tourism creates an important policy trade-off for host countries. Foreign patients can generate revenue for private hospitals and support healthcare-sector growth, but they may also draw capacity away from domestic patients who rely on the same private providers and the public hospital system. We study when medical tourism benefits or harms domestic patients and society in the host country, and how policymakers can regulate the balance between foreignpatient demand from developed countries and domestic healthcare access in developing countries. Methodology/results: We develop an analytical model of a host country healthcare market with a private hospital, a public hospital, domestic patients, and foreign medical tourists. The model captures hospitals' capacity and pricing decisions and patients' hospital choices. We compare outcomes with and without medical tourism and examine two policy levers: public hospital capacity and restrictions on the private hospital's foreign-to-domestic capacity mix. We find that medical tourism can reduce domestic patient welfare by shifting private capacity toward foreign patients, but its effect on overall welfare depends on the cost of expanding private capacity and on how prices, congestion, profits, and market coverage adjust. Public capacity can discipline private hospital behavior, while proportionality rules that link foreign-patient capacity to domestic-patient capacity can protect domestic access. Managerial implications: The paper provides a framework for evaluating medical tourism through data-driven country contextualization. Using publicly available country and healthcare-market data, we show how the same policy can have different welfare consequences across host countries. In cost-driven settings such as India, policy should protect domestic access and redistribute provider-side gains, whereas in highly internationalized settings such as Thailand, regulating the private hospital's foreign-to-domestic capacity mix is more effective. The model helps decision makers tailor medical tourism policy to measurable local conditions.

title: Coherent Drawdown-Adjusted Performance: Replication and Extension Across International Equity Markets

detail.title: Coherent Drawdown-Adjusted Performance: Replication and Extension Across International Equity Markets
detail.abstract: Mechanical drawdown rules are among the most widely used risk management tools in institutional trading, yet their statistical properties remain poorly understood. This paper extends Varma (2025) by replicating and testing the Coherent Drawdown-Adjusted Performance (CDAP) metric out-of-sample across European equity ETFs and a range of drawdown thresholds motivated by pod shop practice. Using rolling 22-day windows over 1993–2024, we confirm that traditional Drawdown-Adjusted Performance (DAP) ranked the worst 22-day window across four major crises - the Dot-com crash, the GFC, COVID, and the 2022 rate shock - between the 8th and 25th percentile for SPY in every case, treating each event as unremarkable, while CDAP correctly ranked all four windows in the bottom 2% of the full sample. This pathology generalises: DAP ranked the same period at approximately the 32nd percentile for both EWU and EWG, while CDAP ranked it below the 0.1th percentile in both cases. Threshold sensitivity analysis shows that Millennium-style 5% drawdown rules applied to SPY since 1993 produce a terminal portfolio value of 5x versus 24x for buy-and-hold, with 280 individual transactions. These results suggest that mechanical drawdown rules substantially underperform buy-and-hold benchmarks across equity markets and that CDAP offers a more coherent basis for risk-adjusted evaluation.
