detail.abstract: Monetary policy transmission to equity markets in frontier economies remains incompletely understood, particularly regarding nonlinear dynamics, distributional heterogeneity, and structural instability. This study investigates how monetary policy shocks affect equity market performance in Ghana-a frontier economy characterised by persistent macroeconomic volatility, shallow financial markets, and recurrent structural breaks-over the period January 2007 to December 2024 (N = 216 monthly observations). We employ a multi-method framework integrating Bayesian Quantile Regression (BQR), Toda-Yamamoto augmented VAR causality testing, impulse response functions (IRF), forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD), and continuous Morlet wavelet coherence analysis. Zivot-Andrews structural break unit root tests account for endogenous breaks associated with the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis, the 2014-2015 exchange rate crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2022-2023 sovereign debt and inflation crisis. Monetary policy rate shocks are associated with statistically significant, asymmetric, and quantile-dependent negative effects on both the Ghana Stock Exchange Composite Index (GSE-CI) and the Financial Stock Index (GSE-FSI), with the largest contractionary effects concentrated at upper return quantiles. Toda-Yamamoto tests indicate unidirectional causality from monetary policy to equity returns. Wavelet coherence identifies medium-run co-movement (6-18 months) as the dominant transmission band, while FEVD estimates attribute approximately 21.4 percent of forecast error variance in GSE-CI returns to monetary policy innovations at a twelve-month horizon. These findings have practical relevance for investors managing interest rate risk, policymakers balancing disinflation against capital market development, and regulators designing macroprudential frameworks in frontier market contexts.

title: Media Over Intermediaries: Edutainment, Gender, and Social Change in Upper Egypt
affiliations: Yale University, Institute for Advanced Study in Toulouse (IAST), Toulouse School of Economics and Columbia University

detail.title: Media Over Intermediaries: Edutainment, Gender, and Social Change in Upper Egypt
detail.abstract: Can narrative entertainment dislodge harmful practices-and if so, how can such changes be measured unobtrusively? We report results from a randomized edutainment intervention in Egypt, in which participants were assigned to view a state-backed drama targeting female genital mutilation (FGM) and early marriage, family planning, or a placebo storyline. Outcomes were measured through surveys and interviewerblinded conversations six months later, analyzed at scale using large language models. The FGM drama increased opposition to the practice, driven by corrections to health and religious misperceptions-corrections the state cannot reliably engineer through local intermediaries, who undermine it. Effects for family planning, which does not face such opposition, were weak and inconsistent. Interview-based measures reveal the spontaneous salience of FGM without elevated signs of respondent re-traumatization. Edutainment works when the state lacks trusted messengers on the ground, and these boosts can be ethically captured by incorporating open-ended measurement into experimental evaluations.

title: The Semiconductors Race-Understanding the Challenges in India’s Technology and Industrial Ecosystem, and Learning From Global Strategies

detail.title: The Semiconductors Race-Understanding the Challenges in India’s Technology and Industrial Ecosystem, and Learning From Global Strategies
detail.abstract: Semiconductors have transitioned from a technological input to a strategic asset, underpinning economic competitiveness and national security. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerabilities of a geographically concentrated global semiconductor supply chain, accelerating the “semiconductors race” worldwide. India has also launched its own policy architecture through the India Semiconductor Mission. This study argues that the semiconductor industry is shaped by three mutually reinforcing forces – Technology, Industry, and Geopolitics – and that national semiconductor strategies succeed or fail depending on whether these three pillars are mutually interacting with each other. Drawing on the historical trajectories of countries that have fared strongly in the semiconductor industry, this study uses the three-pillar framework and applies it as a diagnostic tool to evaluate India's semiconductor ambitions. Applied to India, the diagnostic reveals structural weaknesses across all three pillars. India's R&D spending at 0.7% of GDP, less private sector participation in R&D, weak industry-academia linkages, and a projected shortfall of 2.5 to 3 lakh semiconductor professionals by 2027 point to a fragile technology pillar. India's electronics manufacturing base, despite its recent growth, remains in low-value assembly with domestic value addition as low as 15-20%, and infrastructure bottlenecks in power, water, and land constrain its industrial pillar. And while India has built a significant diplomatic architecture through the TRUST initiative, Quad, Pax Silica, and bilateral agreements with Taiwan, Japan, and Singapore, the technology being transferred is limited to mature nodes, and India's ties with Russia create a credibility gap that limits deeper integration into the US-led semiconductor alliance network. This study recommends a sequenced approach for India: Prioritizing ATMP and design in the short term, expanding the downstream industrial base and reforming the R&D ecosystem in the medium term, and aligning fabrication expansion with ecosystem maturity in the long term.

title: The Lived Experiences Of The Barangay Peacekeeping Action Team In Kibungan, Benguet
affiliations: King’s College of the Philippines, King’s College of the Philippines, King’s College of the Philippines, King’s College of the Philippines, King’s College of the Philippines, King’s College of the Philippines and King’s College of the Philippines

detail.title: The Lived Experiences Of The Barangay Peacekeeping Action Team In Kibungan, Benguet
detail.abstract: This study explored the lived experiences of Barangay Peacekeeping Action Team (BPAT) members in selected barangays of Kibungan, Benguet. It aimed to identify the challenges they encounter and the coping mechanisms they employ in carrying out their duties. The findings indicated that BPAT members face several challenges, including youth engagement in vices, limited road accessibility and transportation, curfew-related concerns, public disturbances, and instances of disrespect from community members. Among these, youth involvement in vices emerged as the most significant challenge. To address these difficulties, BPAT members rely on coping mechanisms, such as seeking support and guidance from law enforcement authorities, demonstrating resilience through patience and hard work, and fostering unity and a heart of service. Based on the findings, the study concludes that addressing youth engagement in vices remains a critical concern. Therefore, it is highly recommended that the Municipality of Kibungan enhance BPAT incentives through increased financial support. The Municipality is also encouraged to implement proactive community-oriented activities, such as clean-up drives, team-building, and sports programs. Furthermore, the Local Government Unit (LGU) is encouraged to conduct anti-vice seminars and campaigns and launch youth development programs. In addition, the municipality is encouraged to provide functional radios or communication devices, flashlights, reflective vests, and basic first aid kits to ensure safety and efficiency during patrols and emergency responses.

title: Learning via Routing: Regret-Estimation Trade-offs in Route-Constrained Combinatorial Bandits
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong (HKU), , Beijing Jiaotong University - School of Economics and Management  and The University of Hong Kong - University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Learning via Routing: Regret-Estimation Trade-offs in Route-Constrained Combinatorial Bandits
detail.abstract: We introduce and study the route-constrained combinatorial bandit problem, a new combinatorial multiarmed bandit model in which each super arm must be realized as a feasible route on a spatial network. In each period, a learner selects a budget-constrained route and observes semi-bandit rewards only at the visited locations. This route-induced action space captures mobile operational settings such as retailing on wheels and mobile healthcare outreach. Beyond the standard goal of regret minimization, we study a closely coupled objective: full-map estimation, which requires the learner to accurately recover the reward landscape over the entire network. We show that these two objectives exhibit an intrinsic trade-off. Specifically, we establish a worst-case lower bound eµ(T) Reg * µ (T) = Ω(1) via route-geometric hard instances. We then design a learning policy that combines route-based coverage with optimistic route selection. Under an (α, β)approximation routing oracle, the policy achieves eµ(T) Reg µ,α,β (T) = O(1); in the exact-oracle case, this matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. We further demonstrate the breadth of the framework through three operationally motivated and technically distinct variants: multi-objective reward-and-edge-cost routing, where the learner estimates both node rewards and edge costs under a Pareto criterion; switching environments, where unknown regime changes require detection and re-learning of the spatial reward map; and risk-aware route evaluation, where route utilities depend on both reward means and variability. For each variant, we design a tailored route-constrained learning policy and establish tight regret-estimation guarantees.

title: A Multidimensional National Defence and Strategic Resilience Framework for Saudi Arabia in the Aftermath of the 2026 Iran–GCC Conflict

detail.title: A Multidimensional National Defence and Strategic Resilience Framework for Saudi Arabia in the Aftermath of the 2026 Iran–GCC Conflict
detail.abstract: The 2026 Iran-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) conflict-initiated on 28 February 2026 by joint United States and Israeli military operations against Iran under the codenames Operation Epic Fury and Operation Roaring Lion respectively (Britannica 2026; The Soufan Center 2026)-has constituted the most consequential operational stress-test of Gulf Arab state defence architecture in modern history. For the first time since the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis, all six GCC member states were simultaneously targeted by Iranian ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones in a sustained multi-week campaign. United States and Gulf partner forces collectively expended in excess of 1,800 Patriot interceptors in the first sixteen days alone (Aerotime 2026), at a unit cost of approximately USD 4.2-5.3 million per PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement round (Norsk Luftvern 2026; TWZ 2026), creating an adverse cost-exchange ratio that is fiscally unsustainable at scale. This paper presents a comprehensive ground-executable multidimensional national defence and strategic resilience framework engineered specifically for Saudi Arabia. The framework is organised across eight mutually reinforcing strategic pillars-layered air and missile defence; critical infrastructure hardening; accelerated indigenous defence industrialisation; supply chain sovereignty; GCC integrated command; cybersecurity, electronic warfare and C5ISR; sovereign space-based situational awareness; and civil defence and societal resilience-over an indicative ten-year investment envelope of approximately USD 131 billion (2026-2035), of which an estimated USD 42-50 billion represents net additional sovereign investment beyond foreign procurement displacement. The principal analytical contribution is the integration of two distinct empirical streams: (i) the documented operational record of the first 96 hours of Operation Epic Fury and its aftermath, including the geographic distribution of Iranian strikes across the Eastern Province, Riyadh, and the Ras Tanura refining complex; and (ii) the demonstrated efficacy of Ukrainian counter-drone doctrine, in which interceptor drones such as the Wild Hornets Sting platform have achieved 80-90 percent kill rates against Shahed-type loitering munitions at unit costs of USD 1,400-2,500 (Defense Innovation Review 2026; Fox News 2026). The author argues that Saudi Arabia possesses the financial, institutional, and political prerequisites to translate the post-conflict urgency into durable strategic autonomy, contingent on the establishment of a National Defence Transformation Council within sixty days and the activation of a National Counter-Drone Emergency Programme through the newly-launched SAMI Autonomous Company (SAMI 2026a; Defensehere 2026). Each pillar is presented with named lead entities, quarterly milestone gates, measurable key performance indicators, and accountability triggers, with the intent that the framework can serve as an operational blueprint rather than a purely analytical contribution.

title: From Trade War to Green Transition: Optimal Electric Vehicle Tariffs with Revenue-Funded Subsidies
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, Yale University - Department of Economics, Stanford University and

detail.title: From Trade War to Green Transition: Optimal Electric Vehicle Tariffs with Revenue-Funded Subsidies
detail.abstract: We study the optimal design of trade and industrial policy when governments pursue environmental objectives alongside traditional welfare goals. Motivated by the global transition to electric vehicles (EVs) and growing concerns about competitiveness, energy security, and climate change, we develop a framework in which policymakers choose tariffs and domestic production subsidies to maximize welfare, defined as the sum of consumer surplus, domestic profits, environmental benefits, and tariff revenue. We combine a theoretical model of differentiated-product oligopoly with a structural demand model estimated using vehicle-level data from 13 countries that together account for the vast majority of global EV sales. Our central finding is that the optimal policy combines a moderate tariff on imported EVs with a subsidy to domestic EV production financed through tariff revenue. This policy substantially outperforms both outright protectionism and laissez-faire. Relative to current policies, it preserves consumer access to affordable EVs, accelerates fleet electrification, supports domestic producers, and remains budget-neutral. For the United States, the optimal policy more than doubles EV market share, generates over $45 billion in annual welfare gains, and avoids approximately 95 million tons of lifetime CO2 emissions. A key mechanism underlying these results is the pass-through of tariffs and subsidies to prices, which depends critically on demand curvature, product substitution, and market structure. More broadly, our results suggest that effective industrial policy requires careful attention to market structure and country-specific conditions, balancing consumer, producer, fiscal, and environmental objectives rather than adhering to ideological prescriptions.
